Therefore he assures him of the truth of what has been said, saying: [[5:27|Behold|Ecce]] (which is a sign of earnestness) [[5:27|this is even so, as we have searched out|hoc ut investigavimus, ita est]]. Then he exhorts him to a watchful remembrance of what he has heard and to showing it in deeds, adding: [[5:27|which thou having heard, consider it thoroughly in thy mind|Quod auditum mente pertracta]].

6.title: Explanatio litteralis capituli sexti: Respondens autem Job, dixit.
6.title_en: Literal explanation of the sixth chapter: Then Job answered, and said

paras.t: Veritatis zelo sanctus Job se falsitati opponit, veritatem defendit, ad singula sibi objecta respondet: non ad sui jactantiam, sed ad divinæ justitiæ ac modi providentiæ ejus declarationem, atque ne aliquis ex sua percussione scandalizaretur.
paras.en: With zeal for the truth holy Job sets himself against falsehood, defends the truth, and answers each of the things laid to his charge: not to boast of himself, but to make plain the justice of God and the manner of His providence, and so that no one should be scandalized at his being stricken.

paras.t: Respondens autem Job, dixit: Utinam appenderentur peccata mea quibus iram, id est plagam pœnamve, ut tu, Eliphaz, asseris, merui a Deo, et calamitas, id est miseria tribulationis, quam patior in anima et corpore, filiis quoque et rebus sublatis, in improperio conjugis, in convitiis amicorum, in statera: id est, in libratione justitiæ hæc ad invicem comparentur. Quasi arena maris, id est innumerabiliter, sicut arena maris innumerabilis est, hæc calamitas mea gravior appareret, id est major quam mea peccata requirant.
paras.en: [[6:1|But Job answered, and said|Respondens autem Job, dixit]]: [[6:2|O that my sins, whereby I have deserved wrath|Utinam appenderentur peccata mea quibus iram]], that is, the stroke or punishment which, as thou assertest, Eliphaz, I have deserved from God, [[6:2|and the calamity that I suffer|et calamitas quam patior]], that is, the misery of tribulation which I suffer in soul and body, with my children and my goods taken away, under the reproaches of my wife and the railing of my friends, [[6:2|were weighed in a balance|in statera]]: that is, that these were compared with one another in the scales of justice. [[6:3|As the sand of the sea|Quasi arena maris]], that is, beyond counting, as the sand of the sea cannot be counted, this calamity of mine [[6:3|would appear heavier|gravior appareret]], that is, greater than my sins require.

paras.t: Sed nonne verba hæc præsumptuosa et falsa videntur? Job namque quotidianis venialibusque peccatis non caruit, præsertim quum scriptum sit: Septies in die cadet justus et resurget. Et Jacobus contestatur: In multis offendimus omnes. Si autem gravitas peccati venialis pensetur per relationem ad infinitam majestatem divinam, quæ per ipsum aliquo modo inhonoratur, apparet quod secundum rigorem justitiæ, quæcumque temporalis afflictio vix aut non sufficiat pro satisfactione illius, et potissime, quod calamitas Job non suffecit pro universis venialibus, quæ per tot vitæ suæ incurrerat annos: mirumque omnino videtur, quod ait pœnam sibi inflictam, incomparabiliter esse graviorem universis peccatis suis.
paras.en: But do not these words seem presumptuous and false? For Job was not without daily and venial sins, especially since it is written: [[Prov 24:16|a just man shall fall seven times, and shall rise again|Septies in die cadet justus et resurget]] [Denis reads "seven times in a day"; the margin gives Prov. xxi, 16, a misreading of xxiv, 16]. And James bears witness: [[Jas 3:2|in many things we all offend|In multis offendimus omnes]]. Now if the gravity of venial sin is weighed by its relation to the infinite majesty of God, which is in some way dishonoured by it, it appears that by the rigour of justice any temporal affliction whatever would scarcely, or not at all, suffice to make satisfaction for it; and above all, that Job's calamity did not suffice for all the venial sins he had incurred through so many years of his life. And it seems altogether astonishing that he says the punishment laid on him is beyond comparison heavier than all his sins.

paras.t: Et respondendum, quod sanctus Job loquitur contra errorem Eliphaz, affirmantis non infligi pœnam a Deo, nisi pro propria prævia culpa afflictis, ita quod pro culpa majori major infligeretur punitio. Contra hoc loquens Job adstruit multo majorem sibi calamitatem inflictam, quam peccata sua exegerint: quia de gravibus sibi excessibus non exstitit conscius, sed de minutis dumtaxat. Quum ergo fuerit sibi inflicta gravissima pœna, patet quod pœna vehementer excesserit culpam. Rursus, Deus gravitatem peccati venialis non solum attendit ut est suæ majestatis inhonoratio aliqua, sed etiam secundum quod procedit ex fragilitate humana, quæ tanta est, quod licet homo possit singula, non tamen omnia venialia vitare peccata. Ideo Deus levissima inter venialia, quæ ex mera et maxime excusante fragilitate et subreptione humana proveniunt, qualia fuerunt venialia beati Job ac ceterorum Sanctorum, facillime donat, nec solet ea in vita hac graviter vindicare. Sicque loquitur Job de venialibus suis peccatis, videlicet non solum ut gravitatem aliquam habuerunt per comparationem ad Deum, sed etiam ut excusationem habuerunt ex parte ipsius. Imo quoniam viri perfecti pro suis venialibus quotidie satisfacere solent per multa remedia contra illa, præsertim per frequentem atque ferventem affectionem suæ mentis ad Deum, peccata ipsius Job per ejus sanctissimam conversationem, quoad pœnam et culpam, deleta vel omnino, vel pro maxima parte fuerunt. Idcirco pro eis tanta adversa non meruit, sed ista sua calamitas peccatis suis sic consideratis, quasi incomparabiliter gravior fuit. Quod tamen per hyperbolen dictum intelligi potest, secundum quod homines ex magna affectione loquentes, hyperbolicis uti solent sermonibus.
paras.en: The answer is that holy Job is speaking against the error of Eliphaz, who affirmed that punishment is not inflicted by God on the afflicted except for their own previous fault, so that for a greater fault a greater punishment would be inflicted. Speaking against this, Job maintains that a far greater calamity has been laid on him than his sins demanded: for he was not conscious of any grave excesses in himself, but only of small ones. Since, then, a most grievous punishment was laid on him, it is plain that the punishment far exceeded the fault. Again, God regards the gravity of venial sin not only as it is some dishonour to His majesty, but also as it proceeds from human frailty, which is so great that, though a man can avoid each venial sin singly, he cannot avoid them all. Therefore the lightest among venial sins, those that come from mere frailty, which greatly excuses them, and from human surprise [*subreptio*: the first stirrings that steal upon a man before reason can deliberate], such as were the venial sins of blessed Job and of the other Saints, God forgives most readily, and is not wont to punish them heavily in this life. And so Job speaks of his venial sins, namely not only as they had some gravity by comparison with God, but also as they had an excuse on the part of man himself. Indeed, since perfect men are wont to make satisfaction daily for their venial sins by many remedies against them, above all by the frequent and fervent affection of their mind toward God, the sins of Job himself, through his most holy manner of life, were blotted out as to punishment and guilt, either altogether or for the greater part. Hence he did not deserve such great adversities for them; but this calamity of his, his sins being so considered, was as it were beyond comparison heavier. This, however, may be understood as said by hyperbole, in the way that men speaking from great feeling are wont to use hyperbolical speech.

paras.t: Unde et verba mea, quibus dixi, Pereat dies in qua natus sum, et quæ nunc profero, dolore sunt plena, id est, ex vehementi dolore proveniunt, et eumdem significant. Ideo non impatientiæ, sed dolori sunt adscribenda, prout in expositione secundi capituli plenius dictum est. Quia sagittæ Domini, id est improvisæ atque acutissimæ afflictiones mihi, Deo permittente, inflictæ, in me sunt, id est, usque ad intima viscera mea pervenerunt; quarum indignatio, id est pressura, ebibit spiritum meum, id est, animam seu vitam animalem quasi consumit et de corpore extrahit, anhelitum impedit, me respirare non sinens; spiritum quoque corporalem, qui est vector virtutis et vitæ, quasi deglutit.
paras.en: [[6:3|therefore, my words|Unde et verba mea]], in which I said, [[Job 3:3|Let the day perish wherein I was born|Pereat dies in qua natus sum]], and those I utter now, [[6:3|are full of sorrow|dolore sunt plena]], that is, they come from vehement sorrow and betoken it. They are therefore to be put down not to impatience but to sorrow, as was said more fully in the exposition of the second chapter. [[6:4|For the arrows of the Lord|quia sagittæ Domini]], that is, the sudden and most piercing afflictions laid on me by God's permission, [[6:4|are in me|in me sunt]], that is, they have reached to my inmost bowels; [[6:4|the rage whereof|quarum indignatio]], that is, their pressure, [[6:4|drinketh up my spirit|ebibit spiritum meum]], that is, as it were consumes my soul or animal life and draws it out of the body, hinders my breath, not letting me breathe; and as it were swallows up the bodily spirit too, which is the carrier of strength and life.

paras.t: Sed quum percussio sancti Job non venerit ex ira indignationeve Dei contra eum, cur pœnam suam appellat indignationem Dei, videlicet in quantum fuit signum indignationis? Et respondendum, quod loquitur ita propter apparentiam exteriorem et similitudinem cum flagellis, quæ ex indignatione Dei contra peccata peccatoribus infliguntur, et propter acerbitatem pœnarum suarum in se. Sic enim et Christus ait ad Patrem: Super me confirmatus est furor tuus. Vel etiam ideo ait, Indignatio, etc., quia forte pro aliquibus suis venialibus partim percussus est: non quod illa fuerunt percussionis suæ causa totalis aut principalis, sed concausa forsitan aliqualis.
paras.en: But since holy Job's being stricken did not come from God's wrath or indignation against him, why does he call his punishment the indignation [Douay-Rheims "rage"] of God, that is, in so far as it was a sign of indignation? The answer is that he speaks so because of the outward appearance and the likeness to the scourges which are laid on sinners from God's indignation against sins, and because of the bitterness of his punishments in themselves. For so Christ too says to the Father: [[Ps 87:8|Thy wrath is strong over me|Super me confirmatus est furor tuus]]. Or else he says [[6:4|the rage|Indignatio]], etc., because perhaps he was stricken in part for some venial sins of his: not that they were the whole or chief cause of his being stricken, but perhaps in some way a contributing cause.

paras.t: Et terrores Domini, id est horribiles adversitates ab ipso mihi inflictæ. Vel, Terrores Domini, id est formidines, quibus vereor mihi a Deo graviora infligi, vel ista diu continuari. Sapiens enim in omnibus metuit. Et quoniam sanctus Job sibi de culpa, ob quam hæc pateretur, non fuerat conscius, metuebat ne rursus ex causa secreta occulto Dei judicio plagaretur. Ideo subditur, Militant contra me, impugnando me et opprimendo. His verbis Job consonat quod in Psalmo loquitur Christus ad Patrem: In me transierunt iræ tuæ, et terrores tui conturbaverunt me. Nam et Christus naturali timore expavit pœnas instantes: quem timorem sponte assumpsit, et potestative deposuit.
paras.en: [[6:4|and the terrors of the Lord|Et terrores Domini]], that is, the dreadful adversities He has laid on me. Or, [[6:4|the terrors of the Lord|Terrores Domini]], that is, the fears with which I dread that heavier things will be laid on me by God, or that these will long continue. For [[Ecclus 18:27|A wise man will fear in every thing|Sapiens enim in omnibus metuit]] [the margin's numeral is misread; the verse is Ecclus. xviii, 27]. And since holy Job had not been conscious in himself of a fault for which he should suffer these things, he feared lest he should again be stricken for some secret cause by the hidden judgement of God. Therefore it is added: [[6:4|war against me|Militant contra me]], assailing and oppressing me. With these words of Job agrees what Christ says to the Father in the Psalm: [[Ps 87:17|Thy wrath hath come upon me: and thy terrors have troubled me|In me transierunt iræ tuæ, et terrores tui conturbaverunt me]]. For Christ too, with natural fear, shrank in dread from the pains that were at hand: a fear which He took upon Himself of His own will, and laid aside by His own power.

paras.t: Deinde probat ista a simili, ostendens propositum in opposito. Numquid rugiet onager quum habuerit herbam? id est, asinus silvestris vocem doloris non profert, dum victui necessaria habet, sed dum talibus caret ex terræ sterilitate, juxta id Jeremiæ: Onagri steterunt, traxerunt ventum quasi dracones, defecerunt oculi eorum, quia non erat herba. Aut mugiet bos quum ante præsepe plenum steterit? Non utique tunc vocem mœroris emittet, nisi forte aliunde sit causa mugitus, ut languor aut aliquid tale. Itaque, sicut bruta non in præsentia, sed in absentia delectabilis et in præsentia contristabilis dolent, doloremque exprimunt; sic naturale est homini, quantum ad partem sensitivam, tempore magnæ adversitatis et pœnæ dolere, dolorosaque verba proferre: præsertim quum homo calamitatem suam penset et ponderet, quod bruta facere nequeunt. Bos itaque mugit necessariis carens, juxta illud Joelis: Mugierunt greges armenti, quia non est pascua eis.
paras.en: Next he proves this by a likeness, showing what he means from its opposite. [[6:5|Will the wild ass bray when he hath grass?|Numquid rugiet onager quum habuerit herbam?]] that is, the wild ass gives no cry of pain while it has what it needs to live, but only when it lacks such things through the barrenness of the land; according to that of Jeremias: [[Jer 14:6|And the wild asses stood|Onagri steterunt]], [[Jer 14:6|they snuffed up the wind like dragons, their eyes failed, because there was no grass|traxerunt ventum quasi dracones, defecerunt oculi eorum, quia non erat herba]]. [[6:5|or will the ox low when he standeth before a full manger?|Aut mugiet bos quum ante præsepe plenum steterit?]] Certainly it will not then give out a cry of grief, unless perhaps the cause of its lowing comes from elsewhere, as sickness or some such thing. So, as the beasts feel pain and express it not when what delights them is present, but when it is absent, and when what grieves them is present, so it is natural to man, as regards his sensitive part, to grieve in time of great adversity and punishment and to utter words of sorrow: above all since man weighs and ponders his calamity, which the beasts cannot do. The ox, then, lows when it lacks what it needs; according to that of Joel: [[Joel 1:18|why did the herds of cattle low? because there is no pasture for them|Mugierunt greges armenti, quia non est pascua eis]].

paras.t: Deinde idem in rationali natura declarat. Aut poterit comedi insulsum quod non est sale conditum? id est, nullus libenter manducat escam insipidam, nec sale temperate permixtam, nisi forte necessitate cogatur, aut corruptum habeat gustum. Job autem loquitur secundum communem cursum ac naturalem processum. Nam et subjungit, aut gustare aliquis potest, quod gustatum affert mortem? id est, nullus secundum naturalem sensitivumque appetitum edere vult cibum mortiferum. Unde probatur, quod naturalis appetitus hominis adversa atque pœnalia detestatur; sed detestatio hæc per rationem virtuose moderatur.
paras.en: Then he shows the same in rational nature. [[6:6|Or can an unsavoury thing be eaten, that is not seasoned with salt?|Aut poterit comedi insulsum quod non est sale conditum?]] that is, no one willingly eats tasteless food, not mixed with salt in due measure, unless perhaps necessity forces him, or his taste is spoiled. But Job is speaking of the common course and natural way of things. For he adds: [[6:6|or can a man taste that which, when tasted, bringeth death?|aut gustare aliquis potest, quod gustatum affert mortem?]] that is, no one, by natural and sensitive appetite, wishes to eat deadly food. Whence it is proved that man's natural appetite abhors adversities and pains; but this abhorrence is moderated virtuously by reason.

paras.t: Animæ enim esurienti, id est homini magnam famem patienti: ponit namque partem pro toto; etiam amara dulcia videntur, præ aviditate et indigentia alimenti, et quoniam talia pœnam famis aliqualiter minuunt. Ex quo etiam innotescit, quantum appetitus naturalis ex absentia objecti delectabilis doleat. Hinc in Proverbiis scribitur: Anima saturata calcabit favum; anima esuriens etiam amarum pro dulce sumet. Quod autem tam ingens fuerit sua afflictio, subditur: Quæ prius tangere nolebat anima mea, id est per gustum contingere, sed quasi insulsa abhorruit, nunc præ angustia, id est pressura tribulationis atque inopiæ meæ, cibi mei sunt, mihi accepti, quemadmodum divites depauperati edunt, quæ tempore opulentiæ abhorrebant.
paras.en: For to a hungry soul, that is, to a man suffering great hunger (for he puts the part for the whole), even bitter things seem sweet, through eagerness and want of food, and because such things somewhat lessen the pain of hunger. From this it is also known how much natural appetite grieves at the absence of what delights it. Hence it is written in Proverbs: [[Prov 27:7|A soul that is full shall tread upon the honeycomb: and a soul that is hungry shall take even bitter for sweet|Anima saturata calcabit favum; anima esuriens etiam amarum pro dulce sumet]]. And that his affliction was so very great is added: [[6:7|The things which before my soul would not touch|Quæ prius tangere nolebat anima mea]], that is, touch by taste, but loathed as tasteless, [[6:7|now, through anguish|nunc præ angustia]], that is, through the pressure of my tribulation and want, [[6:7|are my meats|cibi mei sunt]], welcome to me; as rich men who have become poor eat what they loathed in the time of their wealth.

paras.t: Deinceps ostendit se mortem appetere propter rationabilem causam, videlicet ne adversitatis magnitudine perdurante, ad impatientiam ruat, et ut ad vitam quietiorem perducatur in limbo patrum. Quomodo autem quis mortem propter præsentis vitæ miserias rationabiliter queat appetere, dictum est in elucidatione tertii capituli. Quis mihi det, id est, utinam mihi detur, ut veniat petitio mea, id est, opere compleatur, et quod exspecto, tribuat mihi Deus?
paras.en: Next he shows that he desires death for a reasonable cause, namely lest, while the greatness of his adversity lasts, he fall into impatience, and that he may be brought to a quieter life in the limbo of the fathers. How a man may reasonably desire death because of the miseries of the present life was said in the explanation of the third chapter [the margin refers to Art. XI, towards the end]. [[6:8|Who will grant|Quis mihi det]], that is, O that it may be granted me, [[6:8|that my request may come|ut veniat petitio mea]], that is, be fulfilled in deed, [[6:8|and that God may give me what I look for?|et quod exspecto, tribuat mihi Deus?]]

paras.t: Et, pro id est, qui cœpit me conterere, scilicet Deus per Satan, ipse Deus me conterat per mortem, solvat manum suam, id est, potestatem suam magis in opus extendat: quæ manus quasi ligata videtur, dum operari aliquid cessat. Tunc enim quantum ad aliquem, fertur ligata, quamvis incessabiliter operetur. Et succidat me, id est, de vita hac tollat. Et hæc mihi sit consolatio, ut affligens me dolore, non parcat, id est, affligere non desistat donec inteream, sicque de invalescentia pœnæ consoler, in quantum est acceleratio mortis et abbreviatio vitæ odibilis.
paras.en: [[6:9|And that he that hath begun|qui cœpit]] (*and* stands for "that is"), he who has begun to crush me, namely God through Satan, that God Himself [[6:9|may destroy me|me conterat]] by death, [[6:9|that he may let loose his hand|solvat manum suam]], that is, stretch out His power further into act: for the hand seems as it were bound while it ceases to work at anything; at such a time it is said to be bound as regards some person, though it works unceasingly. [[6:9|and cut me off|Et succidat me]], that is, take me from this life. [[6:10|And that this may be my comfort, that afflicting me with sorrow, he spare not|Et hæc mihi sit consolatio, ut affligens me dolore, non parcat]], that is, may not cease to afflict me until I perish, and so I may be comforted by the growing strength of the pain, in so far as it is a hastening of death and a shortening of a hateful life.

paras.t: Porro, quod ista non ex impatientia oret, pandit subjungens, nec contradicam sermonibus Sancti, id est verbis Dei per essentiam sancti, quibus licentiavit me taliter flagellari, contra eum murmurando, aut per impatientiam corruendo: hoc est, oro ut detur mihi gratia non contradicendi Deo in universis quæ patior; atque idcirco mortem efflagito, ne forte in doloribus diu vivens, tandem per impatientiam vincar.
paras.en: Further, that he does not pray for these things out of impatience he makes plain by adding: [[6:10|nor I contradict the words of the Holy one|nec contradicam sermonibus Sancti]], that is, the words of God, who is holy by His essence, by which He gave leave for me to be scourged in this way: by murmuring against Him, or falling through impatience. That is: I pray that the grace may be given me not to contradict God in all that I suffer; and it is for this that I beg for death, lest perhaps, living long in pains, I be at last overcome by impatience.

paras.t: Quæ est enim fortitudo mea, ut sustineam? id est, per naturalem et propriam animi fortitudinem ista diu ferre non potero, scilicet prout fortitudo est virtus naturalis et acquisita, per gratiam non adjuta. Vel dicit hoc de fortitudine, ut est virtus infusa seu donum, quæ tanta non fuit in eo, quin poterat superari, quoniam ipse nondum confirmatus fuit in bono: ideo caute expavit periculum, non pusillanimiter desperavit Dei subsidium. Aut quis finis meus, id est terminus tribulationum istarum, ut patienter agam? id est, quia tempus mortis meæ ignoro, eam cito venire desidero. Qui enim in tribulationibus sunt, ex hoc potissime consolantur, quod norunt determinate quando sint liberandi, et tunc intuitu finis illius patienter se habent. Job vero finem istum determinate non prænoscebat. Ideo ne tædio obrueretur patientia ejus, mortem expetiit.
paras.en: [[6:11|For what is my strength, that I can hold out?|Quæ est enim fortitudo mea, ut sustineam?]] that is, by the natural strength of mind that is my own I shall not be able to bear these things long: taking fortitude, that is, as it is a natural and acquired virtue, not helped by grace. Or he says this of fortitude as it is an infused virtue or gift, which was not so great in him that he could not be overcome, since he was not yet confirmed in good [that is, made secure against falling, as the blessed are]: and so he prudently dreaded the danger, but did not faint-heartedly despair of God's help. [[6:11|or what is my end|Aut quis finis meus]], that is, the end of these tribulations, [[6:11|that I should keep patience?|ut patienter agam?]] that is, because I do not know the time of my death, I desire it to come quickly. For those in tribulations are chiefly consoled by knowing definitely when they are to be set free, and then, looking to that end, they bear themselves patiently. But Job did not know that end beforehand definitely. So, lest his patience should be overwhelmed by weariness, he longed for death.

paras.t: Hinc etiam patet, firmiter dictum non esse quod quidam hic scribit, dicendo quod verbum istud, scilicet, Aut quis finis meus, Job expresse dicat contra errorem Eliphaz, negantis adversa vitæ præsentis ordinari ad finem vitæ beatæ in futuro, quasi Job verbum hoc dixerit non secundum propriam mentem, sed secundum Eliphaz erroneam positionem: quasi dicat, Quum juxta tuam opinionem, o Eliphaz, non sit mihi finis beatificus in futuro exspectandus, non est ratio cur debeam patienter hæc ferre. Imo verba ista, ut jam patuit, aliter rationabiliter exponuntur. Neque ex hoc verbo potest probari, quod Eliphaz negavit beatitudinem vitæ futuræ.
paras.en: Hence it is also plain that what someone writes here is not soundly said: namely that this saying, [[6:11|or what is my end|Aut quis finis meus]], Job says expressly against the error of Eliphaz, who denied that the adversities of the present life are ordered to the end of the blessed life to come; as though Job said this not according to his own mind but according to Eliphaz's erroneous position, as if to say: Since by thy opinion, O Eliphaz, no beatifying end is to be looked for by me in the future, there is no reason why I should bear these things patiently. Rather, as has now appeared, these words are reasonably expounded otherwise. Nor can it be proved from this saying that Eliphaz denied the beatitude of the life to come.

paras.t: Nec fortitudo lapidum fortitudo mea, id est, non est tam insuperabilis et sine sensu, ut lapidum fortitudo: quod de corporali fortitudine clarius verificatur, et de spirituali fortitudine accipi potest propter fragilitatem subjecti fortitudinis talis. Anima namque fragilis est atque instabilis. Nec caro mea ænea est, sed mollis, tenera ac multum passibilis. Ideo gravissimam sentit pœnam, ob cujus vehementiam timeo de periculo patientiæ meæ.
paras.en: [[6:12|My strength is not the strength of stones|Nec fortitudo lapidum fortitudo mea]], that is, it is not so unconquerable and without feeling as the strength of stones: which is more clearly true of bodily strength, and may be taken of spiritual strength too, because of the frailty of the subject in which such strength is; for the soul is frail and unstable. [[6:12|nor is my flesh of brass|Nec caro mea ænea est]], but soft, tender and very open to suffering. Therefore it feels a most grievous pain, for the violence of which I fear for the danger to my patience.

paras.t: Insuper gravitatem tribulationis suæ demonstrat ex carentia auxilii atque solatii contra adversa sibi inflicta. Ecce non est auxilium mihi in me, id est, me ipsum juvare non valeo, nec damna mihi illata recuperare, quum tam graviter læsus sim corpore, cunctisque facultatibus ac filiis spoliatus; et necessarii quoque mei, id est familiares atque domestici et amici, recesserunt a me, tempore necessitatis afflictionisque meæ, dum eis magis indigeo. Et forte aliqui eorum corporaliter obierunt, alii spiritualiter, non impendendo opera caritatis, imo caritati contraria irrogantes, sicut hi tres qui ad consolandum venerunt, ad contumelias proruperunt.
paras.en: Moreover he shows the weight of his tribulation from his want of help and comfort against the adversities laid on him. [[6:13|Behold there is no help for me in myself|Ecce non est auxilium mihi in me]], that is, I cannot help myself, nor recover the losses brought on me, since I am so grievously hurt in body and stripped of all my goods and my children; [[6:13|and my familiar friends also|et necessarii quoque mei]] [*necessarii*: those bound to one by close ties], that is, those of my household and family, and my friends, [[6:13|are departed from me|recesserunt a me]] in the time of my need and affliction, when I need them most. And perhaps some of them died bodily, others spiritually, by not doing the works of charity, nay, by doing things contrary to charity: as these three who came to comfort him broke out into insults.

paras.t: Qui tollit ab amico suo, id est eo quem se diligere dilexisseve asserit, seu dilexit tempore prosperitatis, misericordiam, id est compassionem et pietatis affectum seu subventionem tempore necessitatis et afflictionis, timorem Domini derelinquit, id est contra filialem Dei timorem agit: quoniam contra caritatem, et contra divinum agit præceptum; sicque peccando mortaliter, caritatem et timorem castum ex ea prodeuntem amittit. In quo verbo beatus Job notat Eliphaz, quod ipsemet inciderit culpam, quam superius dixerat incidisse Job, loquens ad eum: Ubi est timor tuus? Itaque tempore adversitatis comprobatur amicus. Propter quod scriptum est in Ecclesiastico: Si possides amicum, in tentatione posside eum. Est enim amicus secundum tempus suum, et non permanet in die tribulationis. Hinc quoque Joannes ait in prima sua Canonica: Non diligamus verbo neque lingua, sed opere et veritate.
paras.en: [[6:14|He that taketh away|Qui tollit]] [[6:14|from his friend|ab amico suo]], that is, from him whom he says he loves or has loved, or whom he loved in the time of prosperity, [[6:14|mercy|misericordiam]], that is, compassion and loving feeling, or help, in the time of need and affliction, [[6:14|forsaketh the fear of the Lord|timorem Domini derelinquit]], that is, acts against the filial fear of God: since he acts against charity and against the divine commandment; and so, sinning mortally, he loses charity and the chaste fear that springs from it. In this saying blessed Job taxes Eliphaz with having himself fallen into the fault into which he had said above that Job had fallen, when he said to him: [[Job 4:6|Where is thy fear|Ubi est timor tuus]]? So a friend is proved in the time of adversity. For this reason it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 6:7|If thou wouldst get a friend, try him before thou takest him|Si possides amicum, in tentatione posside eum]] [Denis's Latin: "if thou possessest a friend, possess him in trial"]. [[Ecclus 6:8|For there is a friend for his own occasion, and he will not abide in the day of thy trouble|Est enim amicus secundum tempus suum, et non permanet in die tribulationis]]. Hence also John says in his first Canonical Epistle: [[1 John 3:18|let us not love in word nor in tongue, but in deed and in truth|Non diligamus verbo neque lingua, sed opere et veritate]].

paras.t: Fratres mei, id est non amici dumtaxat, sed et cognati ac proximi, præterierunt me, id est, in afflictionibus positum reliquerunt, ad sua commoda festinantes. Est autem consuetudo Scripturæ, ut omnes consanguinei alicujus, fratres ejus vocentur, sicut in Genesi Abraham ait ad Lot: Fratres sumus. Et secundo Regum Joab ait ad Amasam suum nepotem: Salve, mi frater. Joannes quoque evangelista in Evangelio suo testatur, quod fratres Christi quem peperit Virgo, non crediderunt in eum. Utrum vero Job fratres carnales proprie dictos habuerit, et an illi in tribulatione sua præterierunt eum, quis novit? Sicut torrens qui raptim transit in convallibus, id est, improvise, impetuose, ac subito me reliquerunt, quemadmodum torrens fluit in imis cum impetu. Torrens autem, secundum Albertum, dicitur aqua liquefacta torrore solis in montibus, ex nubibus et glacie dissoluta, præcipitanter decurrens in ima.
paras.en: [[6:15|My brethren|Fratres mei]], that is, not only my friends but my kinsmen and neighbours also, [[6:15|have passed by me|præterierunt me]], that is, have left me when I was set in afflictions, hurrying after their own advantage. Now it is the custom of Scripture that all of a man's blood relations are called his brethren, as in Genesis Abraham says to Lot: [[Gen 13:8|we are brethren|Fratres sumus]]. And in the second book of Kings Joab says to Amasa his nephew: [[2 Kings 20:9|God save thee, my brother|Salve, mi frater]]. John the evangelist also testifies in his Gospel that the brethren of Christ, whom the Virgin bore, did not believe in Him[[John 7:5||]] [the margin gives John vi, 3; the passage is John vii, 5]. But whether Job had brothers in the flesh properly so called, and whether they passed him by in his tribulation, who knows? [[6:15|as the torrent that passeth swiftly in the valleys|Sicut torrens qui raptim transit in convallibus]], that is, they left me unforeseen, violently and suddenly, as a torrent flows down into the depths with violence. Now a torrent, according to Albert, is the name for water melted by the scorching [*torror*: the word *torrens* is taken from *torrere*, "to scorch"] of the sun on the mountains, loosed from the clouds and the ice, rushing headlong down into the depths.

paras.t: Qui timent pruinam, irruet super eos nix, id est, qui ita ab amico discedunt, atque a me taliter discesserunt, impuniti non erunt, nisi pœniteant: quia dum amico subvenire omittunt, timore damni minoris, quod exprimitur per pruinam, majus incommodum patientur, quod per nivem notatur. Dicit enim Philosophus in libro Meteororum, quod pruina est nix parva, et nix, pruina magna seu multa.
paras.en: [[6:16|They that fear the hoary frost, the snow shall fall upon them|Qui timent pruinam, irruet super eos nix]], that is, those who so depart from a friend, and who have so departed from me, shall not go unpunished unless they repent: for while they fail to help a friend for fear of a lesser loss, which is expressed by the hoary frost, they shall suffer a greater harm, which is signified by the snow. For the Philosopher says in the book of the Meteorologica that hoar frost is a little snow, and snow is a great or abundant hoar frost.

paras.t: Tempore quo fuerint dissipati, id est per magna adversa destructi, divisi, depauperati, peribunt, id est, spiritualiter morientur per impatientiæ culpam; vel, quum fuerint dissipati per mortem, peribunt damnatione æterna. Et ut incaluerint, id est, igne tribulationis, seu ira divinæ punitionis fuerint tacti, solventur de loco suo, id est, de terra tollentur, atque in tartarum projicientur, quemadmodum pruina seu nix solis calore attacta, dissolvitur statim ac defluit.
paras.en: [[6:17|At the time when they shall be scattered|Tempore quo fuerint dissipati]], that is, destroyed, divided and made poor by great adversities, [[6:17|they shall perish|peribunt]], that is, they shall die spiritually through the fault of impatience; or, when they are scattered by death, they shall perish by eternal damnation. [[6:17|and after it groweth hot|Et ut incaluerint]] [Denis reads "after they have grown hot"], that is, when they have been touched by the fire of tribulation or by the wrath of divine punishment, [[6:17|they shall be melted out of their place|solventur de loco suo]], that is, they shall be taken from the earth and cast into hell; as hoar frost or snow, touched by the heat of the sun, melts at once and runs away.

paras.t: Involutæ sunt semitæ gressuum eorum. Quod involvitur, in se ipso replicatur, et quadam tortuositate in se ipsum revertitur. Hinc involutum vocamus, cujus fines occulti sunt. Itaque, Semitæ gressuum eorum, id est media quibus falsi amici accedunt, et juvare se monstrant amicum afflictum seu alium, involutæ sunt fraudulentiis atque astutiis, et ad proprium commodum reflectuntur, dum amicitiam ante ostendunt, finem amicitiæ sub velamine hypocrisis clam involvunt, juxta illud Ecclesiastici: Est amicus qui convertitur ad inimicitiam, et est amicus qui rixam ac odium denudabit. Itemque: Est amicus socius mensæ, et non permanet in tempore necessitatis. Ambulabunt in vacuum, id est, infructuose vivent, nec finem sortientur beatum; et peribunt, quia non solum beatitudine privabuntur, sed et pœnam incurrent æternam, juxta illud Jacobi: Judicium sine misericordia fiet ei, qui non fecerit misericordiam. Isaias quoque: Væ impio in malum; retributio enim manuum ejus fiet ei. Salomon quoque fatetur: Vir versutus odiosus est.
paras.en: [[6:18|The paths of their steps are entangled|Involutæ sunt semitæ gressuum eorum]]. What is entangled [*involutum*: rolled up, wrapped in on itself] is folded back on itself and turns back into itself with a certain twisting; hence we call that involved whose ends are hidden. So, [[6:18|The paths of their steps|Semitæ gressuum eorum]], that is, the means by which false friends approach, and make a show of helping a friend in affliction or anyone else, are entangled with frauds and cunning, and are bent back to their own advantage: while they first show friendship, they secretly wrap up the end of friendship under the veil of hypocrisy; according to that of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 6:9|there is a friend that turneth to enmity; and there is a friend that will disclose hatred and strife|Est amicus qui convertitur ad inimicitiam, et est amicus qui rixam ac odium denudabit]]. And again: [[Ecclus 6:10|there is a friend a companion at the table, and he will not abide in the day of distress|Est amicus socius mensæ, et non permanet in tempore necessitatis]]. [[6:18|they shall walk in vain|Ambulabunt in vacuum]], that is, they shall live fruitlessly and shall not obtain a blessed end; [[6:18|and shall perish|et peribunt]], for they shall not only be deprived of beatitude, but shall also incur eternal punishment; according to that of James: [[Jas 2:13|judgment without mercy to him that hath not done mercy|Judicium sine misericordia fiet ei, qui non fecerit misericordiam]]. And Isaias: [[Is 3:11|Woe to the wicked unto evil: for the reward of his hands shall be given him|Væ impio in malum; retributio enim manuum ejus fiet ei]]. And Solomon declares: [[Prov 14:17|the crafty man is hateful|Vir versutus odiosus est]].

paras.t: Considerate semitas Theman, id est processum, verba et gesta Eliphaz venientis de terra Theman, itinera Saba, id est aliorum qui de illa terra venerunt. Aliqui tamen per Saba intelligunt apertos adversarios sancti Job, puta Sabæos, de quibus supra dictum est, quod bona ejus diripuerunt. Sicque intendit, quod Eliphaz conformatus est illis, quia ad improperia Job prorupit; ita quod sicut illi persecuti sunt ipsum Job factis, sic Eliphaz verbis: quod de aliis duobus amicis quando dixit Job hæc, nondum innotuit. Et exspectate paulisper, præstolando finem disputationis atque negotii hujus.
paras.en: [[6:19|Consider the paths of Thema|Considerate semitas Theman]], that is, the proceeding, the words and deeds of Eliphaz, who came from the land of Theman, [[6:19|the ways of Saba|itinera Saba]], that is, of the others who came from that land. Some, however, understand by Saba the open adversaries of holy Job, namely the Sabeans, of whom it was said above that they plundered his goods[[Job 1:15||]]. And so he means that Eliphaz has made himself like them, since he broke out into reproaches against Job; so that as they persecuted Job himself by deeds, so Eliphaz did by words: which, when Job said this, had not yet been shown of the other two friends. [[6:19|and wait a little while|Et exspectate paulisper]], awaiting the end of this disputation and business.

paras.t: Confusi sunt, id est, nunc ex verbis meis confusionem incurrerunt, erubescentes, vel ex hoc, quod maledixi tempori nativitatis meæ: amicus quippe erubescit, dum audit amicum suum coram aliis multum irrationabiliter loqui; hi autem tres amici Job, putaverunt eum irrationabilissime esse locutum: vel ex responsione ipsius Job, qua eos reprobavit atque concludit. Quia speravi, id est, fiducialiter et audenter locutus sum ex testimonio bono conscientiæ meæ, qua asserui et assero me absque culpa mea percussum, et esse me justum.
paras.en: [[6:20|They are confounded|Confusi sunt]], that is, they have now incurred confusion from my words, blushing: either at this, that I cursed the time of my birth (for a friend blushes when he hears his friend speak very unreasonably before others, and these three friends of Job thought he had spoken most unreasonably); or at the answer of Job himself, by which he rebuked and refuted them. [[6:20|because I have hoped|Quia speravi]], that is, I have spoken confidently and boldly from the good witness of my conscience, by which I have asserted and assert that I was stricken without fault of mine and that I am just.

paras.t: Porro Thomas exponit sic: Confusi sunt venire ad me, quia speravi, id est, quoniam tempus erat in quo auxilium ab eis sperare debebam. Homines enim qui auxiliari nolunt, confunduntur visitare illos, quos putant a se auxilium petituros. Ista expositio incerta videtur. Dictum est enim secundo capitulo, quod amici Job venerunt ut consolarentur eum. Ideo non apparet, quod non voluerint ei ferre auxilium, vel quod ideo venire confusi sunt, quia noluerunt succurrere. Imo, ut in expositione secundi capituli ostensum est, bona intentione et ex amicitia vera venerunt. Postea vero, ex verbis Job, quæ non satis intellexerunt, permittente Deo et instigante diabolo, ex zelo veritatis indiscreto ad verba ignominiosa delapsi sunt.
paras.en: Thomas, however, expounds it thus: [[6:20|They are confounded|Confusi sunt]] to come to me, [[6:20|because I have hoped|quia speravi]], that is, since it was a time in which I ought to hope for help from them. For men who are unwilling to help are ashamed to visit those whom they think will ask help of them. This exposition seems doubtful. For it was said in the second chapter that Job's friends came to comfort him[[Job 2:11||]]. So it does not appear that they were unwilling to bring him help, or that they were ashamed to come because they would not succour him. Rather, as was shown in the exposition of the second chapter[[Job 2:11||]], they came with a good intention and out of true friendship. But afterwards, because of Job's words, which they did not well understand, by God's permission and at the devil's instigation, they slipped into shameful words out of an indiscreet zeal for the truth.

paras.t: Denique Albertus exponit sic: Confusi sunt, id est, in proximo confundentur, quia speravi, id est, spem de justitia judicis habui. Venerunt quoque usque ad me, gratia consolationis impendendæ, et pudore cooperti sunt, id est totaliter circumfusi, vehementissime erubescentes de tam insolita ac invisa mea dejectione. Quoniam enim vere amabant Job, quando primo eum in tanta calamitate intuiti sunt, non dubium quin erubuerint: et præsertim, quia putabant eum suis peccatis id meruisse.
paras.en: Lastly Albert expounds it thus: [[6:20|They are confounded|Confusi sunt]], that is, they shall shortly be confounded, [[6:20|because I have hoped|quia speravi]], that is, I have had hope in the justice of the Judge. [[6:20|they are come also even unto me|Venerunt quoque usque ad me]], for the sake of giving comfort, [[6:20|and are covered with shame|et pudore cooperti sunt]], that is, wholly overspread, blushing most vehemently at so unwonted and unheard-of a casting down of mine. For since they truly loved Job, when they first saw him in so great a calamity there is no doubt that they blushed: and the more so because they thought he had deserved it by his sins.

paras.t: Deinde alloquitur eos. Nunc venistis, et modo videntes plagam meam timetis, ne et vobis tale quid accidat, vel ne petam a vobis subsidium. Numquid dixi: Afferte mihi, id est aliquid de bonis vestris mihi adducite, et de substantia vestra, id est facultatibus, donate mihi, pro relevamine inopiæ meæ? quasi dicat: Non timeatis quod gravabo vos vestra petendo, quia hucusque non petii. Vel, Liberate me de manu hostis, et de manu robustorum eruite me? id est, auxilium non postulavi a vobis contra adversarios meos, qui mea nuper abstulerunt, Chaldæos et Sabæos, aut similes.
paras.en: Then he addresses them. [[6:21|Now you are come|Nunc venistis]], [[6:21|and now, seeing my affliction, you are afraid|et modo videntes plagam meam timetis]], lest some such thing befall you too, or lest I ask help of you. [[6:22|Did I say: Bring to me|Numquid dixi: Afferte mihi]], that is, bring me something of your goods, [[6:22|and give me of your substance?|et de substantia vestra donate mihi?]] [*substantia*: goods, wealth], that is, of your means, for the relief of my want? as if to say: Do not fear that I shall burden you by asking for what is yours, for I have not asked till now. [[6:23|Or deliver me from the hand of the enemy, and rescue me out of the hand of the mighty?|Vel, Liberate me de manu hostis, et de manu robustorum eruite me?]] that is, I have not asked help of you against my adversaries who lately took away what was mine, the Chaldeans and the Sabeans, or the like.

paras.t: Docete me, et ego tacebo: id est, si aliqua vera atque salubria documenta convenienter proposueritis mihi, cum reverentia atque silentio audiam ea et acceptabo; et si quid forte ignoravi, eorum quæ vos scitis, et quæ scire me decet: de illis etenim loquitur, non absolute de quibuscumque, quum certum fuerit sibi, quod multa nescivit; instruite me. Sapientis equidem est, libenter informari et docilem esse. Nam et docilitas pars est prudentiæ. In Proverbiis quoque habetur: Doce justum, et festinabit accipere. Da sapienti occasionem, et addetur ei sapientia. Alibi quoque: Audiens sapiens, sapientior erit.
paras.en: [[6:24|Teach me, and I will hold my peace|Docete me, et ego tacebo]]: that is, if you set before me fittingly any true and wholesome teachings, I will hear them with reverence and silence and accept them; [[6:24|and if I have been ignorant of any thing|et si quid forte ignoravi]] of the things that you know and that it befits me to know (for he speaks of these, not absolutely of any things whatever, since he was certain that he did not know many things), [[6:24|instruct me|instruite me]]. For it belongs to the wise man to be gladly informed and to be teachable. For teachableness is a part of prudence. In Proverbs too we have: [[Prov 9:9|Teach a just man, and he shall make haste to receive it|Doce justum, et festinabit accipere]]. [[Prov 9:9|Give an occasion to a wise man, and wisdom shall be added to him|Da sapienti occasionem, et addetur ei sapientia]]. And elsewhere: [[Prov 1:5|A wise man shall hear, and shall be wiser|Audiens sapiens, sapientior erit]].

paras.t: Verumtamen quod ait, Docete me, etc., accipi potest ut superioribus condependens, non quasi sententia per se dicta: ut sit sensus, Numquid dixi, Docete me? id est, doctrinam a vobis non postulavi, non quod ex elatione omiserim hoc, sed quoniam tantæ sapientiæ vos non novi.
paras.en: However, his saying "Teach me", etc., may be taken as hanging on what goes before, not as a sentence said by itself; so that the sense is: [[6:22|Did I say|Numquid dixi]]: "Teach me"? that is, I have not asked teaching of you; not that I left this out from pride, but because I did not know you to be of such wisdom.

paras.t: Quare detraxistis sermonibus veritatis, id est veris verbis, quibus me innocentem ac justum asserui, ceterisque eloquiis meis, quæ in deploratione mea seu lamentatione deprompsi veritatis amore, dicentes quod ex impatientia sim locutus? Quum ex vobis nullus sit qui me possit arguere: quia nec auctoritate, nec vita, nec sapientia me ita excellitis, ut me rationabiliter reprehendere valeatis: quod zelo justitiæ dicitur. Ad increpandum tantum, non ad utilitatem, eloquia concinnatis, id est, disputationes curiose componitis, et in ventum verba profertis, id est, infructuose et jactanter loquimini. Super pupillum irruitis, id est, me omni humano auxilio destitutum verbis invaditis, et subvertere, id est a recta sententia retrahere, et ad vestros errores inducere, seu impium comprobare, nitimini me amicum vestrum. Amicus est, qui in eadem disputatione concordat ad veritatis inquisitionem. Econtra, secundum Philosophum in Topicis, Pravus est socius, qui impedit commune opus in inquisitione veritatis.
paras.en: [[6:25|Why have you detracted the words of truth|Quare detraxistis sermonibus veritatis]], that is, my true words, in which I asserted that I am innocent and just, and my other utterances, which I brought forth in my weeping or lamentation out of love of the truth, saying that I spoke from impatience? [[6:25|whereas there is none of you that can reprove me?|Quum ex vobis nullus sit qui me possit arguere]] for you do not so excel me in authority, nor in life, nor in wisdom, that you can reasonably rebuke me: which is said out of zeal for justice. [[6:26|only to rebuke|Ad increpandum tantum]], not for profit, [[6:26|You dress up speeches|eloquia concinnatis]], that is, you put together disputations with care, [[6:26|and you utter words to the wind|et in ventum verba profertis]], that is, you speak fruitlessly and boastfully. [[6:27|You rush in upon the fatherless|Super pupillum irruitis]], that is, you assail with words me who am bereft of all human help, [[6:27|and you endeavour to overthrow|et subvertere]], that is, to draw me back from a right opinion and lead me into your errors, or to prove me wicked, [[6:27|your friend|nitimini me amicum vestrum]]. A friend is one who agrees in the same disputation for the search after truth. On the contrary, according to the Philosopher in the Topics, he is a bad companion who hinders the common work in the search after truth.

paras.t: Verumtamen quod cœpistis implete, id est, cœptam disputationem prosequamini, quatenus ex collatione disputatoria veritas amplius declaretur. Hoc addit, ne putent se territum, quasi eis respondere non possit. Præbete aurem, id est, dociles estote, et patienter audite, et videte, id est considerate, an mentiar. Respondete, obsecro, absque contentione. Contentio enim rationis impedit actum, et per consequens veritatis inquisitionem disputationisque fructum. Propter quod ait Apostolus: Noli verbis contendere: ad nihil enim utile est, nisi ad subversionem audientium. Contentio quippe, teste Ambrosio, est impugnatio veritatis cum confidentia clamoris. Ideo litigiosi seu contentiosi in disputationibus prævalere quærunt injuriosis clamoribus, magis quam rationabilibus argumentis. Et loquentes in disputatione id quod justum est judicate, id est, recte discernite, seu judicando prosequamini quod est justum, ut scilicet quæ vera videntur, concedatis, et quæ falsa, negetis. Quod si feceritis, non invenietis in lingua mea iniquitatem, id est, non audietis verba iniqua de ore meo procedere, nec in faucibus meis stultitia personabit, id est, sermo veræ sapientiæ contrarius non proferetur a me: quod non jactanter præsumptuoseve dixit, suis viribus innitendo, sed ex magnanimitate, et spe ac securitate gratiosæ adsistentiæ Dei. Sic nempe et Salomon ait: Veritatem meditatur guttur meum, et labia mea detestabuntur impium. Sic ergo Job profitetur, quod locutio sua nec veritati, nec æquitati contrariabitur, nec in Deum, neque in proximum prævaricabitur.
paras.en: [[6:28|However, finish what you have begun|Verumtamen quod cœpistis implete]] [the margin notes the reading *explete*, as in the Vulgate], that is, carry on the disputation you have begun, so that the truth may be made plainer by the comparing of arguments. He adds this lest they should think him frightened, as though he could not answer them. [[6:28|give ear|Præbete aurem]], that is, be teachable and listen patiently, [[6:28|and see|et videte]], that is, consider, [[6:28|whether I lie|an mentiar]]. [[6:29|Answer, I beseech you, without contention|Respondete, obsecro, absque contentione]]. For contention hinders the act of reason, and in consequence the search for truth and the fruit of disputation. For this reason the Apostle says: [[2 Tim 2:14|Contend not in words: for it is to no profit, but to the subverting of the hearers|Noli verbis contendere: ad nihil enim utile est, nisi ad subversionem audientium]] [the margin's reference is misread; the verse is II Tim. ii, 14]. For contention, as Ambrose witnesses, is the assailing of the truth with the confidence of clamour. Therefore the quarrelsome or contentious seek to prevail in disputations by abusive clamour rather than by reasonable arguments. [[6:29|and speaking|Et loquentes]] in the disputation [[6:29|that which is just, judge ye|id quod justum est judicate]], that is, discern rightly, or follow out in judging what is just: that is, that you grant what seems true and deny what seems false. If you do this, [[6:30|And you shall not find iniquity in my tongue|non invenietis in lingua mea iniquitatem]], that is, you shall not hear wicked words come out of my mouth, [[6:30|neither shall folly sound in my mouth|nec in faucibus meis stultitia personabit]], that is, no speech contrary to true wisdom shall be uttered by me. This he said not boastfully or presumptuously, leaning on his own strength, but from greatness of soul, and from hope and assurance of God's gracious assistance. For so Solomon too says: [[Prov 8:7|My mouth shall meditate truth, and my lips shall hate wickedness|Veritatem meditatur guttur meum, et labia mea detestabuntur impium]]. So, then, Job professes that his speech will not be contrary to truth or to equity, and will not transgress against God or against his neighbour.

6.title: Elucidatio ejusdem capituli sexti mystica.
6.title_en: Mystical explanation of the same sixth chapter

paras.t: Sanctus Gregorius, in exordio libri septimi Moralium, sentire videtur, quod præsens capitulum, potissime principium ejus, ad litteram exponi non debeat, forsitan propter rationes in præcedentis articuli initio tactas. Unde ad allegorias ac tropologias convertitur. Verum Albertus et Thomas exponunt istud ad litteram: quos præcedenti articulo sum secutus. Et puto, quod dictum eorum verbis Gregorii aut non, aut parum repugnet. Varias nempe considerationes circa verba hæc habuerunt, et juxta eas diversa protulerunt judicia. Verumtamen quidquid inde dicatur, constat quod mystica horum declaratio fructuosior, subtilior, delectabiliorque consistat quam litteralis.
paras.en: St. Gregory, at the beginning of the seventh book of the Morals, seems to hold that the present chapter, and above all its beginning, ought not to be expounded according to the letter, perhaps for the reasons touched on at the beginning of the preceding article. And so he turns to allegories and tropologies [that is, to the allegorical and the moral sense]. But Albert and Thomas expound it according to the letter, and I followed them in the preceding article. And I think that what they say is either not at all, or only a little, at odds with the words of Gregory. For they had different considerations in view concerning these words, and in keeping with them they gave different judgements. Yet whatever may be said of this, it is certain that the mystical explanation of these words is more fruitful, subtler and more delightful than the literal.

paras.t: Itaque Job sui humanique generis voce loquens: Utinam, inquit, appenderentur peccata mea quibus iram merui, et calamitas quam patior, in statera. Quasi arena maris hæc gravior appareret. Per stateram exprimitur Christus, qui ad ponderandum ac metiendum nostræ vitæ meritum venit, secumque misericordiam atque justitiam detulit; qui quasi statera miri libraminis factus, hinc in se calamitatem nostram, et illinc peccata suspendit; ante cujus adventum genus humanum pœnas, quas pro originali peccato ac aliis suis vitiis patiebatur, videlicet mentis excæcationem, dæmonum dominationem, jugum iniquitatis, multiplicem corporis corruptionem atque naturæ infectionem, præsensque exsilium, ignoravit. Job ergo in ejus loquens persona, optavit Christi adventum, ut in ipso suspenderentur nostra peccata, ita quod ipse pro eis satisfaciendo ac moriendo, ea quasi super se caperet. Unde et in Isaia scribitur: Dominus posuit in eo iniquitatem omnium nostrum. Et Petrus in prima sua epistola: Peccata, inquit, nostra pertulit in corpore suo super lignum. Calamitas quoque, quam per peccata meruimus, Christo inducta est, scilicet mors amara, quemadmodum ait in Psalmo: Quæ non rapui, tunc exsolvebam. Et Isaias: Vere languores nostros ipse tulit, et dolores nostros ipse portavit. Joannesque: Ecce Agnus Dei, ecce qui tollit peccata mundi. Ex qua appensione peccatorum et calamitatis in Christo, innotuit quam gravis fuit calamitas exsilii et pœnarum generis humani. Ex hoc enim quod ob eam tollendam unigenitus Dei Filius passus est, constat quod utique fuit gravissima. Ideo ait: Quasi arena maris hæc gravior appareret, id est, gravior appareret tunc, et postea quum per apostolicam prædicationem mundo innotuit, quam ante apparuit. Quasi arena maris, id est, quemadmodum arena ad littus maris sita, multum gravis est simul collecta.
paras.en: And so Job, speaking in his own voice and in that of the human race: [[6:2|O that|Utinam]], he says, [[6:2|my sins, whereby I have deserved wrath, and the calamity that I suffer, were weighed in a balance|appenderentur peccata mea quibus iram merui, et calamitas quam patior, in statera]]. [[6:3|As the sand of the sea, this would appear heavier|Quasi arena maris hæc gravior appareret]]. By the balance Christ is expressed, who came to weigh and measure the merit of our life, and brought mercy and justice with him; who, made as it were a balance of wondrous poise, hung our calamity upon himself on the one side and our sins on the other. Before his coming the human race did not know [the weight of] the punishments which it suffered for original sin and for its other vices: namely blindness of mind, the dominion of the demons, the yoke of iniquity, the manifold corruption of the body and the infection of nature, and the present exile. Job therefore, speaking in its person, longed for the coming of Christ, that our sins might be hung upon him, so that he, by making satisfaction and dying for them, might take them as it were upon himself. Hence it is written in Isaias: [[Is 53:6|the Lord hath laid on him the iniquity of us all|Dominus posuit in eo iniquitatem omnium nostrum]]. And Peter in his first epistle: He [[1 Pet 2:24|bore our sins|Peccata]], he says, [[1 Pet 2:24|in his body upon the tree|nostra pertulit in corpore suo super lignum]]. The calamity too which we deserved by our sins was brought upon Christ, namely a bitter death, as he says in the Psalm: [[Ps 68:5|then did I pay that which I took not away|Quæ non rapui, tunc exsolvebam]]. And Isaias: [[Is 53:4|Surely he hath borne our infirmities and carried our sorrows|Vere languores nostros ipse tulit, et dolores nostros ipse portavit]]. And John: [[John 1:29|Behold the Lamb of God. Behold him who taketh away the sin of the world|Ecce Agnus Dei, ecce qui tollit peccata mundi]]. From this hanging of our sins and calamity upon Christ it became known how heavy was the calamity of the exile and of the punishments of the human race. For from the fact that the only-begotten Son of God suffered to take it away, it is clear that it was very heavy indeed. Therefore he says: [[6:3|As the sand of the sea, this would appear heavier|Quasi arena maris hæc gravior appareret]], that is, it would appear heavier then, and afterwards, when it became known to the world through the preaching of the apostles, than it appeared before. [[6:3|As the sand of the sea|Quasi arena maris]], that is, as the sand lying on the sea-shore is very heavy when gathered together.

paras.t: Deinde Job in persona cujuslibet justi, vitæ hujus exsilium deplorantis, subjecit: Unde et verba mea dolore sunt plena, propter calamitates quibus premitur genus humanum, et maxime homo justus, cujus vita tribulationibus plena est, ad patriamque gemens suspirat. Porro filii sæculi hujus, exsilium pro patria diligentes, atque futuris ac cœlestibus præsentia et terrena præferentes, in suis exsultant miseriis, et animarum suarum vulnera ac dolores non sentiunt; tantoque infeliciores sunt, quo minus infelices se esse perpendunt. Quia sagittæ Domini in me sunt, id est variæ tribulationes ac pœnæ pro peccatis inflictæ. Quatuor namque sunt vulnera animæ pro originali peccato inflicta, videlicet, concupiscentia, infirmitas, ignorantia atque malitia: quibus velut sagittis transfigitur homo. Quarum indignatio ebibit spiritum meum. Ex his quippe vehementer affligitur justus, sentiens aliquam legem in membris ac sensualitate, repugnantem jugiter legi mentis. Propter quod continuum gerit contra vitium prælium, abstinens a carnalibus desideriis, qui militant adversus animam, implensque illud Apostoli: Spiritu ambulate, et desideria carnis non perficietis. Caro enim concupiscit adversus spiritum, et spiritus adversus carnem. Hæc enim sibi invicem adversantur, ut non quæcumque vultis, illa faciatis. Præterea, quid molestius quam contra propriam ignorantiam rationis, contra pronitatem voluntatis ad culpam, contra infirmitatem appetitus irascibilis ad resistendum contrariis veræ salutis, contra concupiscentiam appetitus concupiscibilis quotidie, imo omni hora, debite decertare? Et quia ex hac præliatione, pressura et pœna pro peccato inducta, humiliat homo se ipsum, miseriam suam experiens, potest hoc loco per spiritum, animositas seu spiritus elationis intelligi. Et terrores Domini militant contra me. Justus namque et sapiens non tantum deflet præsentes ærumnas pœnæ et culpæ, sed et futura pericula magis veretur, ne rursus Deum offendat, ne in manus incidat Dei viventis, ne a vultu gloriæ supergloriosissimi Dei pellatur, et pœnas irruat sempiternas. De hoc felici terrore in Proverbiis habetur: Beatus homo qui semper est pavidus. Itemque: Timor Domini fons vitæ, ut declinet a ruina mortis.
paras.en: Then Job, in the person of any just man lamenting the exile of this life, added: [[6:3|therefore, my words are full of sorrow|Unde et verba mea dolore sunt plena]], because of the calamities by which the human race is weighed down, and above all the just man, whose life is full of tribulations, and who sighs and groans for his homeland. But the children of this world, who love the exile in place of the homeland and prefer things present and earthly to things to come and heavenly, exult in their miseries and do not feel the wounds and pains of their souls; and they are the more unhappy, the less they reckon themselves unhappy. [[6:4|For the arrows of the Lord are in me|Quia sagittæ Domini in me sunt]], that is, the various tribulations and punishments inflicted for sins. For there are four wounds of the soul inflicted for original sin, namely concupiscence, weakness, ignorance and malice [the four "wounds of nature" of the scholastics], by which man is pierced through as by arrows. [[6:4|the rage whereof drinketh up my spirit|Quarum indignatio ebibit spiritum meum]]. For by these the just man is sorely afflicted, feeling a certain law in his members and sensuality that fights continually against the law of the mind[[Rom 7:23||]]. Because of this he wages a continual battle against vice, refraining from [[1 Pet 2:11|carnal desires which war against the soul|carnalibus desideriis, qui militant adversus animam]], and fulfilling that word of the Apostle: [[Gal 5:16|Walk in the spirit: and you shall not fulfill the lusts of the flesh|Spiritu ambulate, et desideria carnis non perficietis]]. [[Gal 5:17|For the flesh lusteth against the spirit: and the spirit against the flesh: For these are contrary one to another: so that you do not the things that you would|Caro enim concupiscit adversus spiritum, et spiritus adversus carnem. Hæc enim sibi invicem adversantur, ut non quæcumque vultis, illa faciatis]]. Moreover, what is more irksome than to strive as one ought, daily, nay every hour, against the ignorance proper to reason, against the proneness of the will to sin, against the weakness of the irascible appetite in resisting what is contrary to true salvation, and against the concupiscence of the concupiscible appetite [the two powers of the sense appetite: the irascible, which meets what is hard, and the concupiscible, which seeks what is pleasant]? And since through this battling, this pressure and punishment brought on by sin, man humbles himself, learning his own misery by experience, by *spirit* in this place may be understood haughtiness, or the spirit of pride. [[6:4|and the terrors of the Lord war against me|Et terrores Domini militant contra me]]. For the just and wise man not only bewails the present troubles of punishment and of sin, but fears still more the dangers to come: lest he offend God again, lest he [[Heb 10:31|fall into the hands of the living God|in manus incidat Dei viventis]], lest he be driven from the face of the glory of the supremely glorious God and fall into everlasting punishments. Of this happy terror it is said in Proverbs: [[Prov 28:14|Blessed is the man that is always fearful|Beatus homo qui semper est pavidus]]. And again: [[Prov 14:27|The fear of the Lord is a fountain of life, to decline from the ruin of death|Timor Domini fons vitæ, ut declinet a ruina mortis]].

paras.t: Præterea, quoniam Job fuit evidens Christi figura, possunt hæc verba de Christo exponi. Quemadmodum enim amici Job imputabant ei, quod pro suis affligeretur peccatis, sic Judæi Christum pro suis dixerunt excessibus comprehensum, tentum et tortum, coram Pilato clamantes: Si non esset malefactor hic, non tibi eum tradidissemus. Et rursus: Hunc invenimus subvertentem gentem nostram, et prohibentem tributa dari Cæsari, et dicentem se Christum regem esse. Quibus Christus poterat respondere verba præhabita: Utinam appenderentur peccata mea, non quæ commisi, sed quæ imponitis mihi, quibus iram merui, id est pœnam mortis, secundum vestram censuram, qua de me dixistis, Reus est mortis; et calamitas acerbissimæ passionis, quam patior, in statera, secundum sensum expositum. Quasi arena maris, id est incomparabiliter, hæc calamitas gravior appareret, quam peccata præfata: quia in veritate nulli peccato obnoxius fui. Unde, id est ob amaritudinem passionis, mihi pro aliorum excessu instantis, verba mea dolore sunt plena. Dolorosa plane fuerunt verba Christi, quando passione jam imminente, cum clamore valido et lacrimis preces fudit ad Patrem, secundum Apostolum. Terque rogavit, ut si fieri posset, transiret ab eo calix. Similiter verba quæ dixit in cruce, Deus meus, Deus meus, ut quid dereliquisti me, ac cetera ibi prolata, nonne dolore fuere plenissima? Quia sagittæ Domini, id est amarissimæ mortis puncturæ, præsertim tempore distensionis in cruce, in me sunt: quas, Deo Patre disponente atque volente, sustinui, quemadmodum Pater ait de Christo per Isaiam: Propter scelus populi mei percussi eum. Et rursus ibidem: Dominus voluit conterere eum in infirmitate. Quarum indignatio, in quantum fuerunt velut in ultionem, castigationem seu correctionem peccatorum generis humani, juxta illud Isaiæ, Disciplina pacis nostræ super eum; ebibit spiritum meum: quia per pœnæ illius acerbitatem vere mortuus fuit Christus, per separationem animæ ejus a corpore, quamvis utrumque manserit Verbo unitum.
paras.en: Moreover, since Job was a manifest figure of Christ, these words can be expounded of Christ. For just as Job's friends charged him with being afflicted for his own sins, so the Jews said that Christ had been seized, held and tortured for his own misdeeds, crying out before Pilate: [[John 18:30|If he were not a malefactor, we would not have delivered him up to thee|Si non esset malefactor hic, non tibi eum tradidissemus]]. And again: [[Luke 23:2|We have found this man perverting our nation and forbidding to give tribute to Caesar and saying that he is Christ the king|Hunc invenimus subvertentem gentem nostram, et prohibentem tributa dari Cæsari, et dicentem se Christum regem esse]]. To them Christ could have answered in the words given above: [[6:2|O that my sins|Utinam appenderentur peccata mea]], not those which I committed, but those which you lay upon me, [[6:2|whereby I have deserved wrath|quibus iram merui]], that is, the punishment of death, according to your verdict, by which you said of me: [[Matt 26:66|He is guilty of death|Reus est mortis]]; [[6:2|and the calamity|et calamitas]] of my most bitter passion [[6:2|that I suffer, were weighed in a balance|quam patior, in statera]], in the sense explained. [[6:3|As the sand of the sea|Quasi arena maris]], that is, beyond all comparison, [[6:3|this would appear heavier|hæc calamitas gravior appareret]] [Denis adds *calamitas*: this calamity] than the sins just named, since in truth I was guilty of no sin. [[6:3|therefore|Unde]], that is, because of the bitterness of the passion that stands over me for the transgression of others, [[6:3|my words are full of sorrow|verba mea dolore sunt plena]]. Full of sorrow indeed were the words of Christ when, his passion now at hand, he poured out prayers to the Father [[Heb 5:7|with a strong cry and tears|cum clamore valido et lacrimis]], as the Apostle says. And three times he asked that, if it might be, the chalice might pass from him[[Matt 26:39||]][[Matt 26:42||]][[Matt 26:44||]]. Likewise the words that he spoke on the cross, [[Mark 15:34|My God, My God, Why hast thou forsaken me?|Deus meus, Deus meus, ut quid dereliquisti me]] and the rest that he uttered there: were they not most full of sorrow? [[6:4|For the arrows of the Lord|Quia sagittæ Domini]], that is, the piercings of a most bitter death, above all at the time when I was stretched out on the cross, [[6:4|are in me|in me sunt]]: and these I bore, God the Father so disposing and willing, as the Father says of Christ through Isaias: [[Is 53:8|for the wickedness of my people have I struck him|Propter scelus populi mei percussi eum]]. And again in the same place: [[Is 53:10|And the Lord was pleased to bruise him in infirmity|Dominus voluit conterere eum in infirmitate]]. [[6:4|the rage whereof|Quarum indignatio]], inasmuch as they were, as it were, for the punishment, chastisement or correction of the sins of the human race, according to that of Isaias, [[Is 53:5|the chastisement of our peace was upon him|Disciplina pacis nostræ super eum]]; [[6:4|drinketh up my spirit|ebibit spiritum meum]]: because through the bitterness of that suffering Christ truly died, by the separation of his soul from his body, although both remained united to the Word.

paras.t: Insuper, verba inducta possent exponi de quocumque innocente ac justo, gravissime afflicto, non vitæ suæ demerito, sed propter probationem ipsius et patientiæ demonstrationem, ad aliorum ædificationem, atque ob incrementum sui profectus ac felicitatis: quod in multis electissimis factum constat martyribus. Sed quia ex præinductis clarissime innotescit, quomodo ad hoc valeat littera applicari, pertranseo, ad difficilioraque propero.
paras.en: Furthermore, the words set down could be expounded of any innocent and just man who is most grievously afflicted, not through any fault in his life, but for his testing and the showing of his patience, for the edification of others, and for the increase of his own progress and happiness: as is known to have happened in many most chosen martyrs. But since it is very clear from what was said before how the letter can be applied to this, I pass over it and hasten on to harder things.

paras.t: Numquid rugiet onager quum habuerit herbam? Per onagrum designatur plebs gentilis indomita, voluptatique dedita, cujus non parva pars exspectavit Christum venturum, sicut et Job et patriarchæ gentilium cum subditis ac discipulis suis. Qui populus quo Christi adventum magis optavit, eo ipsius dilationem dolorosius tulit. Quum vero per apostolicam prædicationem evangelicam legem sortitus est, Christo unitus, et gratiæ ac sacramentorum ejus particeps factus, non rugiit, sed lætus effectus est, habens herbam, id est incarnationis dominicæ gratiam et virtutem, seu Christum dulcissimum, qui testatur: Caro mea vere est cibus. Aut mugiet bos, id est populus Judæorum, jugo legis assuetus ac subditus, ad Judaismum proselytos colligens, sicque per corda eorum vomerem legis trahens, quum ante præsepe plenum steterit, id est, Christum corporaliter præsentem agnoverit, sibi in lege diu promissum, jamque in ea positum ac oblatum? Quod de electis Judæorum reliquiis accipi congruit, qui Christi adventum cordialiter optaverunt, eumque præsentem viderunt, aut venisse crediderunt cum ingenti lætitia. Idcirco non mugierunt tristantes, sed psallebant gaudentes. Denique, de discipulis suis dixit Christus Judæis incredulis: Numquid lugere possunt filii sponsi, quamdiu cum illis est sponsus? Itaque, præsepe fuit Scriptura veteris Testamenti, seu lex, quæ sine Christo vacua fuit, et ipso incarnato repleta est. Aut poterit comedi, id est mente sumi ac masticari, insulsum, id est vetus Testamentum, seu lex et Scriptura ipsius ad litteram intellecta, non spiritualiter sumpta? Non utique. Sic enim non reficit, sed occidit, dicente Apostolo: Littera occidit, Spiritus autem vivificat. Sal ergo litteræ legis, est intelligentia spiritualis: qua si fuerit Scriptura illa condita, erit salubriter refectiva. Aut gustare aliquis potest, quod gustatum, affert mortem? Hoc plane rationabiliter et scienter non fit proprio motu gustantis, quanquam aliqui martyrum venena pro fide potaverint. Mysticus igitur sensus est, quod sanctorum Prophetarum vaticinium secundum litteræ superficiem sumptum, frequenter mortiferum esset: ideo taliter gustari non debet.
paras.en: [[6:5|Will the wild ass bray when he hath grass?|Numquid rugiet onager quum habuerit herbam?]] By the wild ass is signified the untamed Gentile people, given over to pleasure, no small part of which awaited the coming of Christ, as did Job too and the patriarchs of the Gentiles with their subjects and disciples. And the more this people longed for Christ's coming, the more painfully it bore its delay. But when through the preaching of the apostles it received the law of the Gospel, being united to Christ and made partaker of his grace and his sacraments, it did not bray but was made glad, having *grass*, that is, the grace and power of the Lord's incarnation, or the most sweet Christ, who testifies: [[John 6:56|my flesh is meat indeed|Caro mea vere est cibus]]. [[6:5|or will the ox low|Aut mugiet bos]], that is, the people of the Jews, accustomed and subject to the yoke of the Law, gathering proselytes to Judaism and so drawing the ploughshare of the Law through their hearts, [[6:5|when he standeth before a full manger?|quum ante præsepe plenum steterit]] that is, when it has recognized Christ present in the body, long promised to it in the Law and now set forth and offered in it? This is fitly taken of the chosen remnant of the Jews, who longed from the heart for the coming of Christ, and saw him present, or believed that he had come, with great joy. Therefore they did not low in sadness, but sang psalms in gladness. And indeed Christ said of his disciples to the unbelieving Jews: [[Matt 9:15|Can the children of the bridegroom mourn, as long as the bridegroom is with them?|Numquid lugere possunt filii sponsi, quamdiu cum illis est sponsus?]][[Mark 2:19||]] The manger, then, was the Scripture of the Old Testament, or the Law, which was empty without Christ and was filled when he became incarnate. Or can there [[6:6|be eaten|Aut poterit comedi]], that is, be taken and chewed by the mind, [[6:6|an unsavoury thing|insulsum]], that is, the Old Testament, or the Law and its Scripture understood according to the letter and not taken spiritually? Not at all. For so it does not refresh but kills, as the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 3:6|the letter killeth: but the spirit quickeneth|Littera occidit, Spiritus autem vivificat]]. The salt of the letter of the Law, then, is the spiritual understanding: if that Scripture is seasoned with it, it will give wholesome refreshment. [[6:6|or can a man taste that which, when tasted, bringeth death?|Aut gustare aliquis potest, quod gustatum, affert mortem?]] This plainly is not done reasonably and knowingly by the taster's own motion, although some of the martyrs drank poisons for the faith. The mystical sense, then, is that the prophecy of the holy Prophets, taken according to the surface of the letter, would often be deadly: and so it ought not to be tasted in that way.

paras.t: Deinde Job tanquam vivum membrum Ecclesiæ, voce ejus subjungit: Quæ prius, id est ante Christi adventum, tangere nolebat anima mea, videlicet veteris Testamenti cibum seu documentum, nunc, post Christi passionem, per apostolicam prædicationem, præ angustia pœnitentiæ et amoris, cibi mei sunt, id est mentis meæ refectiones. Hoc Ecclesiæ ex gentibus collectæ est competens. Potest nihilo minus de conversa electaque Synagoga exponi, quæ Unigenito Dei nondum incarnato ac passo, contempsit gentiles, nolens eis communicare aut jungi, quemadmodum loquitur Petrus gentilibus: Vos scitis quomodo abominatum sit viro Judæo accedere aut conjungi ad alienigenam. Unde et post quidam conversi Judæi, locuti sunt Petro: Quare introisti ad viros præputium habentes, et manducasti cum eis? Postea autem, misso Spiritu Sancto, orsi sunt sancti Apostoli prædicare gentilibus præ angustia æstuantis amoris, incorporaveruntque eos sibi, et de eorum conversione atque salute mente refecti sunt non mediocriter deliciose.
paras.en: Then Job, as a living member of the Church, adds in her voice: [[6:7|The things which before|Quæ prius]], that is, before the coming of Christ, [[6:7|my soul would not touch|tangere nolebat anima mea]], namely the food or teaching of the Old Testament, [[6:7|now|nunc]], after the passion of Christ, through the preaching of the apostles, [[6:7|through anguish|præ angustia]] of penance and of love, [[6:7|are my meats|cibi mei sunt]], that is, the refreshments of my mind. This befits the Church gathered from the Gentiles. It can none the less be expounded of the converted and chosen Synagogue, which, before the Only-begotten of God was incarnate and had suffered, despised the Gentiles, unwilling to have dealings with them or be joined to them, as Peter says to the Gentiles: [[Acts 10:28|you know how abominable it is for a man that is a Jew to keep company or to come unto one of another nation|Vos scitis quomodo abominatum sit viro Judæo accedere aut conjungi ad alienigenam]]. Hence also afterwards certain converted Jews said to Peter: [[Acts 11:3|Why didst thou go in to men uncircumcised and didst eat with them?|Quare introisti ad viros præputium habentes, et manducasti cum eis?]] But afterwards, when the Holy Ghost had been sent, the holy Apostles began to preach to the Gentiles through the anguish of a burning love, and incorporated them into themselves, and were refreshed in mind, and that most delightfully, by their conversion and salvation.

paras.t: Quis mihi det ut veniat petitio mea, et quod exspecto, tribuat mihi Deus? et qui cœpit, ipse me conterat, etc.? Juxta sensum, quo præcedenti articulo verbum hoc de sancto Job exstat expositum, intelligi potest de quocumque justo in gravissimis tribulationibus constituto, qui timore offendendi Deum et tædio malorum culpæ sæculi hujus, desiderioque visionis beatificæ summi Dei, cupit dissolvi, et tribulationem sibi inflictam continuari ac ingravescere, quousque auferatur de vita præsenti. Sic nempe dixit Apostolus: Infelix ego homo, quis me liberabit de corpore mortis hujus? Et Psalmista: Heu mihi quia incolatus meus prolongatus est. Deinde accipi potest de contritione bona et succisione salubri, qua Deus per gratiam et virtutes conterit in nobis, quod a nobis ipsis habemus et sumus, videlicet peccata nostra, passiones et vitia: sicque spiritualiter atque vitaliter mortificemur, et nos ipsos relinquamus ac abnegemus, ut ab alto elationis succisi, ad propriæ parvitatis humilia descendamus: ipsa quoque flagella paternæ castigationis Dei libenter feramus, in quantum sunt criminum sanativa; imo in vita hac corrigi peroptemus, ne æternaliter cruciemur. Hinc ait Gregorius: Sancti viri cum de occulta erga se dispositione Dei suspecti sunt, prospera pertimescunt, tentari appetunt, flagellari desiderant, quatenus incautam mentem metus et dolor erudiat, ne in hac peregrinatione hoste ex insidiis erumpente, sua eam securitas deterius sternat. Hinc ait Psalmista: Proba me, Domine, et tenta me. Itemque: Quoniam ego in flagella paratus.
paras.en: [[6:8|Who will grant that my request may come: and that God may give me what I look for?|Quis mihi det ut veniat petitio mea, et quod exspecto, tribuat mihi Deus?]] [[6:9|And that he that hath begun may destroy me|et qui cœpit, ipse me conterat]], etc.?
