In the sense in which this saying was expounded of holy Job in the preceding article, it can be understood of any just man set in the most grievous tribulations, who, from fear of offending God, from weariness of the evils of sin in this world, and from desire of the beatific vision of the most high God, longs to be dissolved, and wishes the tribulation laid upon him to continue and grow heavier until he is taken out of the present life. So indeed the Apostle said: [[Rom 7:24|Unhappy man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?|Infelix ego homo, quis me liberabit de corpore mortis hujus?]] And the Psalmist: [[Ps 119:5|Woe is me, that my sojourning is prolonged!|Heu mihi quia incolatus meus prolongatus est]] Next, it can be taken of the good *crushing* [*contritio*, from *conterat*, "destroy me"] and the wholesome *cutting off* [*succisio*, from *succidat me*, "cut me off"], by which God, through grace and the virtues, crushes in us what we have and are of ourselves, namely our sins, passions and vices: so that we may be put to death spiritually and in a life-giving way, and may leave and deny ourselves, so that, cut down from the height of pride, we may come down to the lowliness of our own littleness; and may bear willingly the very scourges of God's fatherly chastisement, inasmuch as they heal our sins; nay, may earnestly desire to be corrected in this life, lest we be tormented for ever. Hence Gregory says: Holy men, when they are uneasy about God's hidden disposition towards them, are afraid of prosperity, long to be tried, desire to be scourged, so that fear and sorrow may instruct the unwary mind, lest on this pilgrimage, while the enemy bursts out from ambush, its own security should lay it lower still. Hence the Psalmist says: [[Ps 25:2|Prove me, O Lord, and try me|Proba me, Domine, et tenta me]]. And again: [[Ps 37:18|For I am ready for scourges|Quoniam ego in flagella paratus]].

paras.t: Ideo subditur, et hæc mihi sit consolatio, ut affligens me dolore, non parcat. Electi quippe quum peccasse se norunt, nec tamen ob hoc adversa perpessos se meminerunt, pavore tabescunt et æstuant, ne eos in æternum deseruerit gratia, quos in præsenti non custodit culpæ suæ punitio aliqua: timent ne ultio quæ differtur, gravior in fine servetur: ideo nunc paterna castigatione feriri desiderant. Nec contradicam sermonibus Sancti, Dei me corripientis, impatienter ferendo, murmurando aut male loquendo, sed gratias referam in adversis. Unde in Threnis legitur: Quid murmuravit homo vivens, vir pro peccatis suis? Scrutemur vias nostras, et quæramus, et revertamur ad Dominum. Nos inique egimus, et ad iracundiam provocavimus Dominum. Rursusque scriptum est: Sapiens non murmurabit correptus.
paras.en: Therefore it follows: [[6:10|And that this may be my comfort, that afflicting me with sorrow, he spare not|et hæc mihi sit consolatio, ut affligens me dolore, non parcat]]. For the elect, when they know that they have sinned and yet do not remember having suffered adversity for it, waste away with dread and are in a fever lest grace should have forsaken them for ever, since no punishment of their sin guards them in the present: they fear that the vengeance which is put off may be kept, heavier, for the end; and so they long to be struck now by a father's chastisement. [[6:10|nor I contradict the words of the Holy one|Nec contradicam sermonibus Sancti]], that is, of God rebuking me, by bearing it impatiently, murmuring or speaking ill; but I will give thanks in adversity. Hence we read in Lamentations: [[Lam 3:39|Why hath a living man murmured, man suffering for his sins?|Quid murmuravit homo vivens, vir pro peccatis suis?]] [[Lam 3:40|Let us search our ways, and seek, and return to the Lord|Scrutemur vias nostras, et quæramus, et revertamur ad Dominum]]. [[Lam 3:42|We have done wickedly, and provoked thee to wrath|Nos inique egimus, et ad iracundiam provocavimus Dominum]]. And again it is written: The wise man [[Ecclus 10:28|will not murmur when he is reproved|non murmurabit correptus]] [the margin here could not be read; the words are close to Ecclus 10:28, "a man that is prudent and well instructed will not murmur when he is reproved"].

paras.t: Quæ est enim fortitudo mea, ut sustineam tormenta vitæ futuræ? Ideo in præsenti cupio emendari. Aut quis finis meus, ut patienter agam? id est, nulla est ratio habendi patientiam plenam in pœnis inferni, quum non sit spes evadendi, nec exspectatio alicujus finis beati, cujus intuitu solet in adversis patientia conservari. Nec fortitudo lapidum, fortitudo mea, nec caro mea ænea est. Multi jam dignos pœnitentiæ fructus agere renuunt, religionem intrare verentur, dicentes se pati dura non posse jejunia, vigilias, disciplinas, ceteraque similia abhorrentes: qui utinam passibilitatem ac teneritudinem suam prudenter intuerentur, per comparationem ad futura pravorum supplicia. Sicque pensantes quam ineffabiliter graviora sint illa præsentibus pœnis, viriliter aggrederentur arctam viam salutis, omneque exercitium pœnitentiale ac virtuosum.
paras.en: [[6:11|For what is my strength, that I can hold out|Quæ est enim fortitudo mea, ut sustineam]] the torments of the life to come? Therefore I long to be amended in the present. [[6:11|or what is my end, that I should keep patience?|Aut quis finis meus, ut patienter agam?]] That is, there is no means of having full patience in the pains of hell, since there is no hope of escape, nor expectation of any blessed end, in view of which patience is usually kept in adversity. [[6:12|My strength is not the strength of stones, nor is my flesh of brass.|Nec fortitudo lapidum fortitudo mea, nec caro mea ænea est.]] Many now refuse to bring forth fruits worthy of penance and are afraid to enter religion, saying that they cannot bear hard fasts, vigils and disciplines, and shrinking from everything of the kind: if only they would look wisely at their own frailty and tenderness by comparison with the torments to come of the wicked! Then, weighing how unspeakably heavier those are than present pains, they would set out manfully on the narrow way of salvation, and on every exercise of penance and virtue.

paras.t: Ecce non est auxilium mihi in me: id est, propria virtute seu naturali fortitudine, aut per sola et nuda dona naturæ salvari non valeo; a peccatis purgari, meritorie operari, dæmonibus reluctari sine supernaturali Dei subventione et dono gratioso non queo. Itaque nullus de se præsumat, nemo sibi bonum quod agit aut habet, adscribat; sed totam suam fiduciam ponat in Deo, qui ait per Osee: Perditio tua ex te, in me tantummodo auxilium tuum. Et Christus loquitur: Sine me nihil potestis facere. Denique Apostolus, Fiduciam, inquit, talem habemus ad Deum: non quod sufficientes simus cogitare aliquid ex nobis quasi ex nobis, sed sufficientia nostra ex Deo est. Jeremias quoque loquitur Deo: Scio, Domine, quia non est hominis via ejus, nec viri est ut ambulet et dirigat gressus suos.
paras.en: [[6:13|Behold there is no help for me in myself|Ecce non est auxilium mihi in me]]: that is, by my own power or natural strength, or by the gifts of nature alone and bare, I cannot be saved; without the supernatural help of God and the gift of grace I cannot be cleansed from sins, work meritoriously, or resist the demons. Let no one, then, presume on himself, let no one ascribe to himself the good that he does or has, but let him put all his trust in God, who says through Osee: [[Osee 13:9|Destruction is thy own|Perditio tua ex te]], [[Osee 13:9|thy help is only in me|in me tantummodo auxilium tuum]]. And Christ says: [[John 15:5|without me you can do nothing|Sine me nihil potestis facere]]. And the Apostle: [[2 Cor 3:4|such confidence|Fiduciam]], he says, [[2 Cor 3:4|we have|talem habemus]] [[2 Cor 3:4|towards God|ad Deum]]: [[2 Cor 3:5|Not that we are sufficient to think any thing of ourselves, as of ourselves: but our sufficiency is from God|non quod sufficientes simus cogitare aliquid ex nobis quasi ex nobis, sed sufficientia nostra ex Deo est]]. Jeremias too says to God: [[Jer 10:23|I know, O Lord, that the way of a man is not his: neither is it in a man to walk, and to direct his steps.|Scio, Domine, quia non est hominis via ejus, nec viri est ut ambulet, et dirigat gressus suos.]]

paras.t: Necessarii quoque mei recesserunt a me. Hoc dicere potest is, a quo amici ejus tempore necessitatis aut indigentiæ avertuntur, manum adjutricem non porrigentes, sive in spiritualibus, sive in corporalibus bonis. Sic nempe ait Psalmista: Amici mei et proximi mei adversum me appropinquaverunt, et steterunt. Atque Apostolus: In prima mea defensione omnes me dereliquerunt. Qui tollit ab amico suo misericordiam, timorem Domini derelinquit. Hoc de omni proximo intelligi potest. Omnem etenim proximum tanquam amicum et fratrem, imo sicut nos ipsos amare tenemur, eique auxiliari quando ratio dictat, dum scilicet locus, tempus et causa requirunt: quod qui omittit, præceptum caritatis transgreditur, non faciens alteri sicut vellet fieri sibi.
paras.en: [[6:13|and my familiar friends also are departed from me|Necessarii quoque mei recesserunt a me]]. He can say this from whom his friends turn away in the time of need or want, not holding out a helping hand, whether in spiritual or in bodily goods. So indeed the Psalmist says: [[Ps 37:12|My friends and my neighbours have drawn near, and stood against me|Amici mei et proximi mei adversum me appropinquaverunt, et steterunt]]. And the Apostle: [[2 Tim 4:16|At my first answer|In prima mea defensione]] [[2 Tim 4:16|all forsook me|omnes me dereliquerunt]]. [[6:14|He that taketh away mercy from his friend, forsaketh the fear of the Lord.|Qui tollit ab amico suo misericordiam, timorem Domini derelinquit.]] This can be understood of every neighbour. For we are bound to love every neighbour as a friend and a brother, nay as ourselves, and to help him when reason prescribes, that is, when place, time and cause require it: and he who fails to do so transgresses the precept of charity, not doing to another as he would wish to be done to himself.

paras.t: Fratres mei præterierunt me, non condolendo aut succurrendo. Tempore quo fuerint dissipati, id est peccato corrupti, corde divisi, ab integritate virtutum collapsi, peribunt perpetuo: juxta id Osee, Divisum est cor eorum, nunc interibunt; et ut incaluerint, fervore passionum, videlicet iræ, impatientiæ, indignationis seu concupiscentiæ, solventur de loco suo, id est, impetum passionis sequentur, nec stabiles erunt in ratione, in qua homo debet quasi in loco quiescere. Unde scriptum est in Isaia: Impii quasi mare fervens, quod quiescere non potest. Involutæ sunt semitæ gressuum eorum. Hoc omnibus versutis et callidis, duplicibus, adulatoribus ac simulatoribus competit, qui dum aliud mente intendunt, aliud verbis actibusve ostendunt, involutis gressibus gradiuntur et se ipsos a vero virtutum profectu impediunt: imo instar cancri retrogrediuntur, in tartarumque labuntur. Propter quod subditur: Ambulabunt in vacuum, et peribunt. De talibus Jeremias inducit: Sagitta vulnerans, lingua eorum; in ore suo pacem cum amico suo loquitur, et occulte ponit ei insidias. Recti ergo et plani sint gressus nostri, quoniam scriptum est: Deus proteget gradientes simpliciter.
paras.en: [[6:15|My brethren have passed by me|Fratres mei præterierunt me]], by not grieving with me or coming to my help. [[6:17|At the time when they shall be scattered|Tempore quo fuerint dissipati]], that is, corrupted by sin, divided in heart, fallen away from the integrity of the virtues, [[6:17|they shall perish|peribunt]] for ever: according to that of Osee, [[Osee 10:2|Their heart is divided: now they shall perish|Divisum est cor eorum, nunc interibunt]]; [[6:17|and after it groweth hot|et ut incaluerint]] [Denis reads *incaluerint*, "when they grow hot"] with the heat of the passions, namely of anger, impatience, indignation or concupiscence, [[6:17|they shall be melted out of their place|solventur de loco suo]], that is, they will follow the rush of passion and will not stand firm in reason, in which man ought to rest as in his place. Hence it is written in Isaias: [[Is 57:20|the wicked are like the raging sea, which cannot rest|Impii quasi mare fervens, quod quiescere non potest]]. [[6:18|The paths of their steps are entangled|Involutæ sunt semitæ gressuum eorum]]. This fits all the crafty and cunning, the double-dealers, flatterers and dissemblers, who, while they intend one thing in their mind and show another in their words or deeds, walk with entangled steps and hinder themselves from true progress in the virtues: nay, like a crab they go backwards, and slip down into hell. For which reason it is added: [[6:18|they shall walk in vain, and shall perish|Ambulabunt in vacuum, et peribunt]]. Of such men Jeremias says: [[Jer 9:8|Their tongue is a piercing arrow|Sagitta vulnerans, lingua eorum]]: [[Jer 9:8|with his mouth one speaketh peace with his friend, and secretly he lieth in wait for him|in ore suo pacem cum amico suo loquitur, et occulte ponit ei insidias]]. Let our steps, then, be straight and plain, since it is written: God will [[Prov 2:7|protect them that walk in simplicity|proteget gradientes simpliciter]].

paras.t: Considerate semitas Theman, itinera Saba, et exspectate paulisper. Per Theman, quod interpretatur Auster, qui dissolvit afflata teporibus membra, animi remissio designatur. Itaque considerandæ sunt semitæ Theman, id est actus remisse viventium, qui Deo negligenter serviunt cum tepore; ut agnitis eorum dispendiis atque periculis, Domino fervide obsequamur, pensantes quod loquitur Deus: Scio opera tua, quia nec calidus es, neque frigidus; et nunc quia tepidus es, incipiam te evomere ex ore meo. Porro, per Saba, quod interpretatur rete, significantur dolosi, qui aliis deceptionum modos extendunt et moliuntur insidias, capiuntque intra rete suæ versutiæ innocentes ac simplices. Contra quos Isaias asserit: Fraudulenti vasa pessima sunt. Ipse enim cogitationes concinnabit ad perdendos mites in sermone mendacii. Et in Psalmo: Virum sanguinum et dolosum abominabitur Dominus. Tales docet Salomon esse vitandos: Fili, inquiens, si te lactaverint peccatores, ne acquiescas eis. Si dixerint, Veni nobiscum, insidiemur sanguini, abscondamus tendiculas contra insontem frustra; ne ambules cum eis. Horum damnationem videbimus, si paululum præstolemur.
paras.en: [[6:19|Consider the paths of Thema|Considerate semitas Theman]], [[6:19|the ways of Saba, and wait a little while|itinera Saba, et exspectate paulisper]]. By Theman, which is interpreted *south wind*, which loosens the limbs it breathes upon with its warmth, slackness of soul is signified. So we are to consider the paths of Theman, that is, the doings of those who live slackly, who serve God negligently and with lukewarmness; so that, knowing their losses and dangers, we may serve the Lord fervently, weighing what God says: [[Apoc 3:15|I know thy works, that thou art neither cold nor hot|Scio opera tua, quia nec calidus es, neque frigidus]]; and now, [[Apoc 3:16|because thou art lukewarm|quia tepidus es]], [[Apoc 3:16|I will begin to vomit thee out of my mouth|incipiam te evomere ex ore meo]]. Further, by Saba, which is interpreted *net*, are signified the deceitful, who spread out ways of deceiving others and contrive snares, and catch the innocent and simple within the net of their cunning. Against them Isaias declares: [[Is 32:7|The vessels of the deceitful are most wicked: for he hath framed devices to destroy the meek, with lying words|Fraudulenti vasa pessima sunt. Ipse enim cogitationes concinnabit ad perdendos mites in sermone mendacii]]. And in the Psalm: [[Ps 5:7|The bloody and the deceitful man the Lord will abhor|Virum sanguinum et dolosum abominabitur Dominus]]. Solomon teaches that such men are to be shunned: [[Prov 1:10|My son|Fili]], he says, [[Prov 1:10|if sinners shall entice thee, consent not to them|si te lactaverint peccatores, ne acquiescas eis]]. [[Prov 1:11|If they shall say: Come with us, let us lie in wait for blood, let us hide snares for the innocent without cause|Si dixerint, Veni nobiscum, insidiemur sanguini, abscondamus tendiculas contra insontem frustra]]; [[Prov 1:15|walk not thou with them|ne ambules cum eis]] [the margin gives Prov. i, 10, 11, 13; these last words are in v. 15]. We shall see their damnation if we wait a little while.

paras.t: Confusi sunt, quia speravi. Dum reprobi et perversi bonos turbare, a via virtutum retrahere, ab animi constantia impedire nituntur, exhilarantur, si quod moliuntur, ad effectum perducunt: juxta id Psalmistæ, Qui tribulant me, exsultabunt si motus fuero. Dum vero quis tota mente in Deo confidit, nec ab animi tranquillitate dejicitur, confunduntur tanquam spe sua frustrati. Venerunt quoque usque ad me, et pudore cooperti sunt. Hoc in persona cujuslibet justi profertur, quem iniqui aggressi subvertere nequiverunt, ideo erubescunt.
paras.en: [[6:20|They are confounded, because I have hoped|Confusi sunt, quia speravi]]. When the reprobate and perverse strive to trouble the good, to draw them back from the way of the virtues, to shake their constancy of soul, they are delighted if they bring about what they are contriving: according to that of the Psalmist, [[Ps 12:5|They that trouble me, will rejoice when I am moved|Qui tribulant me, exsultabunt si motus fuero]]. But when someone trusts in God with his whole mind and is not cast down from his tranquillity of soul, they are confounded, as men cheated of their hope. [[6:20|they are come also even unto me, and are covered with shame|Venerunt quoque usque ad me, et pudore cooperti sunt]]. This is said in the person of any just man whom the wicked set upon but could not overthrow: and so they blush.

paras.t: Nunc venistis, et modo videntes plagam meam timetis. Vitiosi, qui Deum non amant, neque in prosperis eum verentur, frequenter quodam servili concutiuntur timore, dum aliquem, præsertim suorum propinquorum seu amicorum justorum, viderint horribiliter plagatum, molestatum aut cæsum: quos justus vir tribulatus redarguit, quod non in prosperis quoque Deum formidant, nec eum ex timore filialiter timent. Numquid dixi: Afferte mihi, et de substantia vestra donate mihi? Substantia impiorum, mundana atque carnalis prudentia dicitur: quam justus, ab eis non petit, sed aspernatur, nec per eam consolari dignatur. Vel: Liberate me de manu hostis, et de manu robustorum eruite me? Virtuosi ab invisibilibus ac visibilibus hostibus impugnantur. Scientes vere reprobam vitam pravorum, non quærunt eorum suffragio ab invisibilis hostis tentatione salvari. Et quoniam eos non timent qui corpus occidunt, dum fides vel justitia exigit, parati sunt a visibilibus inimicis occidi, nec quærunt de eorum tyrannide erui.
paras.en: [[6:21|Now you are come: and now, seeing my affliction, you are afraid.|Nunc venistis; et modo videntes plagam meam, timetis.]] The vicious, who do not love God and do not fear him in prosperity, are often shaken by a kind of servile fear when they see someone, especially one of their just kinsmen or friends, horribly stricken, harassed or beaten: and the just man in his tribulation rebukes them because they do not fear God in prosperity as well, nor fear him as sons with a filial fear. [[6:22|Did I say: Bring to me, and give me of your substance?|Numquid dixi: Afferte mihi, et de substantia vestra donate mihi?]] The *substance* of the wicked is the name given to worldly and carnal prudence: the just man does not ask it of them, but scorns it, and does not deign to be consoled by it. [[6:23|Or deliver me from the hand of the enemy, and rescue me out of the hand of the mighty?|Liberate me de manu hostis, et de manu robustorum eruite me?]] The virtuous are attacked by enemies invisible and visible. Knowing the life of the wicked to be truly reprobate, they do not seek to be saved by their support from the temptation of the invisible enemy. And since they do not fear them that kill the body[[Matt 10:28||]], when faith or justice requires it they are ready to be killed by their visible enemies, and do not seek to be rescued from their tyranny.

paras.t: Docete me, et ego tacebo. Multoties carnales, pigri ac passionati putant et jactant se melius scire et sanius sapere, quam virtuosi ac fervidi: unde præsumunt eos arguere ac docere. Quibus justus vereque sapiens ironice zelo æquitatis respondet: Docete me. Quasi dicat: Aut vere me informate, aut ab insipienti instructione cessate.
paras.en: [[6:24|Teach me, and I will hold my peace|Docete me, et ego tacebo]]. Very often the carnal, the slothful and those ruled by passion think and boast that they know better and judge more soundly than the virtuous and fervent: and so they presume to reprove and teach them. To them the just and truly wise man answers ironically, with zeal for what is right: [[6:24|Teach me|Docete me]]. As if to say: Either truly instruct me, or leave off your foolish instruction.

paras.t: Quare detraxistis sermonibus veritatis? Tales equidem verba virtuosorum irrationabilia vanaque arbitrantur, quum dicat Apostolus: Animalis homo non percipit quæ sunt Spiritus Dei. Ideo detrahit verbis verissimis, asserens ea aut non vera, aut non recta intentione prolata. Et dum videt se ratione justum superare non posse, ad increpationes et exprobrationes convertitur, inaniterque verba multiplicat. Ideo sequitur: Ad increpandum tantum eloquia concinnatis, et in ventum verba profertis.
paras.en: [[6:25|Why have you detracted the words of truth|Quare detraxistis sermonibus veritatis?]]? Such men indeed judge the words of the virtuous to be unreasonable and empty, since, as the Apostle says, [[1 Cor 2:14|the sensual man perceiveth not these things that are of the Spirit of God|Animalis homo non percipit quæ sunt Spiritus Dei]] [the margin gives II Cor. ii, 14; the words are 1 Cor 2:14]. So he disparages the truest words, asserting that they are either untrue or not spoken with a right intention. And when he sees that he cannot overcome the just man by reason, he turns to rebukes and reproaches, and multiplies words to no purpose. Therefore there follows: [[6:26|You dress up speeches only to rebuke, and you utter words to the wind.|Ad increpandum tantum eloquia concinnatis, et in ventum verba profertis.]]

paras.t: Ceterum, quomodo sequentia textus verba ad moralitatem valeant applicari, ex præcedenti articulo facillime consideratur.
paras.en: For the rest, how the following words of the text can be applied to the moral sense is very easily seen from the preceding article.

7.title: Elucidatio litteralis capituli septimi.
7.title_en: Literal explanation of the seventh chapter

paras.t: Docet beatus Job in hujus capituli exordio, vitam præsentem ordinari ad aliam magis perfectam; eamque anxietatibus esse plenam, atque ob id rationabiliter appeti posse terminum ejus. Aliqui vero opinati sunt, ipsum Job principium præsentis capituli inducere ad reprobandum errorem Eliphaz, asserentis ultimam hominis felicitatem esse in vita hac, animam quoque rationalem esse mortalem. Verum (ut clare jam ante probatum est, et demum probabitur amplius) illa non fuit opinio Eliphaz: imo in verbis quarti capituli, quæ sibi perhibet desuper revelata, evidenter innuit animæ immortalitatem, atque futuram impiorum perpetuam calamitatem, inter cetera loquens: Et quia nullus intelligit, in æternum peribunt. Itaque verba hujus capituli Job inducit ad suæ declarationem sententiæ, qua intendit defendere, quod justis in vita hac multa contingant adversa sine eorum prævia culpa; quod item ad aliam et ipsam vere felicem vitam adspirent.
paras.en: Blessed Job teaches at the opening of this chapter that the present life is ordered to another, more perfect one; that it is full of anxieties, and that its end may therefore reasonably be longed for. Some, however, have thought that Job brings in the beginning of this chapter to refute the error of Eliphaz, who held that man's final happiness lies in this life, and also that the rational soul is mortal. But (as has already been clearly proved, and will be proved more fully later on) that was not the opinion of Eliphaz: indeed in the words of the fourth chapter, which he declares were revealed to him from above, he plainly hints at the immortality of the soul and at the everlasting calamity to come for the wicked, saying among other things: [[Job 4:20|and because no one understandeth, they shall perish for ever|Et quia nullus intelligit, in æternum peribunt]]. Job, then, brings in the words of this chapter to set out his own view, in which he means to defend this: that many adversities befall the just in this life without any previous fault of theirs; and also that they aspire to another life, one truly happy.

paras.t: Ait ergo: Militia est vita hominis super terram. Ubi Hieronymus transtulit, Militia, Septuaginta transtulerunt, Tentatio. Sed, ut docet S. Gregorius, sensus redit in idem. Tentatio namque est pugna contra hostes spiritusque malignos; militia vero exercitium contra adversarios appellatur. Itaque vita bonorum, militia tentatioque vocatur: quoniam contra desideria carnis passionesque animæ, contra mundi vanitates, contra dæmonum suggestiones, omnem quoque impietatem indesinenter ac fortiter præliantur. Unde ob gravitatem ac multitudinem tentationum hominis in hac via, vita ejus non tentationem habere, sed tentatio dicitur, quamvis nonnunquam sine actuali tentatione vivamus, et mente tranquilla Deo sine lucta vacemus. Sed in hoc parva est mora, nisi fortasse viris perfectis ex gratia singulari, qui revelata facie gloriam Domini speculantes, in deiformem transformantur imaginem a claritate in claritatem. Circa hoc verbum, sicut et circa cetera sancti Job verba, scribit multa pulchra illuminatus Gregorius: quæ vitandæ prolixitatis causa omitto, et quoniam scripta ejus (ut decet) ubique habentur. Præterea verbum inductum, ipsi Job tanto litteralius competit, quanto passus est duriora, fortioremque habuit contra invisibilem hostem luctam.
paras.en: He says, then: [[7:1|The life of man upon earth is a warfare|Militia est vita hominis super terram]]. Where Jerome translated *Militia* [warfare, military service], the Septuagint translated *Tentatio* [trial, temptation]. But, as St. Gregory teaches, the sense comes back to the same thing. For temptation is a fight against enemies and evil spirits, while warfare is the name for an exercise against adversaries. And so the life of the good is called warfare and temptation, because they battle unceasingly and bravely against the desires of the flesh and the passions of the soul, against the vanities of the world, against the suggestions of the demons, and against all ungodliness. Hence, because of the weight and number of man's temptations on this way, his life is said not to have temptation but to be temptation, although now and then we live without actual temptation and, with a tranquil mind, are free for God without struggle. But in this the respite is short, unless perhaps for men made perfect by a singular grace, who, [[2 Cor 3:18|beholding the glory of the Lord with open face|revelata facie gloriam Domini speculantes]], are transformed into a godlike image [[2 Cor 3:18|from glory to glory|a claritate in claritatem]]. On this saying, as on the other words of holy Job, the enlightened Gregory writes many beautiful things, which I leave out to avoid length, and because his writings (as is fitting) are to be had everywhere. Moreover, the saying brought in fits Job himself the more literally, the harsher the things he suffered and the stronger the struggle he had against the invisible enemy.

paras.t: Et sicut dies mercenarii dies ejus. Hoc primo ita exponitur: Quoniam vita hominis est militia super terram, propter continuum atque durissimum contra passiones ac vitia prælium; ideo dies ejus comparantur diebus mercenariorum, quorum dies sunt laboribus interdumque tædiis pleni. Ita et dies hominis viatoris graves et anxii sunt, præsertim tempora electorum, quoniam multæ tribulationes justorum. Nilque laboriosius exstat, quam mentem in vera puritate cordis Deo semper servare, Deum in nullo inhonorare, vanas cogitationes, inordinatas affectiones, viles occupationes, omissiones et commissiones iniquas vitare, abjicere, detestari. Secundo exponitur sic: Quemadmodum mercenarius finem dierum sui laboris desiderat, ut præmium assequatur; sic homo viator hujus optat finem exsilii ac laboris, ut ad æternam beatitudinem perducatur, prout ait Apostolus: Cupio dissolvi et esse cum Christo. Et Psalmista: Convertere, anima mea, in requiem tuam. Tertio sic: Quemadmodum mercenarius in alienis rebus seu aliorum bonis laborat, et sibi mercedem adipisci conatur; ita electi nunc in rebus occupantur divinis ac Christi negotiis, et tamen sibi ipsis præmium adipiscuntur.
paras.en: [[7:1|and his days are like the days of a hireling|Et sicut dies mercenarii dies ejus]]. This is explained, first, thus: since the life of man upon earth is a warfare, because of the continual and very hard battle against passions and vices, his days are therefore compared to the days of hirelings, whose days are full of labours and at times of weariness. So too the days of man the wayfarer [that is, man still on the way to his homeland, in this life] are heavy and anxious, above all the times of the elect, since [[Ps 33:20|Many are the afflictions of the just|multæ tribulationes justorum]]. And nothing is more laborious than always to keep the mind for God in true purity of heart, to dishonour God in nothing, and to shun, cast off and detest vain thoughts, disordered affections, base occupations, and wicked omissions and commissions. Secondly it is explained thus: as the hireling longs for the end of the days of his labour, so as to receive his wages, so man the wayfarer longs for the end of this exile and labour, so as to be brought to everlasting beatitude, as the Apostle says: [[Phil 1:23|having a desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ|Cupio dissolvi et esse cum Christo]] [Denis has *Cupio*, "I desire", for the Vulgate's *desiderium habens*]. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 114:7|Turn, O my soul, into thy rest|Convertere, anima mea, in requiem tuam]]. Thirdly thus: as the hireling labours on another's things, or on others' goods, and strives to win wages for himself, so the elect are now busied with divine things and the affairs of Christ, and yet gain a reward for themselves.

paras.t: Denique, quoniam duo homini in vita ista incumbunt, videlicet impedimentis suæ salutis resistere, et suæ beatitudinis accommoda operari: ideo, quantum ad primum, comparat vitam humanam militi, cujus est hostibus pacis occurrere; quantum vero ad secundum, diebus mercenarii, cujus est utilia suæ mercedis peragere. Insuper, ex his declaratur vita humana providentiæ subesse divinæ: quia et milites sub duce exercitus militant, ejusque directione aguntur; mercenarii quoque a domino operis inducuntur, ac præmium præstolantur. Rursus, ex his error Eliphaz reprobatur, dicentis tribulationes et pœnas non nisi pro peccatis infligi, nec adversitates majores nisi pro gravioribus culpis. Dux namque exercitus frequenter melioribus magisque strenuis militibus graviora luctamina atque pericula sapienter injungit, secundum quod pro communi expedit bono, ut expleto labore, eos amplius veneretur. Similiter paterfamilias interdum melioribus operariis graviores committit labores: quibus, opere consummato, præmia largitur majora. Itaque superaltissimus omnium princeps Deus, sanctus ac sapiens, suos pugnatores electos ac milites meliores, frequenter adversitatibus exponit majoribus, efficacioresque operarios fortioribus laboribus applicat, ut in fine, adepto triumpho ac Dei obsequio consummato, sublimius honorentur, abundantiusque munerentur in cœlo.
paras.en: Lastly, since two things are laid upon man in this life, namely to resist what hinders his salvation and to work what serves his beatitude: therefore, as to the first, he compares human life to a soldier, whose task is to meet the enemies of peace; and as to the second, to the days of a hireling, whose task is to carry out what is useful for his wages. Further, these words show that human life is subject to divine providence: for soldiers serve under the leader of the army and are moved by his direction, and hirelings too are brought in by the master of the work and wait for their reward. Again, these words refute the error of Eliphaz, who said that tribulations and punishments are inflicted only for sins, and greater adversities only for graver faults. For the leader of an army often wisely lays heavier struggles and dangers on the better and more vigorous soldiers, as is expedient for the common good, so that when the labour is over he may honour them the more. Likewise a householder sometimes gives the heavier labours to the better workmen, and when the work is finished bestows greater rewards on them. So God, the most high Prince of all, holy and wise, often exposes His chosen fighters and better soldiers to greater adversities, and sets the more effective workmen to harder labours, so that in the end, the triumph won and the service of God fulfilled, they may be honoured more highly and rewarded more abundantly in heaven.

paras.t: Deinde beatus Job adducit similitudines ad prædicta. Exempla enim in moralibus quo particulariora ac planiora exstiterint, eo plus instruunt. Moralia quippe circa particularia versantur, quum agere et pati sint suppositorum, secundum Philosophum. Sicut cervus æstu afflictus desiderat umbram, id est locum refrigerativum, quo post laborem et cursum quiescat, sicut et cervus a venantibus agitatus, festinat ad aquæ fluenta, secundum illud Psalmi: Quemadmodum desiderat cervus ad fontes aquarum; et sicut mercenarius præstolatur finem operis sui, id est moram qua suum obsequium compleat, ut sortiatur mercedem; sic et ego habui menses vacuos, id est, menses annorum quibus vixi, sine consecutione optatæ felicitatis expendi, et affectuose semper ad veram felicitatem futuram, tanquam ad præmium consummatum mentaliter acceleravi; et noctes laboriosas enumeravi mihi, id est, noctes vitæ meæ reputavi, et quasi diu durantes computavi laboribus plenas. Virtuosi enim in noctibus solent meditationibus insudare, futura pensare, pœnitentiæ lamentis insistere, juxta quod scriptum est: Anticipaverunt vigilias oculi mei; turbatus sum, et non sum locutus. Cogitavi dies antiquos, et annos æternos in mente habui: et meditatus sum nocte cum corde meo. Et iterum: Laboravi in gemitu meo, lavabo per singulas noctes lectum meum. Itemque: Consurge, lauda in nocte, in principio vigiliarum, et effunde sicut aquam cor tuum ante conspectum Domini Dei tui. Constat quoque quod homines frequenter numerent tempus, quod eis diu durare videtur atque molestum est. Iterum, noctes hujusmodi laboriosæ dicuntur, propter optati boni dilationis difficultatem. Laboriosum etenim esse solet, diu exspectare bonum vehementer cupitum, juxta illud Proverbiorum: Spes quæ differtur, affligit animam; lignum vitæ, desiderium veniens.
paras.en: Then blessed Job brings in likenesses for what he has said. For in moral matters, the more particular and plain the examples are, the more they instruct; for moral matters are concerned with particulars, since acting and being acted upon belong to individual subjects [*supposita*, that is, concrete individual beings], according to the Philosopher. As a hart [Denis reads *cervus*, "hart", where the Vulgate has *servus*, "servant", which the Douay-Rheims follows; an unread note in the margin is probably about this], afflicted by the heat, [[7:2|longeth for the shade|desiderat umbram]], that is, a cooling place where it may rest after toil and running, as the hart too, driven by the hunters, hastens to the streams of water, according to that of the Psalm: [[Ps 41:2|As the hart panteth after the fountains of water|Quemadmodum desiderat cervus ad fontes aquarum]]; [[7:2|as the hireling looketh for the end of his work|et sicut mercenarius præstolatur finem operis sui]], that is, the time in which he may complete his service so as to receive his wages; [[7:3|So I also have had empty months|sic et ego habui menses vacuos]], that is, the months of the years I have lived I have spent without attaining the happiness I longed for, and with longing I have ever hastened in mind towards the true happiness to come, as to a reward made complete; [[7:3|and have numbered to myself wearisome nights|et noctes laboriosas enumeravi mihi]], that is, I have reckoned up the nights of my life, and counted them as lasting long and full of labours. For the virtuous are wont in the nights to toil at meditation, to ponder the things to come, to persevere in the laments of penance, according to what is written: [[Ps 76:5|My eyes prevented the watches: I was troubled, and I spoke not|Anticipaverunt vigilias oculi mei; turbatus sum, et non sum locutus]]. [[Ps 76:6|I thought upon the days of old: and I had in my mind the eternal years|Cogitavi dies antiquos, et annos æternos in mente habui]]: [[Ps 76:7|And I meditated in the night with my own heart|et meditatus sum nocte cum corde meo]]. And again: [[Ps 6:7|I have laboured in my groanings, every night I will wash my bed|Laboravi in gemitu meo, lavabo per singulas noctes lectum meum]]. And likewise: [[Lam 2:19|Arise, give praise in the night, in the beginning of the watches: pour out thy heart like water, before the face of the Lord|Consurge, lauda in nocte, in principio vigiliarum, et effunde sicut aquam cor tuum ante conspectum Domini Dei tui]] thy God. It is plain too that men often count up a time that seems to them to last long and is irksome. Again, such nights are called wearisome because of the hardship of having the good one longs for put off. For it is usually wearisome to wait long for a good that one vehemently desires, according to that of the Proverbs: [[Prov 13:12|Hope that is deferred afflicteth the soul: desire when it cometh, is a tree of life|Spes quæ differtur, affligit animam; lignum vitæ, desiderium veniens]].

paras.t: Si dormiero, id est, me ad dormiendum posuero, aut parum quievero, dicam, expergefactus, seu præ dolore ac tædio dormire non valens: Quando consurgam? id est, diei adventum optabo. Qui enim in tristitia atque doloribus est, ad futurum tempus anhelat, in quo se melius habiturum confidit. Et rursum exspectabo vesperam, id est, orto jam die, noctem fieri præstolabor et cupiam. Dolor namque ea quæ adsunt, non permittit placere, optaturque tempus afflictionis finiri. Et replebor doloribus usque ad tenebras noctis, id est, tota die pœnis afficiar. Cujus causam adjecit: Induta est caro mea putredine et sordibus pulveris, id est, materia et sanie ulcerosa, immunditiisque loci quo sedeo, scilicet sterquilinii, corpus meum circumdatur, impletur ac tegitur, sicut quis veste operitur. Vel, Sordibus pulveris, id est pulverulentis. Sanies enim indurata, scabiem facit: quæ arefacta, in pulverem recidit. Cutis mea aruit et contracta est, id est rugosa effecta ex siccitate. Naturali quippe humore consumpto, et virtute naturali deficiente, caro intus consumitur, forisque siccatur atque rugatur: qui defectus contingit ex senectute, aut infirmitate, vel fame. Unde in Threnis de confectis esurie scribitur: Adhæsit cutis eorum ossibus eorum; facta est quasi lignum.
paras.en: [[7:4|If I lie down to sleep|Si dormiero]], that is, if I lay myself down to sleep, or rest a little, [[7:4|I shall say|dicam]], on waking, or being unable to sleep for pain and weariness: [[7:4|When shall I rise?|Quando consurgam?]] that is, I shall long for the coming of the day. For one who is in sadness and pains yearns for a time to come in which he trusts he will be better. [[7:4|and again, I shall look for the evening|Et rursum exspectabo vesperam]], that is, when the day has already dawned, I shall wait and long for night to come. For pain does not let what is present please, and one longs for the time of affliction to be ended. [[7:4|and shall be filled with sorrows even till darkness|Et replebor doloribus usque ad tenebras]] of night, that is, I shall be afflicted with pains the whole day. And he added the cause of it: [[7:5|My flesh is clothed with rottenness and the filth of dust|Induta est caro mea putredine et sordibus pulveris]], that is, my body is surrounded, filled and covered, as one is covered with a garment, with the matter and the pus of the ulcers, and with the filth of the place where I sit, namely the dunghill. Or, [[7:5|the filth of dust|Sordibus pulveris]], that is, with dusty filth: for pus that has hardened makes a scab, which, when it dries, falls away into dust. [[7:5|my skin is withered and drawn together|Cutis mea aruit et contracta est]], that is, made wrinkled from dryness. For when the natural moisture is used up and the natural strength fails, the flesh is consumed within and dried and wrinkled without: a defect that comes from old age, or sickness, or hunger. Hence in Lamentations it is written of those wasted by hunger: [[Lam 4:8|their skin hath stuck to their bones|Adhæsit cutis eorum ossibus eorum]]; it [[Lam 4:8|is become like wood|facta est quasi lignum]].

paras.t: Dies mei velocius transierunt, quam a texente tela succiditur, id est, tempora quibus vixi, celerrime defluxerunt. Nil enim tam cito decurrit ut tempus, in quo nulla est mora, quies aut fixio, sed defluxus continuus. Sic et Ezechias profatur: Præcisa est velut a texente vita mea. Et Psalmista: Dies mei sicut umbra declinaverunt, et ego sicut fœnum arui. Quamvis autem tempus dum præsens est, longum appareat propter adversa quibus homo afficitur, nihilominus quum fuerit evolutum, ratio intuetur quam breve exstiterit. Et consumpti sunt absque ulla spe, recuperandi tempus præteritum: quod quum fuerit lapsum, idem nequaquam revertitur. Vel, Absque spe, redeundi ad pristinos dies, seu vitam in terra agendam post mortem. Fuit autem Platonis opinio, quod post certa tempora, corrupta in inferioribus istis eodem numero reverterentur; quem errorem sanctus Job pluribus reprobat locis.
paras.en: [[7:6|My days have passed more swiftly than the web is cut by the weaver|Dies mei velocius transierunt, quam a texente tela succiditur]], that is, the times in which I have lived have flowed away most swiftly. For nothing runs on so quickly as time, in which there is no delay, rest or fixity, but a continual flowing away. So too Ezechias declares: [[Is 38:12|My life is cut off, as by a weaver|Præcisa est velut a texente vita mea]]. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 101:12|My days have declined like a shadow, and I am withered like grass|Dies mei sicut umbra declinaverunt, et ego sicut fœnum arui]]. And although time, while it is present, seems long because of the adversities with which a man is afflicted, nevertheless once it has rolled by, reason sees how short it was. [[7:6|and are consumed without any hope|Et consumpti sunt absque ulla spe]] of recovering the time past: for once it has slipped away, the same time never returns. Or, [[7:6|without any hope|Absque spe]] of returning to my former days, that is, to a life to be led on earth after death. Now it was Plato's opinion that after certain periods of time the things corrupted here below would return the same in number [that is, the very same individual things, not merely things of the same kind]; an error which holy Job refutes in several places.

paras.t: Deinde Deum alloquitur: Memento quia ventus est vita mea, id est, duratio temporis qua hic vivo, conformis est vento ob nimiam utriusque fluxibilitatem ac labilitatem et brevitatem; itemque, quoniam sicut ventus idem non redit, ita vita hominis post mortem ad istum non revertitur statum. Hinc scriptum est: Quæ est vita vestra? Vapor est ad modicum parens, deinceps exterminabitur. Et: Omnes morimur, et quasi aquæ dilabimur in terram, quæ non revertuntur. Orat autem ut Deus horum sit memor, non quod in Deo cadat oblivio aut recens memoratio, sed quoniam instar obliviscentis se habet, dum quemquam juste relinquit, aut in æternum condemnat, aut peccatis ignoscit. Dum vero aliquem misericorditer juvat, gratiam tribuit, beatitudinemve largitur, per modum recordantis se habet. Sicque oramus, ut Deus nostræ fragilitatis ac labilitatis meminerit, id est, illas intuendo, pronus sit ad parcendum ac succurrendum, quemadmodum ait Psalmographus: Recordatus est quoniam pulvis sumus; homo sicut fœnum dies ejus, tanquam flos agri sic efflorebit. Et non revertetur oculus meus ut videat bona, id est, ad videnda hujus vitæ bona non redibit post mortem. Nec adspiciet me visus hominis, id est, ab aliis in hoc statu, loco ac sæculo amplius non videbor, quia post mortem huc amplius non revertar. Quibus consonat illud in Isaia: Non adspiciam hominem ultra, et habitatorem quietis: quæ sunt verba Ezechiæ. Sed quum Job post plagam hanc sit ad sanitatem, longamque et prosperam vitam reductus, quomodo protulit verba hæc absque mendacio? Et respondendum, quod naturaliter sanandus non fuit, vel protinus moriturum se æstimavit, vel verba sua retulit ad tempus post mortem suam futurum, sicut expositum est. Oculi tui in me, id est, ab oculis sapientiæ et scientiæ tuæ, o Deus, nusquam nec vivus nec defunctus abscondar, juxta illud Proverbiorum: Respicit Dominus viam hominis, et omnes gressus illius considerat. Alibi quoque ait Scriptura: In omni loco oculi Domini contemplantur bonos et malos. Et non subsistam diu in vita præsenti. Vel, Non subsistam, quia vita præsens instabilis est. Iterum, Non subsistam, id est, coram tua justitia stare non potero, si secundum rigorem ejus sine admixtione clementiæ examinatus judicatusque fuero.
paras.en: Then he addresses God: [[7:7|Remember that my life is but wind|Memento quia ventus est vita mea]], that is, the length of time for which I live here is like the wind, because of the great fluidity, slipperiness and shortness of both; and also because, as the wind does not come back the same, so the life of man after death does not return to this state. Hence it is written: [[Jas 4:15|what is your life? It is a vapour which appeareth for a little while and afterwards shall vanish away|Quæ est vita vestra? Vapor est ad modicum parens, deinceps exterminabitur]]. And: [[2 Kings 14:14|We all die, and like waters that return no more, we fall down into the earth|Omnes morimur, et quasi aquæ dilabimur in terram, quæ non revertuntur]]. Now he prays that God may be mindful of these things, not that forgetting or a fresh remembering can befall God, but because He behaves like one who forgets when He justly abandons someone, or condemns him for ever, or pardons sins; while when He mercifully helps someone, gives grace, or bestows beatitude, He behaves in the manner of one who remembers. And so we pray that God may remember our frailty and our proneness to fall, that is, that in looking upon them He may be inclined to spare and to help, as the Psalmist says: [[Ps 102:14|He remembereth that we are dust|Recordatus est quoniam pulvis sumus]]; [[Ps 102:15|Man's days are as grass, as the flower of the field so shall he flourish|homo sicut fœnum dies ejus, tanquam flos agri sic efflorebit]]. [[7:7|and my eye shall not return to see good things|Et non revertetur oculus meus ut videat bona]], that is, it will not come back after death to see the good things of this life. [[7:8|Nor shall the sight of man behold me|Nec adspiciet me visus hominis]], that is, I shall no more be seen by others in this state, place and world, because after death I shall not return here any more. With which agrees that in Isaias: [[Is 38:11|I shall behold man no more, nor the inhabitant of rest|Non adspiciam hominem ultra, et habitatorem quietis]], which are the words of Ezechias. But since Job after this stroke was brought back to health and to a long and prosperous life, how did he utter these words without lying? The answer must be that he was not to be healed by natural means; or he thought he would soon die; or he referred his words to the time that would follow his death, as has been explained. [[7:8|thy eyes are upon me|Oculi tui in me]], that is, from the eyes of thy wisdom and knowledge, O God, I shall nowhere be hidden, neither living nor dead, according to that of the Proverbs: [[Prov 5:21|The Lord beholdeth the ways of man, and considereth all his steps|Respicit Dominus viam hominis, et omnes gressus illius considerat]]. Scripture also says elsewhere: [[Prov 15:3|The eyes of the Lord in every place behold the good and the evil|In omni loco oculi Domini contemplantur bonos et malos]]. [[7:8|and I shall be no more|Et non subsistam]] [literally "and I shall not subsist", that is, not stand or last], long in the present life. Or, [[7:8|I shall be no more|Non subsistam]] because the present life is unstable. Again, [[7:8|I shall be no more|Non subsistam]], that is, I shall not be able to stand before thy justice, if I am examined and judged according to its rigour without any admixture of mercy.

paras.t: Sicut consumitur nubes et pertransit. Nubes enim ad altiora suspenditur: densata autem impellitur vento ad discurrendum, et solis calore dissolvitur ac dissipatur, ita quod evanescit, nec eadem numero ultra revertitur. Sic qui descendit ad inferos, id est defunctus, quoad animam, ad aliquem locum inferni descendens: ad quem ante Christi passionem omnes descenderunt, videlicet prout inferi nomine etiam limbus patrum et puerorum, ac purgatorium intelliguntur; quantum vero ad corpus, ad loca sepulcrorum sub terra; non ascendet, id est, ad vitam sæculi hujus et ad statum mortalem non revertetur naturaliter utique, quamvis miraculose fieri possit, sæpeque factum sit. Nec revertetur ultra in domum suam, id est ad pristinas opes ac mansiones; neque cognoscet eum amplius locus ejus, id est, in priori vitæ hujus loco non erit, nec cognoscetur ibidem, nec conspicietur. Dicitur autem locus cognoscere, vel quia confert ad habendam rei cognitionem; vel eo modo, quo tempus dicitur ea facere quæ fiunt in tempore.
paras.en: [[7:9|As a cloud is consumed, and passeth away|Sicut consumitur nubes et pertransit]]. For a cloud is held up on high; but once it has thickened it is driven by the wind to run hither and thither, and is dissolved and scattered by the heat of the sun, so that it vanishes and never comes back again the same in number. [[7:9|so he that shall go down to hell|Sic qui descendit ad inferos]], that is, the dead man, going down as to the soul to some place of hell, to which all went down before the passion of Christ, taking the name of hell [*inferi*, the lower regions] to cover also the limbo of the fathers and of children, and purgatory; and as to the body, to the places of the graves beneath the earth; [[7:9|shall not come up|non ascendet]], that is, he will not return to the life of this world and to the mortal state, naturally at least, though it can be done by miracle, and often has been. [[7:10|Nor shall he return any more into his house|Nec revertetur ultra in domum suam]], that is, to his former wealth and dwellings; [[7:10|neither shall his place know him any more|neque cognoscet eum amplius locus ejus]], that is, he will not be in the former place of this life, nor be known there, nor seen. Now a place is said to know either because it helps one to have knowledge of a thing, or in the way that time is said to do the things that are done in time.

paras.t: His verbis excludit Job errorem ponentium circulationem generationum in inferioribus. Quemadmodum enim in libris de Trinitate et Civitate Dei recitat Augustinus, Platonis opinio fuit, quod post certa annorum curricula omnia ista inferiora ad pristinum statum redirent, ita quod idem Plato in eadem urbe Atheniensi eisdem discipulis esset lecturus, qui olim ibi legerat eis. Quorum ratio una fuit, quoniam inferiora disponuntur secundum cœlestium corporum motum. Unde eadem constellatione et influentia post plurima tempora redeunte, ponebant, eamdem rem numero reparari atque ad pristinum statum reverti. Ad quod etiam quidam hæretici, errorem illum partim sequentes (ut Origenes, qui circa hoc gravissime invenitur errasse in libro Periarchon et alibi, prout S. Hieronymus in suis epistolis protestatur), allegabant illud Ecclesiastæ: Quid est quod fuit? ipsum quod futurum est. Quid est quod factum est? ipsum quod faciendum est. Nihil sub sole novum, nec valet aliquis dicere, Ecce hoc recens est. Jam enim præcessit in sæculis quæ fuerunt ante nos. Verum, ut Augustinus exponit, verba hic Salomonis intelligenda sunt non de eisdem numero, sed specie. Hoc quoque Aristoteles secundo de Generatione, docet et probat, scilicet in circulatione cœlestium corporum idem numero redit, videlicet idem sol, quia in illis per motum non corrumpitur, sed quoad situm solum variatur substantia. In motu autem et circulatione inferiorum, seu generabilium et corruptibilium, non redit idem numero post occasum, sed specie, quia res ipsa corrumpitur. Sicque sententia sancti Job consonat fidei christianæ et Peripateticorum philosophiæ.
paras.en: With these words Job excludes the error of those who hold a cycle of generations in the things here below. For as Augustine relates in the books On the Trinity and The City of God, it was Plato's opinion that after certain courses of years all these lower things would return to their former state, so that the same Plato would lecture in the same city of Athens to the same disciples to whom he had once lectured there. One reason they gave was that lower things are disposed according to the motion of the heavenly bodies; hence, when the same constellation and influence came round again after very many ages, they held that the same thing in number would be restored and return to its former state. In support of this some heretics too, partly following that error (such as Origen, who is found to have erred most gravely on this point in the book Periarchon [that is, *Peri Archon*, On First Principles] and elsewhere, as St. Jerome declares in his letters), alleged that saying of Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 1:9|What is it that hath been? the same thing that shall be. What is it that hath been done? the same that shall be done|Quid est quod fuit? ipsum quod futurum est. Quid est quod factum est? ipsum quod faciendum est]]. [[Eccles 1:10|Nothing under the sun is new, neither is any man able to say: Behold this is new: for it hath already gone before in the ages that were before us|Nihil sub sole novum, nec valet aliquis dicere, Ecce hoc recens est. Jam enim præcessit in sæculis quæ fuerunt ante nos]]. But, as Augustine explains, these words of Solomon are to be understood not of the same things in number, but in kind. Aristotle too teaches and proves this in the second book On Generation: namely that in the revolution of the heavenly bodies the same thing in number comes back, for instance the same sun, because in them nothing is corrupted by motion, but the substance varies only as to position; whereas in the motion and cycle of lower things, that is, of things that can be generated and corrupted, the same thing in number does not come back after its passing away, but only the same in kind, because the thing itself is corrupted. And so the view of holy Job agrees with the Christian faith and with the philosophy of the Peripatetics.

paras.t: Quapropter, id est, quia veritas ita se habet circa vitam humanam, ut dixi, et ego non parcam ori meo, id est, a labore seu actu loquendi ipsum non supportabo: et confisus de ipsa veritatis firmitate, non contracto ore loquar vera quæ restant. Bona namque conscientia et vera sententia præstant fiduciam. Ideo tertio Esdræ libro habetur: Super omnia vincit veritas. Et rursus: Veritas invalescit in æternum, et vivit et manet in sæcula sæculorum. Loquar in tribulatione spiritus mei, ita quod ipsa tribulatio instigabit me ad loquendum, atque ex ea sumam loquendi materiam: confabulabor cum amaritudine animæ meæ, id est, causam ipsius inquiram, et (sicut est moris amaricatis) per modum querelæ de ea tractabo. Ipsamque in secreto affabor, considerando qualitatem ipsius.
paras.en: [[7:11|Wherefore|Quapropter]], that is, because the truth stands thus concerning human life, as I have said, [[7:11|I will not spare my mouth|et ego non parcam ori meo]], that is, I will not spare it the labour or act of speaking; and trusting in the very firmness of the truth, I will speak with no tight-shut mouth the true things that remain. For a good conscience and a true judgement give confidence. Hence it is found in the third book of Esdras: Truth conquereth above all things. And again: Truth groweth strong for ever, and liveth and abideth for ever and ever [3 Esdras 3:12 and 4:38 (the margin is unreadable here); this book, printed after the Vulgate among the apocrypha, is not in the Douay-Rheims, so the words are given in a plain translation]. [[7:11|I will speak in the affliction of my spirit|Loquar in tribulatione spiritus mei]], so that the affliction itself will spur me on to speak, and from it I shall take matter for speaking; [[7:11|I will talk with the bitterness of my soul|confabulabor cum amaritudine animæ meæ]], that is, I shall inquire into its cause and (as is the way of the embittered) treat of it by way of complaint. And I shall speak with it in secret, considering what kind of thing it is.

paras.t: Deinde alloquitur Deum. Numquid mare ego sum, aut cetus, quia circumdedisti me carcere? Hoc multipliciter explanatur. Primo sic: Numquid tantæ sum fortitudinis sicut Oceanus, et cetus, qui est maximus piscis, quia implesti me maxima afflictione, ita ut instar incarceratorum non habeam consolationem aut exeundi facultatem? quasi dicat, Supra vires et modum gravasti me: eo modo quo ait Apostolus, Supra modum gravati sumus. Non quod electos permittat Deus tentari absolute supra quod ferre possunt; sed quia supra communem modum aliquando premuntur, et amplius quam propriis viribus possint. Estque in talibus verbis quodammodo hyperbolicus sermo, ad exprimendum lucidius magnitudinem rei. Secundo exponitur ab Alberto sic: Duo imponebantur beato Job. Primo, quod inquietudine avaritiæ suos semper terminos dilataret, quemadmodum mare, quod effluens operit alia, et refluens attrahit multa. De hoc excusat se, dicens: Numquid mare ego sum? quasi dicat, Non. Secundo, quod subjectos devoraret atque opprimeret. Quod excusans, adjecit: Aut cetus? Nihilo minus sum percussus, quia circumdedisti me carcere.
paras.en: Then he addresses God: [[7:12|Am I a sea, or a whale, that thou hast enclosed me in a prison|Numquid mare ego sum, aut cetus, quia circumdedisti me carcere]]? This is explained in several ways. First thus: Am I of such strength as the Ocean, and as the whale, which is the greatest of fishes, that thou hast filled me with the greatest affliction, so that, like men shut in prison, I have no consolation and no means of getting out? As if to say: Thou hast weighed me down beyond my strength and beyond measure; in the way that the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 1:8|we were pressed out of measure|Supra modum gravati sumus]] [the margin's note here is unread; it is evidently 2 Cor. i, 8, given again below]. Not that God allows the elect to be tempted absolutely beyond what they can bear, but that they are sometimes pressed beyond the common measure, and more than they could bear by their own strength. And in such words there is in a manner a hyperbolic speech, to express the greatness of the thing more clearly. Secondly, it is explained by Albert thus: Two things were laid to the charge of blessed Job. First, that through the restlessness of avarice he was ever widening his bounds, like the sea, which flowing out covers other things, and ebbing draws many things back with it. Of this he clears himself, saying: [[7:12|Am I a sea|Numquid mare ego sum]]? as if to say, No. Second, that he devoured and oppressed those under him. Clearing himself of this, he added: [[7:12|or a whale|Aut cetus]]? Nevertheless I am stricken, [[7:12|that thou hast enclosed me in a prison|quia circumdedisti me carcere]].

paras.t: Tertio Thomas exponit, dicendo: Circa creaturas irrationales, quibus non competit meritum aut demeritum, operatur divina providentia, secundum quod competit bono universi. Hinc mare coercet, ne totam terram operiat, ut animalibus et terræ nascentibus remaneat locus; similiter cetum intra Oceanum mare coercet, ne si in alia maria deduceretur, noceret hominibus. Ideo inquirit Job, an simili causa afflictus sit, utpote non ob suum demeritum, sed ob aliquam utilitatem ex sua percussione aliis provenientem; vel, ut ne aliis esset nocivus, si non esset plagatus. Et constat, quod non ideo sit percussus, ne si prosperaretur, aliis adversaretur, quia nec in pristina prosperitate hoc fecit. Una vero suæ percussionis causa fuit, communis utilitas inde proveniens, hoc est ædificatio omnium nostrum, ad patientiam jugiter conservandam.
paras.en: Thirdly, Thomas explains it, saying: With irrational creatures, to which merit and demerit do not belong, divine providence works according as it befits the good of the universe. Hence it holds in the sea, lest it cover the whole earth, so that room may be left for the animals and for the things that grow from the earth; likewise it holds in the whale within the Ocean sea, lest, if it were brought into other seas, it should do harm to men. Job therefore asks whether he has been afflicted for a like cause: that is, not for his own demerit, but for some benefit that would come to others from his being stricken; or else so that he should not be harmful to others, as he would be if he were not smitten. And it is plain that he was not stricken lest, if he prospered, he should be against others, since he did not do this even in his former prosperity. But one cause of his being stricken was the common benefit that comes from it, that is, the edification of us all, for keeping patience at all times.

paras.t: Insuper, ostendit se circumdatum carcere, id est omni privatum solatio. Si dixero, Consolabitur me lectulus meus, id est somnus qui solet esse in lecto. Somnus enim, quemadmodum balneum ac alia quædam, est relevativus tristitiæ, quemadmodum Augustinus asserit se expertum. Somnus quippe et balneum corporalem naturam tristitia deordinatam, ad naturalem statum reformant, ad convenientem quoque processum vitales motus cordis reducunt. Et relevabor loquens mecum in stratu meo: id est, si dixero me habiturum tristitiæ meæ aliquod relevamen ex meditatione seu secreta ad me ipsum locutione in lecto hora quietis, quando anima ad meditandum est aptior, exterioribus sensibus ab actibus suis vacantibus, quietatoque exteriori tumultu atque obstaculo contemplationis. Ipsa equidem meditatio speculativa seu contemplatio, vel sagax ad se ipsum locutio, tristitiam maxime aufert, quia naturaliter delectabilis est veritatis cognitio.
paras.en: Moreover, he shows that he is enclosed in a prison[[7:12||]], that is, deprived of all solace. [[7:13|If I say: My bed shall comfort me|Si dixero, Consolabitur me lectulus meus]], that is, sleep, which is usually had in bed. For sleep, like a bath and certain other things, relieves sorrow, as Augustine declares he found by experience. For sleep and a bath restore to its natural state the bodily nature put out of order by sorrow, and bring the vital motions of the heart back to their proper course. [[7:13|and I shall be relieved, speaking with myself on my couch|Et relevabor loquens mecum in stratu meo]]: that is, if I say that I shall have some relief of my sorrow from meditation, or from speaking secretly to myself in bed at the hour of rest, when the soul is fitter for meditating, the outward senses being free from their acts, and the outward tumult and hindrance to contemplation being stilled. For speculative meditation itself, or contemplation, or a shrewd speaking to oneself, takes away sorrow above all, since the knowledge of truth is naturally delightful.

paras.t: Terrebis me, vel effective, vel permissive, per somnia, quæ dormienti apparent; et per visiones, quæ vigilanti ac exterioribus sensibus alienato apparere solent, horrore concuties. Somnia enim similia esse solent præcedentibus cogitationibus in vigilia habitis. Quoniam ergo Job in vigilia, quæ mortis et tristitiæ sunt cogitabat, similibus phantasmatibus inquietabatur in somno. Satan quoque a Deo permissus, movebat (ut creditur) phantasiam beati Job, immittens ei terribilia afflictivaque somnia: sed et infirmitas corporalis cooperatur ad hoc, ut perturbata phantasmata dormienti appareant. Circa quod dicit Albertus: Infirmitas cujus causa intus est, non sinit somniare nisi terribilia, sicut in medicina dicitur, quod in quo collectio apostematis calidi generatur, somniat se flammis succendi; et in quo colligitur hydrops frigidus, somniat se glacie congelari.
paras.en: [[7:14|Thou wilt frighten me|Terrebis me]], either by doing it or by allowing it, [[7:14|with dreams|per somnia]], which appear to one asleep; [[7:14|with visions|et per visiones]], which usually appear to one awake but withdrawn from the outward senses, [[7:14|and terrify me|horrore concuties]]. For dreams are usually like the thoughts one had before while awake. Since, then, Job when awake was thinking of things of death and sorrow, he was troubled in sleep by phantasms of the same kind. Satan too, by God's leave, stirred (as is believed) the imagination of blessed Job, sending him terrible and distressing dreams; and bodily sickness also works to this end, that disordered phantasms appear to the sleeper. On this Albert says: A sickness whose cause is within lets one dream nothing but terrible things; as it is said in medicine that one in whom a gathering of a hot abscess is forming dreams that he is set on fire with flames, and one in whom a cold dropsy is gathering dreams that he is frozen with ice.

paras.t: Quamobrem, id est, quoniam tot pœnis afficior, omnique consolatione destituor, elegit suspendium anima mea, id est suspensionem influxionis, qua corpori influit vitam. Ab actu namque et officio suspenditur anima, dum corpori vitam non influit, secundum Albertum. Itaque anima ejus desideravit a corpore separari. Thomas exponit de corporali suspendio, ita quod desideravit mortem quantumcumque abjectam et vilem, qua vitam tam pœnosam miseramque finiret. Quod etiam secundum deliberatam rationem se optasse designans, adjecit, et mortem, scilicet corporalem, elegerunt ossa mea, id est quæ robustiora in me sunt, ut sunt actus intellectus ac voluntatis: robustiora quippe per ossa significantur. Quomodo autem istud licuerit, dictum est supra. Sancti enim aliquando mortem optaverunt ut terminum tribulationis præsentis, et ut ingressum vitæ melioris sequentis, non penitus absolute, sed quantum in ipsis fuit, et dummodo Deo placeret, a quo etiam petierunt tolli a vita hac. De hoc dictum est planius atque completius.
paras.en: [[7:15|So that|Quamobrem]], that is, since I am afflicted with so many pains and bereft of all consolation, [[7:15|my soul rather chooseth hanging|elegit suspendium anima mea]] [*suspendium*, "hanging", also means a suspending], that is, the suspending of the inflowing by which it pours life into the body. For the soul is suspended from its act and office when it does not pour life into the body, according to Albert. And so his soul desired to be parted from the body. Thomas explains it of bodily hanging, meaning that he desired death, however abject and vile, by which to end a life so painful and wretched. And showing that he wished this also with deliberate reason, he added: and [[7:15|death|et mortem]], that is, bodily death, [[7:15|my bones|ossa mea]] have chosen [Denis adds *elegerunt*, "have chosen"], that is, the stronger things in me, such as the acts of the intellect and will: for the stronger things are signified by the bones. How this was lawful has been said above [the margin: Art. XI, towards the end]. For the saints have sometimes wished for death as the end of present tribulation and as the entrance into the better life that follows; not wholly absolutely, but as far as in them lay, and provided it pleased God, of whom they even asked to be taken from this life. Of this it has been said more plainly and more fully.

paras.t: Desperavi: non de misericordia Dei et animæ meæ salute, sed, Desperavi, id est, ex causis naturalibus spem convalescendi non habeo. Ideo subditur, nequaquam ultra jam vivam, id est, diu in vita hac naturaliter non durabo. Vel, Non vivam ultra, id est, ad vitam istam mortalem ac animalem post mortem nequaquam redibo.
paras.en: [[7:16|I have done with hope|Desperavi]]: not of the mercy of God and the salvation of my soul; but, [[7:16|I have done with hope|Desperavi]], that is, from natural causes I have no hope of recovering. Therefore it is added: [[7:16|I shall now live no longer|nequaquam ultra jam vivam]], that is, I shall not last long in this life by nature. Or: [[7:16|I shall now live no longer|Non vivam ultra]], that is, after death I shall by no means return to this mortal and animal life.

paras.t: Porro, quod non simpliciter desperaverit, innuit addens: Parce mihi, vel corpus meum sanando, vel ab eo meam animam separando. Sic et Tobias oravit: Fac mecum misericordiam, et præcipe in pace recipi spiritum meum. Et quia ad promerendam Dei clementiam confert potissime humilis propriæ vilitatis ac parvitatis cognitio, subdit, Nihil enim sunt dies mei, id est nihilo comparandi, præsertim respectu æternitatis sequentis, cujus comparatione omne tempus est quasi momentum: et nulla est comparatio finiti ad infinitum. Unde primo Paralipomenon habetur: Dies nostri quasi umbra super terram, et nulla est mora. Specialiter autem Job dicit hoc de se ipso, quia putavit se protinus moriturum, et quoniam dies vitæ suæ pro magna jam parte fluxerunt. Ac si dicat: Tempus est ut corpus sepulturæ tradatur, et anima mea ad limbum patrum transferatur.
paras.en: Further, he shows that he did not despair outright by adding: [[7:16|spare me|Parce mihi]], either by healing my body or by parting my soul from it. So too Tobias prayed: Do with me according to thy mercy[[Tob 3:6||]], and [[Tob 3:6|command my spirit to be received in peace|præcipe in pace recipi spiritum meum]] [Denis's *Fac mecum misericordiam*, "deal mercifully with me", stands for the Vulgate's *secundum voluntatem tuam fac mecum*, "do with me according to thy will"]. And since a humble knowledge of one's own vileness and littleness helps most of all to win God's clemency, he adds: [[7:16|for my days are nothing|Nihil enim sunt dies mei]], that is, they are to be counted as nothing, especially with respect to the eternity that follows, in comparison with which all time is as a moment; and there is no comparison of the finite with the infinite. Hence it is said in the first book of Paralipomenon: [[1 Par 29:15|Our days upon earth are as a shadow, and there is no stay|Dies nostri quasi umbra super terram, et nulla est mora]]. But Job says this of himself in particular because he thought he would die forthwith, and because the days of his life had already for the most part run out. As if to say: It is time for my body to be given to burial and for my soul to be taken to the limbo of the fathers.

paras.t: Quid est homo, quia magnificas eum? id est, tam vilis ac fragilis creatura est homo, potissime quantum ad corpus et originalem infectionem, seu virium corruptionem per quatuor vulnera ex originali peccato secuta, ut mirum appareat, quod per tua beneficia etiam supernaturalia, in tantum magnificas eum. Aut quid apponis erga eum cor tuum, id est mentis tuæ sapientiam, qua eum et omnia ejus consideras, specialique providentia eum gubernas? quasi dicat: In hoc admiranda est bonitas tua. Nam homo indignus videtur secundum modum prædictum, potissime per comparationem ad infinitam excellentiam Creatoris, et quoad supernaturalem beatitudinem, ad quam Deus hominem ordinavit ac dirigit. Tali utique provisione ac directione Dei indignus est homo, quantum ad naturalia sua: qui vilis est, utpote materia lutum, conditione servus, fortuna instabilis, actu pravus, conceptu immundus, ad vitia pronus, morte doloribus plenus. Simili admiratione divinæ clementiæ, non reprobatione divinæ providentiæ, loquitur Deo Psalmista: Quid est homo, quod memor es ejus? aut filius hominis, quoniam visitas eum? Et rursus: Domine, quid est homo, quia innotuisti ei? aut filius hominis, quoniam reputas eum? Homo vanitati similis factus est.
paras.en: [[7:17|What is a man, that thou shouldst magnify him|Quid est homo, quia magnificas eum]]? That is, man is so vile and frail a creature, above all as regards the body and the original infection, or the corruption of his powers through the four wounds that followed from original sin [that is, the wounds of ignorance, malice, weakness and concupiscence], that it seems a marvel that thou dost magnify him so greatly by thy benefits, even supernatural ones. [[7:17|or why dost thou set thy heart upon him|Aut quid apponis erga eum cor tuum]], that is, the wisdom of thy mind, by which thou considerest him and all that is his, and governest him by a special providence? As if to say: In this thy goodness is to be wondered at. For man seems unworthy in the way just said, above all in comparison with the infinite excellence of the Creator, and as regards the supernatural beatitude to which God has ordained man and directs him. Of such providing and directing by God man is indeed unworthy as far as his natural endowments go: for he is vile, being clay in his matter, a servant in his condition, unstable in fortune, wicked in act, unclean in his conception, prone to vices, full of sorrows in death. With a like wonder at the divine clemency, not a reproach of divine providence, the Psalmist speaks to God: [[Ps 8:5|What is man, that thou art mindful of him? or the son of man, that thou visitest him?|Quid est homo, quod memor es ejus? aut filius hominis, quoniam visitas eum?]] And again: [[Ps 143:3|Lord, what is man, that thou art made known to him? or the son of man, that thou makest account of him?|Domine, quid est homo, quia innotuisti ei? aut filius hominis, quoniam reputas eum?]] [[Ps 143:4|Man is like to vanity|Homo vanitati similis factus est]].

paras.t: Visitas eum, id est, tuis beneficiis eum adornas, et per angelum dirigis, diluculo, id est a nativitatis et vitæ ac lucis suæ exordio. Itemque, Diluculo, id est spirituali mane, quando gratiæ tuæ illustratione incipis cordis humani tenebras, vitia et errores expellere, internamque diem in mente producere, lucem infusæ sapientiæ illico diffundendo, quemadmodum in Proverbiis inducitur: Justorum semita quasi lux splendens, procedit et crescit usque ad perfectam diem. Hoc diluculum oritur illucescente parum bonitate Dei super hominem. Ad litteram quoque, homines solent diluculo esse ad devotionem plus dediti, quando sensus adhuc sobrii manent, nec cor negotiis occupatur. Unde primo capitulo de sancto Job dictum est: Consurgens diluculo offerebat holocausta per singulos. Et Isaias alloquitur Deum: De mane vigilabo ad te. Similiter Ecclesiasticus de sapiente justoque dicit: Cor suum tradet ad vigilandum diluculo, ad Dominum qui fecit illum. Ideo dicitur Deus hominem diluculo per inspirationem et motionem Sancti Spiritus visitare.
paras.en: [[7:18|Thou visitest him|Visitas eum]], that is, thou adornest him with thy benefits and directest him through an angel, [[7:18|early in the morning|diluculo]], that is, from the beginning of his birth, his life and his light. And again: [[7:18|early in the morning|Diluculo]], that is, in the spiritual morning, when by the enlightening of thy grace thou beginnest to drive out the darkness, vices and errors of the human heart and to bring forth an inward day in the mind, at once pouring out the light of infused wisdom; as is set forth in Proverbs: [[Prov 4:18|the path of the just, as a shining light, goeth forwards, and increaseth even to perfect day|Justorum semita quasi lux splendens, procedit et crescit usque ad perfectam diem]]. This dawn rises as the goodness of God begins little by little to shine upon man. Literally too, men are usually more given to devotion at dawn, when the senses are still sober and the heart is not taken up with business. Hence it was said of holy Job in the first chapter: [[Job 1:5|rising up early, offered holocausts for every one of them|Consurgens diluculo offerebat holocausta per singulos]]. And Isaias addresses God: [[Is 26:9|in the morning early I will watch to thee|De mane vigilabo ad te]]. Likewise Ecclesiasticus says of the wise and just man: [[Ecclus 39:6|He will give his heart to resort early to the Lord that made him|Cor suum tradet ad vigilandum diluculo, ad Dominum qui fecit illum]] [the margin's numbers here are misread; the passages are Is 26:9 and Ecclus 39:6]. Therefore God is said to visit man at dawn by the inspiration and motion of the Holy Ghost.

paras.t: Et subito, id est statim post hoc, probas illum, id est, tentari permittis, et per adversa exerces ac probas, non ut tu eum agnoscas, sed ut homo cognoscat se ipsum, et aliis qualis sit ostendatur: per tribulationes quoque probatus ac virtuosus reddatur. Sic enim orat Psalmista: Proba me, Domine, et tenta me. Hinc scriptum est in libro Sapientiæ: Tanquam aurum in fornace probavit electos Dominus, et quasi holocausti hostiam accepit eos. In Ecclesiastico quoque: Vasa figuli probat fornax, et homines justos tentatio tribulationis.
paras.en: And [[7:18|suddenly|Et subito]], that is, straightway after this, [[7:18|thou provest him|probas illum]], that is, thou allowest him to be tempted, and dost exercise and prove him by adversities: not that thou mayest know him, but that man may know himself, and that it may be shown to others what he is; and that, proved by tribulations, he may also be made virtuous. For so the Psalmist prays: [[Ps 25:2|Prove me, O Lord, and try me|Proba me, Domine, et tenta me]]. Hence it is written in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 3:6|As gold in the furnace, he hath proved them, and as a victim of a holocaust, he hath received them|Tanquam aurum in fornace probavit electos Dominus, et quasi holocausti hostiam accepit eos]]. And in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 27:6|The furnace trieth the potter's vessels, and the trial of affliction just men.|Vasa figuli probat fornax, et homines justos tentatio tribulationis.]]

paras.t: Usquequo non parcis mihi? id est, cur tam diu differs mihi succurrere, vel miseram vitam hanc terminando, aut ad sanitatem me reducendo? Nec dimittis me ut glutiam salivam meam? id est, nec ad modicum das mihi a doloribus repausationem, sed ita desiccatus sum corpore, exhaustusque viribus, ut salivam aut non, aut vix naturali convenientique modo queam glutire. Et est partim hyperbolica locutio, ad exprimendum magnitudinem suæ pressuræ. Quocirca scribit Albertus: Humidum salivale secundum naturam est, quo omnis sapor nervis gustativis per linguam dispersis infunditur, et quo ad incorporationem glutitur: et est sensus, Dimitte me ut aliquod sapidum vitæ gustem vel glutiam.
paras.en: [[7:19|How long wilt thou not spare me|Usquequo non parcis mihi]]? That is, why dost thou put off so long coming to my help, either by ending this wretched life or by bringing me back to health? [[7:19|nor suffer me to swallow down my spittle|Nec dimittis me ut glutiam salivam meam]]? That is, thou givest me not even a little rest from my pains; but I am so dried up in body and so drained of strength that I either cannot swallow my spittle at all, or can hardly swallow it in the natural and fitting way. And it is partly a hyperbolic way of speaking, to express the greatness of his distress.
