Wherefore Albert writes: The moisture of the spittle is by nature that by which every savour is poured into the nerves of taste spread through the tongue, and by which it is swallowed to be taken into the body; and the sense is: Let me taste or swallow something of the savour of life.

paras.t: Peccavi. Infra sæpe, sed et supra innuit se non peccasse: quomodo ergo nunc ait, Peccavi? Nam infra testatur: Neque enim reprehendit me cor meum in omni vita mea. Et respondendum, quod innuit se non peccasse peccato gravi et tantæ afflictionis meritorio, non autem a quotidianis ac venialibus se excusat, quum et Salomon protestetur: Non est homo super terram, qui faciat bonum, et non peccet. Joannes quoque in prima sua epistola: Si dixerimus quia peccatum non habemus, nos ipsos seducimus, et veritas in nobis non est.
paras.en: [[7:20|I have sinned|Peccavi]]. Often below, and above as well, he gives to understand that he has not sinned: how then does he now say, [[7:20|I have sinned|Peccavi]]? For below he testifies: [[Job 27:6|for my heart doth not reprehend me in all my life|Neque enim reprehendit me cor meum in omni vita mea]]. And the answer is that he gives to understand that he has not sinned with grave sin, deserving so great an affliction; but he does not clear himself of daily and venial sins, since Solomon too declares: [[Eccles 7:21|there is no just man upon earth, that doth good, and sinneth not|Non est homo super terram, qui faciat bonum, et non peccet]][[3 Kings 8:46||]] [Denis's wording, without *justus*, "just", stands between Eccles 7:21 and Solomon's prayer at 3 Kings 8:46, "there is no man who sinneth not"; the margin gives both]. And John in his first epistle: [[1 John 1:8|If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us|Si dixerimus quia peccatum non habemus, nos ipsos seducimus, et veritas in nobis non est]].

paras.t: Quid faciam tibi, id est ad tuam gloriam et honorem? o custos hominum, id est, Deus, hominum gerens curam atque custodiam: juxta illud in Psalmo, Custodiens parvulos Dominus; et, Nisi Dominus custodierit civitatem. Quasi dicat: O Deus, nil condignæ satisfactionis propriis viribus facere valeo, nec sine gratia tua veniam consequi, aut aliquid promereri sufficio.
paras.en: [[7:20|what shall I do to thee|Quid faciam tibi]], that is, for thy glory and honour, [[7:20|O keeper of men|o custos hominum]]? That is, God, who takes care and keeping of men; according to that in the Psalm: [[Ps 114:6|The Lord is the keeper of little ones|Custodiens parvulos Dominus]]; and: [[Ps 126:1|Unless the Lord keep the city|Nisi Dominus custodierit civitatem]]. As if to say: O God, by my own strength I can make no condign satisfaction [that is, satisfaction equal in worth to the debt], nor obtain pardon without thy grace, nor am I able to merit anything.

paras.t: Quare posuisti, id est, poni et esse seu fieri permisisti, me contrarium tibi, id est tuæ voluntati ac legi per culpam? In omni enim peccato est quidam recessus a rectitudine voluntatis divinæ atque ab ordine sapientiæ Dei, et a dictamine seu doctrina legis naturalis aut scriptæ vel evangelicæ. Porro qui peccat, ponit et facit se ipsum Deo contrarium, dissentientem seu displicentem. Itaque eo modo ponit Deus hominem sibi contrarium, quomodo dicitur hominem indurare, videlicet quoniam gratiam non largitur. Potest et ita exponi: Quare posuisti me contrarium tibi? id est, me quasi adversarium habuisti et ostendisti, dum me tam graviter percussisti. Unde et infra Job loquitur Deo: Sto, et non respicis me. Mutatus es mihi in crudelem, et in duritia manus tuæ adversaris mihi.
paras.en: [[7:20|why hast thou set|Quare posuisti]], that is, allowed to be set, and to be or become, [[7:20|me opposite to thee|me contrarium tibi]], that is, to thy will and law, through fault? For in every sin there is a certain turning away from the rightness of the divine will and from the order of God's wisdom, and from the dictate or teaching of the natural law, or the written law, or the law of the Gospel. Now he who sins sets and makes himself opposite to God, at variance with him or displeasing to him. And so God sets man opposite to himself in the way in which he is said to harden man: that is, because he does not bestow grace. It can also be explained thus: [[7:20|why hast thou set me opposite to thee|Quare posuisti me contrarium tibi]]? That is, thou hast held me and shown me as an adversary, in striking me so heavily. Hence below too Job says to God: [[Job 30:20|I stand up, and thou dost not regard me|Sto, et non respicis me]]. [[Job 30:21|Thou art changed to be cruel toward me, and in the hardness of thy hand thou art against me.|Mutatus es mihi in crudelem, et in duritia manus tuæ adversaris mihi.]]

paras.t: Et factus sum mihimetipsi gravis, per pœnas quas patior, atque per culpam ex qua dolor et remorsus conscientiæ oriuntur; ipsumque peccatum quasi pondus est aggravans animam. Denique, ex peccato oritur in viribus animæ pronitas ad peccandum, et difficultas in ratione ad refrenandum passiones et vitia sensualitatis: sicque fit homo sibimet gravis, ita quod difficulter recedit a malo, et laboriose efficit bonum. Hinc ad Hebræos monet Apostolus: Deponentes omne pondus et circumstans nos peccatum, per patientiam curramus ad propositum nobis certamen. De aggravatione vero per pœnam ait ad Corinthios: Supra modum gravati sumus supra virtutem, ita ut tæderet nos vivere.
paras.en: [[7:20|and am I become burdensome to myself|Et factus sum mihimetipsi gravis]] [or "heavy to myself"]: through the pains that I suffer, and through the fault from which grief and remorse of conscience arise; and sin itself is like a weight burdening the soul. Lastly, from sin there arises in the powers of the soul a proneness to sin, and in the reason a difficulty in curbing the passions and vices of sensuality; and so man becomes burdensome to himself, so that he turns away from evil with difficulty and does good with toil. Hence the Apostle admonishes in Hebrews: [[Heb 12:1|laying aside every weight and sin which surrounds us, let us run by patience to the fight proposed to us|Deponentes omne pondus et circumstans nos peccatum, per patientiam curramus ad propositum nobis certamen]]. And of the burdening by pain he says to the Corinthians: [[2 Cor 1:8|we were pressed out of measure above our strength, so that we were weary even of life|Supra modum gravati sumus supra virtutem, ita ut tæderet nos vivere]].

paras.t: Cur non tollis peccatum meum in proximum, si quod est, illud per pœnam hanc dimittendo, vel ex tua clementia ignoscendo? Et quare non aufers iniquitatem meam commissam in te? Omnis autem culpa est aliquo modo iniquitas, quia a perfecta æquitate defectus. Et homines virtuosi etiam parva peccata deflent ac reputant quasi magna; sicque loquitur Job. Præterea contuendum, quod tam audenter ac fiducialiter loquitur Deo, non ex elatione, præsumptione, impatientia aut temeraria divinorum judiciorum inquisitione aut reprehensione; sed potius ex quadam pia querela et humili admiratione, imo ex affectionis magnitudine virtuosa. Quasi dicat: Utinam non posuisses me tibi per peccata contrarium, et utinam omnem culpam meam auferres.
paras.en: [[7:21|Why dost thou not remove my sin|Cur non tollis peccatum meum]], against my neighbour, if there is any, forgiving it through this pain or pardoning it of thy clemency? [[7:21|and why dost thou not take away my iniquity|Et quare non aufers iniquitatem meam]], committed against thee? Now every fault is in some way iniquity [*iniquitas*, literally "unevenness", against *æquitas*, "evenness" or "equity"], since it is a falling short of perfect equity. And virtuous men weep even for small sins and count them as great; and so Job speaks. Further, it is to be considered that he speaks to God so boldly and confidently not from pride, presumption, impatience, or a rash prying into or finding fault with the divine judgments, but rather from a kind of pious complaint and humble wonder, nay, from a virtuous greatness of affection. As if to say: Would that thou hadst not set me opposite to thee through sins, and would that thou wouldst take away all my fault.

paras.t: Ecce nunc in pulvere dormiam, id est, statim moriar, et in sepulcro quiescam, in pulveremque resolvar. Imo tam cito moriturum me reor, secundum naturalem causarum processum, quod et si mane diei sequentis me quæsieris in hac vita, non subsistam in ea. Loquitur autem Job affectu et more graviter atque letaliter infirmantium et mortem optantium, qui sic proloqui solent: Ego mox moriar. Quod et ideo agit, ut innuat se incertum de vitæ suæ duratione usque ad alteram diem. Rursus, quemadmodum in Scripturis per crastinum diem non semper intelligitur dies proxime sequens, sed interdum tempus cito futurum, ut dum in Genesi ait Jacob, Cras respondebit mihi justitia mea; et in libro Josue, Cras dicent filii vestri filiis nostris; talisque modus loquendi frequens est, maxime in Deuteronomio: ita et nunc per Mane, non necessario intelligitur mane diei proxime imminentis, sed alicujus diei non longe distantis.
paras.en: [[7:21|Behold now I shall sleep in the dust|Ecce nunc in pulvere dormiam]], that is, I shall die straightway, and rest in the tomb, and be dissolved into dust. Nay, I think I shall die so soon, by the natural course of causes, that even [[7:21|if thou seek me|me quæsieris]] in this life [[7:21|in the morning|et si mane]] of the following day, [[7:21|I shall not be|non subsistam]] in it. Now Job speaks with the feeling and in the manner of those who are gravely and mortally sick and long for death, who are wont to say: I shall soon die. And he does this to give to understand that he is uncertain of his life lasting until the next day. Again, as in the Scriptures *tomorrow* does not always mean the day next following, but sometimes a time soon to come (as when Jacob says in Genesis: [[Gen 30:33|my justice shall answer for me tomorrow|Cras respondebit mihi justitia mea]]; and in the book of Josue: [[Jos 22:24|To morrow your children will say to our children|Cras dicent filii vestri filiis nostris]]; and this manner of speaking is frequent, above all in Deuteronomy), so here too by [[7:21|in the morning|Mane]] is not necessarily meant the morning of the day just at hand, but of some day not far off.

paras.t: Postremo, ex dictis eliciuntur tres causæ, cur aliquis nunc affligatur a Deo: prima, quatenus coerceatur ejus malitia, ne aliis sit nociva; secunda, ad hominis probationem, ut virtus ejus manifestetur; tertia, in pœnam peccati.
paras.en: Lastly, from what has been said three causes are drawn why anyone is now afflicted by God: the first, that his malice may be held in, lest it do harm to others; the second, for the man's proving, that his virtue may be made manifest; the third, as punishment for sin.

7.title: De intellectu tropologico ejusdem capituli septimi.
7.title_en: On the tropological sense of the same seventh chapter

paras.t: Generalem hominis conditionem, proprietatem ac statum insinuans sanctus Job: Militia, inquit, est vita hominis super terram. Quicumque ergo veraciter Dei servus est, etiam miles est ejus, et contra adversarios ipsius jugiter præliatur, videlicet contra aciem vitiorum, contra insidias tentamentaque dæmonum: imo adversus omnia quæ Dei sunt offensiva, et veræ salutis impeditiva. Quoniam ergo vita nostra militia est, debemus indesinenter spiritualibus armis esse armati, virtutibus roborati, omnem torporem abjicere, stultam securitatem expellere, ad prælia Dei semper parati consistere, totam in rege nostro Deo altissimo spem firmare, ejus auxilium fideliter implorare, ejus adjutorio ubique inniti, hostibus ejus nullatenus conformari. Sed hæc non sine grandi labore implentur; verum (teste Apostolo) non coronatur, nisi legitime certans. Imo frequenter contingit, ut tunc plura proficiendi obstacula nobis occurrant, plura turbantia obvient tam a dæmonibus, quam ab hominibus improbis, dum firmius vitam emendare decrevimus aut cœpimus. Sed non vincamur: quin potius tanto affectuosius recurramus ad Deum, quo sentimus nos importunius impediri ac impugnari.
paras.en: Holy Job, setting forth the general condition, property and state of man, says: [[7:1|The life of man upon earth|est vita hominis super terram]] [[7:1|is a warfare|Militia]]. Whoever, then, is truly a servant of God is also his soldier, and fights unceasingly against his adversaries: that is, against the battle line of the vices, against the snares and temptations of the demons, and indeed against everything that offends God and hinders true salvation. Since, then, our life is a warfare, we ought unceasingly to be armed with spiritual arms and strengthened with the virtues; to cast off all torpor, to drive out foolish security, to stand always ready for the battles of God, to fix all our hope on our King, the most high God, faithfully to implore his help, to lean on his aid everywhere, and in no way to be conformed to his enemies. But these things are not fulfilled without great labour; indeed (as the Apostle witnesses) a man [[2 Tim 2:5|is not crowned, except he strive lawfully|non coronatur, nisi legitime certans]]. Indeed it often happens that more obstacles to our progress meet us, and more troubles come against us, both from the demons and from wicked men, just when we have resolved or begun to amend our life more firmly. But let us not be overcome: rather let us run back to God the more affectionately, the more insistently we feel ourselves hindered and assailed.

paras.t: Et sicut dies mercenarii dies ejus. Circa hoc præcedenti articulo satis dictum videtur. Præterea, væ eis qui viam hanc præsensque exsilium pro patria diligunt; qui æternis atque divinis præferunt carnalia ista vanissima; qui vanis ac frivolis rebus immundissimisque delectationibus magis, quam superdignissimo Deo infinito et incommutabili bono, inhærent; qui in labore hominum non sunt, nec cum hominibus flagellantur; qui vitiis non solum non reluctantur, sed et ad explendas concupiscentias suas conantur, ad satisfaciendum propriis voluptatibus operam largiuntur, ad obtinendos mundi honores, divitias, deliciasque intenti sunt. Isti sunt milites diaboli, hostesque Dei, qui pepigerunt pactum cum morte, et cum inferno fœdus inierunt, diabolo in omnibus concordantes: ideo tenet eos superbia, proditque quasi ex adipe iniquitas eorum: quorum dies non diebus mercenariorum, sed otiosorum, infructuosorum atque ludentium comparantur.
paras.en: [[7:1|and his days are like the days of a hireling|Et sicut dies mercenarii dies ejus]]. Enough seems to have been said about this in the preceding article. Further: woe to those who love this way and present exile instead of the fatherland; who prefer these most vain carnal things to the eternal and divine; who cling to vain and frivolous things and most unclean delights more than to the most supremely worthy God, the infinite and unchangeable good; who [[Ps 72:5|are not in the labour of men: neither shall they be scourged like other men|in labore hominum non sunt, nec cum hominibus flagellantur]]; who not only do not resist the vices, but even strive to fulfil their lusts, give their labour to satisfying their own pleasures, and are intent on gaining the honours, riches and delights of the world. These are the soldiers of the devil and the enemies of God, who have struck a bargain with death and entered into a covenant with hell[[Is 28:15||]] [the margin seems to read Is. xxvii, 13; the words are those of Is 28:15, a little changed], agreeing with the devil in all things: [[Ps 72:6|Therefore pride hath held them fast|ideo tenet eos superbia]], [[Ps 72:7|Their iniquity hath come forth, as it were from fatness|proditque quasi ex adipe iniquitas eorum]]; and their days are compared not to the days of hirelings, but to those of idlers, of the unfruitful and of players.

paras.t: Sicut cervus desiderat umbram, etc., sic et ego habui menses vacuos. Hoc peccator pœnitens dicere potest, qui tempus suum infructuose expendit, sicque menses habuit a bonis operibus vacuos, vanitate et vitiis (quæ nihil sunt) plenos. Ideo ait Ambrosius: Plenitudinem vitæ justi habet; inanes autem sunt dies impiorum. Porro, quod ait, Sicut cervus desiderat umbram, de homine virtuoso potest exponi, qui propter agilitatem devotissimam ad universa quæ Dei sunt, cervus vocatur; umbramque desiderat, quoniam post tentationis fervorem, operisque sudorem, æternæ felicitatis refrigerium quærit, cum Psalmista proclamans: Quemadmodum desiderat cervus ad fontes aquarum, ita desiderat anima mea ad te, Deus.
paras.en: [[7:2|As a servant longeth for the shade|Sicut cervus desiderat umbram]] [Denis's text has *cervus*, “hart”, for the Vulgate's *servus*, “servant”: the two words sound alike, and his second reading of the verse below rests on the hart], etc., [[7:3|So I also have had empty months|sic et ego habui menses vacuos]]. The repentant sinner can say this, who has spent his time fruitlessly, and so has had months empty of good works and full of vanity and vices (which are nothing). Hence Ambrose says: The life of the just has fullness, but the days of the wicked are empty. Moreover, what he says, [[7:2|As a servant longeth for the shade|Sicut cervus desiderat umbram]], can be explained of the virtuous man, who is called a hart for his most devout swiftness towards all the things of God; and he longs for the shade, since after the heat of temptation and the sweat of labour he seeks the refreshment of eternal happiness, crying out with the Psalmist: [[Ps 41:2|As the hart panteth after the fountains of water; so my soul panteth after thee, O God|Quemadmodum desiderat cervus ad fontes aquarum, ita desiderat anima mea ad te, Deus]].

paras.t: Et noctes laboriosas enumeravi mihi. Per noctem intelligitur actio vitiosa, tenebris erroris immixta, juxta illud Proverbiorum: Via impiorum tenebrosa; nesciunt ubi corruunt. Peccatores itaque noctes habent laboriosas, quia in ipsis eorum vitiosis operibus variæ anxietates, fatigationes, pœnæ et difficultates consistunt. Propter quod in libro Sapientiæ fatentur: Lassati sumus in via iniquitatis et perditionis, et ambulavimus vias difficiles. Quemadmodum enim virtus ex sua natura suavis est, et actus ejus delectat; sic peccatum vel amarum est in se, vel amaritudinem habet adjunctam. Propter quod, Augustino testante, animus inordinatus sibi ipsi pœnalis et gravis est. Unde Ecclesiastes ait: Homini bono dedit Deus sapientiam, et scientiam, et lætitiam; peccatori autem afflictionem, et curam superfluam.
paras.en: [[7:3|and have numbered to myself wearisome nights|Et noctes laboriosas enumeravi mihi]]. By night is understood vicious action, mingled with the darkness of error, according to that of Proverbs: [[Prov 4:19|The way of the wicked is darksome: they know not where they fall|Via impiorum tenebrosa; nesciunt ubi corruunt]]. Sinners therefore have wearisome nights, because in their very vicious works lie manifold anxieties, weariness, pains and difficulties. For which reason they confess in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 5:7|We wearied ourselves in the way of iniquity and destruction, and have walked through hard ways|Lassati sumus in via iniquitatis et perditionis, et ambulavimus vias difficiles]]. For just as virtue is by its nature sweet, and its act delights, so sin is either bitter in itself or has bitterness joined to it. For which reason, as Augustine witnesses, the disordered mind is a punishment and a burden to itself. Hence Ecclesiastes says: [[Eccles 2:26|God hath given to a man that is good|Homini bono dedit Deus]] [[Eccles 2:26|wisdom, and knowledge, and joy|sapientiam, et scientiam, et lætitiam]]: [[Eccles 2:26|but to the sinner he hath given vexation, and superfluous care|peccatori autem afflictionem, et curam superfluam]].

paras.t: Si dormiero, id est, ab actu cessavero, et torporem otiumque admisero, dicam, ipso otio attædiatus: Quando consurgam ab otiositate ad opus? Tanta nempe est humanæ naturæ instabilitas, imperfectio atque varietas, ut nec in otio, nec in opere diu delectabiliter perseveret; sed nunc isto, nunc illo fatigetur, et de uno adspiret ad aliud. Ideo sequitur: Et rursum exspectabo vesperam, id est operationis occasum et corporis repausationem. Hinc Ecclesiastes asserit: Cuncti dies hominis doloribus et ærumnis pleni sunt, nec per noctem mente quiescit.
paras.en: [[7:4|If I lie down to sleep|Si dormiero]], that is, if I cease from action and give way to torpor and idleness, [[7:4|I shall say|dicam]], wearied by that very idleness: [[7:4|When shall I rise|Quando consurgam]] from idleness to work? For so great is the instability, imperfection and changeableness of human nature, that it does not persevere with delight for long either in rest or in work, but is wearied now by this, now by that, and from the one longs for the other. Therefore there follows: [[7:4|and again, I shall look for the evening|Et rursum exspectabo vesperam]], that is, the setting of work and the rest of the body. Hence Ecclesiastes asserts: [[Eccles 2:23|All his days are full of sorrows and miseries, even in the night he doth not rest in mind|Cuncti dies hominis doloribus et ærumnis pleni sunt, nec per noctem mente quiescit]] [the margin gives *Ibid.*, that is Ecclesiastes, with its verse misread; the words are Eccles 2:23, where the Vulgate has *dies ejus*, “his days”, for Denis's *dies hominis*, “the days of man”].

paras.t: Potest quoque ita exponi: Si dormiero, id est, ab exterioribus alienatus, in Deo per contemplationem quievero (juxta illud, In pace in id ipsum dormiam, et requiescam: hæc est obdormitio dulcissima in dilecto), dicam intra me verbo affectuoso mentali: Quando consurgam de contemplatione imperfecta hujus viæ, ad contemplationem beatissimam patriæ? Tunc enim ad facialem Dei benedicti intuitum vehementius inflammamur, quando hic per contemplationem theoricam mysticæ theologiæ, visionem internam atque amorem flammigerum succendentem, ad ipsum levamur, in ipso suspendimur et vacamus. Tunc equidem delicias patriæ prægustamus, futuram visionem beatificam inchoamus; tantoque amplius ad claram ac immediatam divinæ superinfinitæ pulchritudinis visionem, atque divinæ, immensæ ac superpurissimæ bonitatis dulcedinisque fruitionem completam appropinquamus et dignificamur, quo in via hac ad sereniorem ac amorosiorem ipsius contemplationem provehimur. Deus enim essentialiter interminabiliterque amabilis, quo clarius se ostendit, eo videntem plus attrahit et delectat. Et rursum exspectabo vesperam, id est contemplativi splendoris cessationem: quia in vita ista mens contemplativa in luce theorica et contemplatione deifica jugiter stare non valet, sed ad defectuositatis suæ tenebras cito relabitur.
paras.en: It can also be explained thus: [[7:4|If I lie down to sleep|Si dormiero]], that is, if, estranged from outward things, I rest in God through contemplation (according to that: [[Ps 4:9|In peace in the self same I will sleep, and I will rest|In pace in id ipsum dormiam, et requiescam]]: this is the sweetest falling asleep in the beloved), [[7:4|I shall say|dicam]] within myself with an affectionate word of the mind: [[7:4|When shall I rise|Quando consurgam]] from the imperfect contemplation of this way to the most blessed contemplation of the fatherland? For we are the more vehemently inflamed towards the face-to-face vision of the blessed God when here, through the theoretical contemplation [that is, the beholding, Greek *theoria*] of mystical theology, through inward vision and the flaming love it kindles, we are raised up to him, hang upon him, and are at leisure in him. Then indeed we foretaste the delights of the fatherland and begin the future beatific vision; and we draw the nearer to the clear and immediate vision of the divine, more than infinite beauty, and to the complete enjoyment of the divine, immense and most supremely pure goodness and sweetness, and are made the worthier of it, the further we are advanced on this way to a more serene and more loving contemplation of him. For God, who is essentially and without limit lovable, the more clearly he shows himself, the more he draws and delights the one who sees him. [[7:4|and again, I shall look for the evening|Et rursum exspectabo vesperam]], that is, the ceasing of contemplative splendour: because in this life the contemplative mind cannot stand continually in theoretical light and deifying contemplation, but soon slips back into the darkness of its own deficiency.

paras.t: Præterea, in persona electi, quamvis peccatoris, ita exponitur: Si dormiero, id est, peccatis sopitus jacuero, motuque vitæ ac sensu spirituali privatus exstitero, dicam: Quando consurgam a somno peccati ad virtutum vigiliam? Electi namque emendationem proponunt, quemadmodum Michæas in persona hujusmodi dicit: Ne læteris, inimica mea, super me, quia cecidi: consurgam. Quum sedero in tenebris, Dominus lux mea est. Et rursus exspectabo vesperam: quia post pœnitentiam rursus metuunt se casuros, imo ad venialium umbras, actualisque illuminationis occasum frequenter labuntur: nam in eodem illustrationis dilectionisque Dei fulgore atque fervore non diu actualiter manent, sed frequentius innovantur et recalescunt.
paras.en: Further, it is explained thus in the person of one of the elect, though a sinner: [[7:4|If I lie down to sleep|Si dormiero]], that is, if I lie lulled to sleep by sins, and have been deprived of the motion of life and of spiritual sense, [[7:4|I shall say|dicam]]: [[7:4|When shall I rise|Quando consurgam]] from the sleep of sin to the watchfulness of the virtues? For the elect resolve on amendment, as Micheas says in the person of such a one: [[Mich 7:8|Rejoice not, thou my enemy, over me, because I am fallen: I shall arise, when I sit in darkness, the Lord is my light|Ne læteris, inimica mea, super me, quia cecidi: consurgam. Quum sedero in tenebris, Dominus lux mea est]]. [[7:4|and again, I shall look for the evening|Et rursus exspectabo vesperam]]: because after penance they fear they will fall again; indeed they often slip into the shadows of venial sins and the setting of actual illumination: for they do not remain long actually in the same brightness and fervour of God's enlightening and love, but are quite often renewed and grow warm again.

paras.t: Et replebor doloribus usque ad tenebras: quia ex hac miserrima instabilitate, defectuositate et lapsu justus vehementer affligitur, ex purissimo Dei amore maxime dolens, quod Creatorem suum supersanctissimum toties inhonorat, offendit, perdit, relinquit, etsi non quantum ad habitum, tamen quantum ad actum: istudque durat usque ad tenebras, id est horam mortis, tenebris angustiarum repletam. Hinc ait Gregorius: Vult in contemplatione mens stare, sed nequit meditationis gressum figere; nititur, sed infirmitatis suæ lapsibus enervatur.
paras.en: [[7:4|and shall be filled with sorrows even till darkness|Et replebor doloribus usque ad tenebras]]: because the just man is grievously afflicted by this most wretched instability, deficiency and falling, grieving exceedingly, out of the purest love of God, that he so often dishonours, offends, loses and forsakes his most supremely holy Creator, if not as to the habit, yet as to the act [that is, not by losing the abiding state of grace and charity, but in his particular acts]: and this lasts until darkness, that is, the hour of death, full of the darkness of anguish. Hence Gregory says: The mind wishes to stand in contemplation, but cannot fix the step of its meditation; it strives, but is unnerved by the falls of its own weakness.

paras.t: Induta est caro mea putredine, id est carnalium vitiorum inquinamentis, et sordibus pulveris, id est immunditiis cogitationis terrenæ sive carnalis. Sic et pœnitens ait: Putruerunt et corruptæ sunt cicatrices meæ a facie insipientiæ meæ: quoniam lumbi mei impleti sunt illusionibus, et non est sanitas in carne mea. Cutis, id est conversationis meæ superficies apparentiave exterior, aruit, id est, aliis exemplaris et fructuosa non fuit, sed potius scandalizativa, et contracta est, id est plicis duplicitatis et rugis tortuosæ injustitiæ deformata. Verumtamen hæc exponi queunt in bono, ut caro pœnitentis dicatur putredine ac sordibus pulveris quasi vestita, id est præ rigore abstinentiæ ac operum pœnitentiæ naturali vigore aliqualiter destituta, et ab æqualitate harmoniæ aliquo modo corrupta ac infirmata. Inter abstinentiam quippe virtutem acquisitam ac naturalem, et inter abstinentiam virtutem infusam, ista distinctio assignatur, quod ad abstinentiam naturalem pertinet tantum accipere alimenti, quantum expedit ad naturalia opera rationis exsequenda, atque ad bonam vitæ naturalis habitudinem in corpore conservandam; ad abstinentiam vero infusam spectat, etiam aliquid necessariorum abstrahere corpori, propter recompensandum ejus in alimentis aliisque excessum, et ut Christo concrucifigatur, aut per hoc plus gratiæ mereatur. Quo facto, cutis aret atque contrahitur, ita quod pallore ac macie, quæ sunt signa amoris, homo afficitur. Sic enim ait Psalmista: Ossa mea sicut cremium aruerunt; a voce gemitus mei adhæsit os meum carni meæ.
paras.en: [[7:5|My flesh is clothed with rottenness|Induta est caro mea putredine]], that is, with the defilements of carnal vices, [[7:5|and the filth of dust|et sordibus pulveris]], that is, with the uncleanness of earthly or carnal thought. So too the penitent says: [[Ps 37:6|My sores are putrefied and corrupted, because of my foolishness|Putruerunt et corruptæ sunt cicatrices meæ a facie insipientiæ meæ]]: [[Ps 37:8|For my loins are filled with illusions; and there is no health in my flesh|quoniam lumbi mei impleti sunt illusionibus, et non est sanitas in carne mea]]. [[7:5|my skin|Cutis]], that is, the surface or outward appearance of my way of life, [[7:5|is withered|aruit]], that is, was not exemplary and fruitful for others, but rather a cause of scandal, [[7:5|and drawn together|et contracta est]], that is, disfigured by the folds of duplicity and the wrinkles of twisted injustice. Yet these words can be explained in a good sense, so that the penitent's flesh is said to be as it were clothed with rottenness and the filth of dust: that is, through the rigour of abstinence and of the works of penance, in some measure deprived of its natural vigour, and in some way impaired and weakened from the evenness of its harmony [that is, the balanced temper of the body]. For between abstinence as an acquired and natural virtue and abstinence as an infused virtue this distinction is given: to natural abstinence it belongs to take as much food as serves for carrying out the natural works of reason and for preserving in the body the good condition of natural life; but to infused abstinence it belongs to withdraw from the body even something of what is necessary, to make amends for its excess in food and other things, and so that it may be crucified with Christ, or may merit more grace by this. When this is done the skin withers and is drawn together, so that the man is marked with pallor and leanness, which are signs of love. For so the Psalmist says: [[Ps 101:4|my bones are grown dry like fuel for the fire|Ossa mea sicut cremium aruerunt]]; [[Ps 101:6|Through the voice of my groaning, my bone hath cleaved to my flesh|a voce gemitus mei adhæsit os meum carni meæ]].

paras.t: Quapropter, id est, quum tanta sit generis humani ac mea calamitas in malis culpæ meæ, et ego non parcam ori meo, id est, propriam vilitatem ac vitia propalare et sacramentaliter confiteri non desinam: sed sponte et copiose me accusabo et humiliabo, ne vulnera animæ meæ intus abscondita permanentia, periculosius, imo et incurabiliter, putrefiant, quum dicat Scriptura: Qui abscondit scelera sua, non dirigetur; qui autem confessus fuerit et reliquerit ea, misericordiam consequetur.
paras.en: [[7:11|Wherefore|Quapropter]], that is, since the calamity of the human race and my own, in the evils of my guilt, is so great, [[7:11|I will not spare my mouth|et ego non parcam ori meo]], that is, I will not cease to make known my own vileness and vices and to confess them sacramentally: but of my own accord and abundantly I will accuse and humble myself, lest the wounds of my soul, remaining hidden within, should fester more dangerously, and even incurably; since Scripture says: [[Prov 28:13|He that hideth his sins, shall not prosper: but he that shall confess, and forsake them, shall obtain mercy|Qui abscondit scelera sua, non dirigetur; qui autem confessus fuerit et reliquerit ea, misericordiam consequetur]].

paras.t: Loquar in tribulatione spiritus mei, verba divina ac consolatoria proferendo: quemadmodum Jacobus edocet: Tristatur aliquis vestrum? oret æquo animo et psallat. Nam et hoc tribulationem tristitiamque internam diminuit, si foris per verba ordinata erumpat: intus etenim permanens clausa, plus cruciat. Hinc primo Regum sancta Anna fatetur: Ex multitudine doloris et mœroris mei locuta sum.
paras.en: [[7:11|I will speak in the affliction of my spirit|Loquar in tribulatione spiritus mei]], uttering divine and consoling words: as James teaches: [[Jas 5:13|Is any of you sad? Let him pray|Tristatur aliquis vestrum? oret]] with an even mind, and [[Jas 5:13|Let him sing|psallat]] [Denis reads *oret æquo animo et psallat*, “let him pray with an even mind, and sing”; the Vulgate has *oret. Æquo animo est? psallat*, “let him pray. Is he cheerful in mind? Let him sing”]. For this too lessens inward tribulation and sadness, if it breaks out outwardly in well-ordered words: for when it stays shut up within it torments the more. Hence in the first book of Kings holy Anna confesses: [[1 Kings 1:16|out of the abundance of my sorrow and grief have I spoken|Ex multitudine doloris et mœroris mei locuta sum]].

paras.t: Confabulabor cum amaritudine animæ meæ, comparando eam ad ea quæ passi sunt Christus et martyres ac alii sancti, quorum comparatione nullius est ponderis, faciliterque suffertur. Confabulabor quoque cum ea, ex qualitate meæ afflictionis seu pœnæ, considerando qualitatem et multitudinem peccatorum meorum. Vexatio namque dat intellectum: ideo multi infirmitatibus deprehensi, pensant, confitentur ac deflent vitia sua. Unde tribulatio vitæ præsentis, inter maxima Dei munera computatur: et nisi hæc esset, paucissimi salvarentur, sicut et S. Brigitta sibi asserit revelatum.
paras.en: [[7:11|I will talk with the bitterness of my soul|Confabulabor cum amaritudine animæ meæ]], comparing it with what Christ and the martyrs and the other saints suffered, in comparison with which it is of no weight and is easily borne. [[7:11|I will talk|Confabulabor]] with it also, considering from the quality of my affliction or punishment the quality and number of my sins. For vexation gives understanding[[Is 28:19||]] [the margin reads Is. xxvii; the saying is from Is 28:19, *sola vexatio intellectum dabit auditui*, “vexation alone shall make you understand what you hear”]: therefore many, overtaken by sickness, weigh, confess and bewail their vices. Hence the tribulation of the present life is counted among the greatest gifts of God: and were it not for this, very few would be saved, as St Bridget too asserts was revealed to her.

paras.t: Deinde anima ad contemplationis libertatem patriamque cœlestem anhelans, subjungit: Numquid mare ego sum aut cetus? secundum expositiones præhabitas; quia circumdedisti me carcere, id est corruptibili corpore me gravante ac deprimente, suisque indigentiis, infectionibus ac motibus, mille contemplandi impedimenta præbente, quemadmodum Plato comprobat in Phædone. Corpus enim quoad multa, carceri assimilatur. Propter quod orat vir sanctus: Educ de custodia (vel, ut alia habet translatio, de carcere) animam meam ad confitendum nomini tuo. Itaque viris heroicis seu divinis molestum est diu in carcere isto teneri, atque a felicitate differri.
paras.en: Then the soul, panting for the freedom of contemplation and for the heavenly fatherland, adds: [[7:12|Am I a sea, or a whale|Numquid mare ego sum aut cetus?]]? according to the explanations given before; [[7:12|that thou hast enclosed me in a prison|quia circumdedisti me carcere]], that is, with the corruptible body weighing me down and pressing on me, and by its needs, infections and movements putting a thousand hindrances in the way of contemplation, as Plato proves in the Phædo. For the body in many respects is likened to a prison. For which reason the holy man prays: [[Ps 141:8|Bring my soul out of prison|Educ de custodia]] (or, as another translation has it, *de carcere*) [the Vulgate has *de custodia*, “out of ward”, which the Douay-Rheims renders “out of prison”; the other translation has *de carcere*, “out of prison”, the word of Job's verse] [[Ps 141:8|that I may praise thy name|animam meam ad confitendum nomini tuo]]. So to heroic or godly men it is irksome to be held long in this prison and kept back from happiness.

paras.t: Si dixero, Consolabitur me lectulus meus, id est cordis cubile seu cogitatio ejus secreta, contemplationisve quies, et relevabor a gravitate afflictionis meæ, loquens mecum in stratu meo, id est intus considerando ea per quorum attentionem minuitur dolor; terrebis me per somnia, et per visiones horrore concuties. Quemadmodum enim homines timorati in die atque vigilia intente perpendunt districtum Dei judicium, angustias mortis, æternum illud intolerabile metuendissimumque supplicium, et quam supergravissimum sit a divino vultu in æternum repelli; sic talia frequenter in somno et visione seu imaginatione nocturna eis non sine pavore occurrunt.
paras.en: [[7:13|If I say: My bed shall comfort me|Si dixero, Consolabitur me lectulus meus]], that is, the chamber of the heart or its secret thought, or the rest of contemplation, [[7:13|and I shall be relieved|et relevabor]] from the weight of my affliction, [[7:13|speaking with myself on my couch|loquens mecum in stratu meo]], that is, considering inwardly the things by attention to which grief is lessened; [[7:14|Thou wilt frighten me with dreams, and terrify me with visions|terrebis me per somnia, et per visiones horrore concuties]]. For just as God-fearing men by day and in their waking hours intently weigh the strict judgment of God, the anguish of death, that eternal, unbearable and most dreadful punishment, and how supremely grievous it is to be driven away from the divine countenance for ever; so these things often come to them, not without dread, in sleep and in vision or nightly imagination.

paras.t: Porro, ut scribit Gregorius, Somnia interdum ventris plenitudine vel inanitate, aliquando vero illusione, aliquando cogitatione simul et illusione, aliquando autem revelatione, aliquando cogitatione simul et revelatione generantur. Prima duo genera omnes in nobis multoties experimur. Porro ex illusione nascuntur, dum ab hoste occulto, scilicet diabolo, ingeruntur. Propter quod scriptum est in Ecclesiastico: Multos errare fecerunt somnia. In Levitico quoque: Non augurabimini, nec observabitis somnia. Quod vero ex illusione simul et cogitatione interdum procedant, constat ex eo quod Salomon asserit: Multas curas sequuntur somnia. Quod autem vicissim ex revelatione sint, patet in somniis Joseph. Postremo, quod nonnunquam ex prævia cogitatione simul et revelatione oriantur, probatur per id quod Daniel somnium Nabuchodonosor regis interpretans ait: Tu, rex, cœpisti cogitare in stratu tuo, quid esset venturum post hæc; et qui revelat mysteria Deus, ostendit tibi quæ futura sunt.
paras.en: Further, as Gregory writes, dreams are produced sometimes by fullness or emptiness of the stomach, sometimes by illusion, sometimes by thought and illusion together, sometimes by revelation, and sometimes by thought and revelation together. The first two kinds we all experience in ourselves many times. They arise from illusion when they are put into us by the hidden enemy, that is, the devil. For which reason it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 34:7|dreams have deceived many|Multos errare fecerunt somnia]]. And in Leviticus: [[Lev 19:26|You shall not divine nor observe dreams|Non augurabimini, nec observabitis somnia]]. That they sometimes come from illusion and thought together is plain from what Solomon asserts: [[Eccles 5:2|Dreams follow many cares|Multas curas sequuntur somnia]]. That they come in turn from revelation is plain in the dreams of Joseph[[Gen 37:5||]][[Gen 37:9||]]. Lastly, that they sometimes arise from foregoing thought and revelation together is proved by what Daniel says when interpreting the dream of king Nabuchodonosor: [[Dan 2:29|Thou, O king, didst begin to think in thy bed, what should come to pass hereafter|Tu, rex, cœpisti cogitare in stratu tuo, quid esset venturum post hæc]]: [[Dan 2:29|and he that revealeth mysteries|et qui revelat mysteria]], God, [[Dan 2:29|shewed thee what shall come to pass|ostendit tibi quæ futura sunt]].

paras.t: Quamobrem, id est, quum tantæ sint meæ afflictiones, elegit suspendium, id est mentis elevationem ad alta, anima mea, ut ab inferioribus per considerationem suspensa, divinorum contemplationi intenta sit, quorum contemplatio contemplationisque delectatio, corporalium obliviscatur dolorum, et delectetur in Deo: quod fortissimum contra dolores exstat remedium. Siquidem quo anima actui unius potentiæ fortius est intendens, eo aliarum actus virium minus advertit. Et mortem ossa mea, id est, virtutes animæ meæ carnis mortificationem vivificam elegerunt: quemadmodum ait Apostolus: Mortificate membra vestra super terram. Caro enim et membra salubriter mortificantur, dum a propriis inclinationibus voluptatibusque frenantur, atque ab omni inordinato usu jugiter compescuntur. Sic namque et Christus jubet oculos erui, manus et pedes (si nos scandalizent) abscindi. Salubrius autem est tempore adversitatis, infirmitatis et afflictionis omnem carnalem delectationem et consolationem contemnere, atque in solo Deo refrigerium quærere, quam ad mitiganda adversa consolationem carnalem admittere, sicut fatetur Psalmista: Renuit consolari anima mea, memor fui Dei, et delectatus sum.
paras.en: [[7:15|So that|Quamobrem]], that is, since my afflictions are so great, [[7:15|my soul|anima mea]] [[7:15|rather chooseth hanging|elegit suspendium]], that is, the lifting up of the mind to high things, so that, held aloft from lower things by consideration and intent on the contemplation of divine things, through the contemplation of them and the delight of that contemplation it may forget bodily pains and delight in God: which is the strongest remedy against pain. For the more intently the soul is bent on the act of one power, the less it notices the acts of its other powers. [[7:15|and my bones death|Et mortem ossa mea]], that is, the virtues of my soul have chosen the life-giving mortification of the flesh: as the Apostle says: [[Col 3:5|Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth|Mortificate membra vestra super terram]]. For the flesh and the members are mortified to our health when they are reined in from their own inclinations and pleasures and continually held back from all disordered use. For so Christ too commands that the eyes be plucked out, and the hands and feet (if they scandalize us) be cut off[[Matt 18:9||]][[Matt 18:8||]]. Now in time of adversity, sickness and affliction it is more wholesome to despise all carnal delight and consolation and to seek refreshment in God alone, than to admit carnal consolation to soften adversity; as the Psalmist confesses: [[Ps 76:3|My soul refused to be comforted|Renuit consolari anima mea]], [[Ps 76:4|I remembered God, and was delighted|memor fui Dei, et delectatus sum]].

paras.t: Ideo subditur: Desperavi, id est, in exterioribus et terrenis nullam fiduciam habui, quia hæc totis præcordiis sprevi, cum Psalmista decantans: Concupiscit et deficit anima mea in atria Domini. Parce mihi, id est, peccatis meis ignosce; nihil enim sunt dies mei; juxta sensum præhabitum. Virtuosi etenim viri, quo verius, quo clarius divina et summa cognoscunt, eo subtilius terrena despiciunt: ideoque præsentis vitæ dies nil esse conspiciunt, quoniam illuminatos mentis suæ oculos in æternitatis consideratione defigunt.
paras.en: Therefore there is added: [[7:16|I have done with hope|Desperavi]], that is, I have put no trust in outward and earthly things, because I have scorned them with my whole heart, singing with the Psalmist: [[Ps 83:3|my soul longeth and fainteth for the courts of the Lord|Concupiscit et deficit anima mea in atria Domini]]. [[7:16|spare me|Parce mihi]], that is, pardon my sins; [[7:16|for my days are nothing|nihil enim sunt dies mei]]; according to the sense given before. For virtuous men, the more truly and the more clearly they know divine and highest things, the more keenly they despise earthly ones; and so they see that the days of the present life are nothing, since they fix the enlightened eyes of their mind on the consideration of eternity[[Eph 1:18||]].

paras.t: Verum, quoniam pars ista hujus capituli in Officiis defunctorum pro lectione assumitur, intuendum quid ad animas defunctorum in pœnis remedialibus exsistentes, pro quibus dumtaxat oratur, ista pertineant, et quomodo applicari his valeant. Itaque in persona hujusmodi animæ loquens Job, ait: Parce mihi. Anima namque in purgatorii pœnis consistens, postulat sibi parci, ne quantum meruit puniatur, sed secundum divinæ magnitudinem pietatis sibi de pœna quid remittatur, etiam per Ecclesiæ militantis suffragia, sed et per preces ac merita Beatorum. Nihil enim sunt dies mei, id est, tempora quibus temporaliter vixi, penitus transierunt, nec habeo tempus merendi, ita quod me ipsam nequeo adjuvare.
paras.en: But since this part of this chapter is taken as a lesson in the Office of the Dead [the first lesson of Matins of the Dead, which begins *Parce mihi, Domine*], we must consider how these words concern the souls of the dead who are in the remedial pains [that is, the cleansing pains of purgatory, as against the punishment of hell], for whom alone prayer is made, and how they can be applied to them. Job, then, speaking in the person of such a soul, says: [[7:16|spare me|Parce mihi]]. For the soul set in the pains of purgatory asks to be spared, that it may not be punished as much as it has deserved, but that something of its punishment may be remitted to it according to the greatness of the divine mercy, both through the suffrages of the Church militant and through the prayers and merits of the Blessed. [[7:16|for my days are nothing|Nihil enim sunt dies mei]], that is, the times in which I lived in time have wholly passed away, and I have no time of meriting, so that I cannot help myself.

paras.t: Insuper talis anima loquitur Deo: Quid est homo, quia magnificas eum? id est, quum tantæ sit fragilitatis, mirum quod opera ejus tam rigorose ac seriose advertis, judicas atque ulcisceris, quasi magnum aliquid sit: quem etiam per dona naturæ, per munera gratiæ, per dotesque gloriæ miro modo magnificas. Aut quid apponis erga eum cor tuum? sibi de necessariis quantum in te est providendo, et omnia ejus opera interiora ac exteriora diligentissime usque ad minimum quadrantem examinando ac judicando. Ideo ait Psalmista: Dominus sollicitus est mei. Verumtamen, non obstante hominis naturali imperfectione, præsertim quantum ad corpus, non injustum, sed penitus justum est, hominem sic curari, gubernari, judicari et præmiari a Deo, in quantum ratione ornatus est atque ad Creatoris sui imaginem factus, inter bonum et malum valens discernere, et quod placeat, libere potens eligere. Non enim dedit homini rationem, nisi ut ea utatur: liberumque arbitrium, nisi ut malis et falsis abjectis, veris ac bonis inhæreat: quod faciens, dignus est laude et præmio; omittens vero et oppositum agens, pœnam meretur. Exigit quoque sapientia et justitia Dei, ut unicuique quod meruit rependatur. Propter quod ait Psalmista ad Dominum: Numquid vane constituisti omnes filios hominum? Unde de insipientibus sapiens quidam scribit: Æstimaverunt lusum esse vitam nostram, et conversationem vitæ ad lucra compositam, et oportere undecumque acquirere. Præterea anima taliter loquitur admirative, ad provocandam Dei clementiam ad parcendum. Nam et in verbis his, quo amplius propriam naturam humiliat, eo plus Dei majestatem insinuat.
paras.en: Moreover such a soul says to God: [[7:17|What is a man, that thou shouldst magnify him|Quid est homo, quia magnificas eum]]? that is, since he is of such frailty, it is a wonder that thou dost so strictly and earnestly mark his works, judge and punish them, as though he were something great: him whom thou dost also wonderfully magnify through the gifts of nature, the gifts of grace, and the dowries of glory [that is, the endowments of the glorified soul and body]. [[7:17|or why dost thou set thy heart upon him?|Aut quid apponis erga eum cor tuum?]] providing him, as far as is in thee, with what he needs, and examining and judging all his works, inward and outward, most carefully, down to the last farthing. Therefore the Psalmist says: [[Ps 39:18|the Lord is careful for me|Dominus sollicitus est mei]]. Yet, notwithstanding man's natural imperfection, especially as to the body, it is not unjust but altogether just that man should be thus cared for, governed, judged and rewarded by God, inasmuch as he is adorned with reason and made to the image of his Creator, able to discern between good and evil and freely able to choose what pleases. For he gave man reason only that he might use it, and free will only that, casting away what is evil and false, he might cleave to what is true and good: doing which he is worthy of praise and reward; but leaving it undone and doing the opposite, he deserves punishment. The wisdom and justice of God also require that each be repaid what he has deserved. For which reason the Psalmist says to the Lord: [[Ps 88:48|hast thou made all the children of men in vain?|Numquid vane constituisti omnes filios hominum?]] Hence a certain wise man writes of the foolish: [[Wis 15:12|they have counted our life a pastime and the business of life to be gain, and that we must be getting every way|Æstimaverunt lusum esse vitam nostram, et conversationem vitæ ad lucra compositam, et oportere undecumque acquirere]]. Further, the soul speaks thus in wonder, to move the mercy of God to spare. For in these words, the more it humbles its own nature, the more it sets forth the majesty of God.

paras.t: Visitas eum diluculo, et subito probas illum. Hoc præcedenti articulo satis explanatum videtur. Visitatio autem Dei in Scripturis interdum in bono accipitur, scilicet pro beneficii impensione, quemadmodum in Luca: Benedictus Dominus Deus Israel, quia visitavit et fecit redemptionem plebis suæ. Quandoque in malo, videlicet pro justa ultione, ut dum per Sophoniam Dominus perhibet: Visitabo super viros defixos in fæcibus suis; et visitabo super omnem qui arroganter ingreditur. Denique probat Deus hominem tempore mortis, judicans qualiter vixit; atque deinceps per purgatorii ignem probat eum, qui sine mortali decedit, non plene mundatus, sicut probatur aurum in igne fornacis. Rursus, lumen gratiæ se habet ad lumen gloriæ, sicut aurora ad diem. Ideo Deus visitat eum diluculo in præsenti, id est, radio gratiæ suæ mentem ejus perfundit; subito autem hunc probat, quoniam vita tribulationibus plena est.
paras.en: [[7:18|Thou visitest him early in the morning, and thou provest him suddenly|Visitas eum diluculo, et subito probas illum]]. This seems to have been explained enough in the preceding article. Now God's visitation is sometimes taken in Scripture in a good sense, namely for the bestowing of a benefit, as in Luke: [[Luke 1:68|Blessed be the Lord God of Israel: because he hath visited and wrought the redemption of his people|Benedictus Dominus Deus Israel, quia visitavit et fecit redemptionem plebis suæ]]. Sometimes in a bad sense, namely for just vengeance, as when the Lord declares through Sophonias: I [[Soph 1:12|will visit upon the men that are settled on their lees|Visitabo super viros defixos in fæcibus suis]]; and [[Soph 1:9|I will visit|et visitabo]] [[Soph 1:9|upon every one that entereth arrogantly|super omnem qui arroganter ingreditur]] [the margin gives only Soph 1:12; these words are from Soph 1:9]. Lastly, God proves man at the time of death, judging how he has lived; and afterwards, through the fire of purgatory, he proves him who departs without mortal sin but not fully cleansed, as gold is proved in the fire of the furnace[[Wis 3:6||]]. Again, the light of grace is to the light of glory as the dawn is to the day. Therefore God visits him early in the morning in the present life, that is, he floods his mind with the ray of his grace; but he proves him suddenly, since life is full of tribulations.

paras.t: Usquequo non parcis mihi? id est, heu quod tam diu me punis et differs a gloria! Gloriæ quippe dilatio, animabus in purgatorio pœnalissima est atque gravissima. Imo gravior omni pœna sensibili vitæ præsentis, prout Thomas super quartum Sententiarum pulchre declarat. Sunt enim hujusmodi animæ vehementer affectuosæ, atque in caritate, et circa spiritualia tantum intentæ, in magno quoque tormento. Hinc breve tempus eis videtur longissimum. Ideo verba hæc querulosa proferunt voce. Nec dimittis me, a suppliciis evolare aut recreari, ut glutiam salivam meam? id est, caritatem aut sapientiæ donum, quibus ornata sum, ad beatificæ fruitionis saporem deducam. Quemadmodum enim saliva corpus humectat et sapidum efficit cibum, sic caritas et sapientia ceteras virtutes saporosas efficiunt, atque gratioso fluento has rigant: quæ glutiuntur, dum ad intimum mentis saporem in patria admittuntur; interim vero quasi aridæ sunt et absque sapore. Vel istud est parabolica locutio, ad insinuandum vehementiam purgatoriarum pœnarum.
paras.en: [[7:19|How long wilt thou not spare me|Usquequo non parcis mihi]]? that is, alas that thou punishest me so long and keepest me back from glory! For the delay of glory is most painful and most grievous to the souls in purgatory; indeed heavier than any pain of sense in the present life, as Thomas finely shows on the fourth book of the Sentences. For such souls are vehemently full of longing, and in charity, and intent on spiritual things alone, and in great torment as well. Hence a short time seems very long to them. Therefore they utter these words in a plaintive voice. [[7:19|nor suffer me|Nec dimittis me]] to fly away from my torments or to be refreshed, [[7:19|to swallow down my spittle?|ut glutiam salivam meam?]] that is, to bring the charity or the gift of wisdom with which I am adorned to the savour of beatific enjoyment. For as spittle moistens the body and makes food savoury, so charity and wisdom make the other virtues savoury [Denis plays on *sapientia*, “wisdom”, and *sapor*, “savour”, which are akin in Latin], and water them with a gracious stream: and they are swallowed when they are admitted to the inmost savour of the mind in the fatherland; but meanwhile they are as it were dry and without savour. Or else this is a figurative way of speaking, to suggest the vehemence of the pains of purgatory.

paras.t: Peccavi: ideo juste hæc patior, imo et citra condignum affligor. Hinc ista non loquor quasi tuæ derogans æquitati. Quid faciam tibi, o custos hominum? id est, jam per me satisfacere nequeo, mereri nil valeo, pro injuria quam tibi exhibui, recompensare nil possum. Itaque alios audi pro me, et quo impotentior ego sum, eo pietas tua ad parcendum sit pronior. Quare posuisti me contrarium tibi? id est, doleo quod me te offendere permisisti; nec in hoc te, sed me ipsum accuso, quoniam juste me taliter reliquisti. Verbum istud, sicut et cetera, in præcedenti articulo plenius habentur exposita. Et factus sum mihimetipsi gravis. Spiritus qui in purgatorio puniuntur, eo sibi ipsis sunt graviores, quo intensiori pœna premuntur. Dolent quoque de peccatis præteritis et Dei offensa, quia in caritate persistunt; hoc tamen dolore nil promerentur, quum non sint in statu merendi, qui terminatur in morte, sicut et via peregrinationis istius. Hinc (secundum Damascenum) quod angelis fuit ruina, hoc hominibus est mors.
paras.en: [[7:20|I have sinned|Peccavi]]: therefore I suffer these things justly, and indeed am afflicted less than I deserve. Hence I do not say these things as though detracting from thy equity. [[7:20|what shall I do to thee, O keeper of men?|Quid faciam tibi, o custos hominum?]] that is, I can no longer make satisfaction by myself, I can merit nothing, I can make no amends for the injury I have done thee. Therefore hear others for me, and the more powerless I am, the readier let thy mercy be to spare. [[7:20|why hast thou set me opposite to thee|Quare posuisti me contrarium tibi]]? that is, I grieve that thou hast permitted me to offend thee; and in this I accuse not thee but myself, since thou didst justly leave me so. This saying, like the others, has been explained more fully in the preceding article. [[7:20|and am I become burdensome to myself?|Et factus sum mihimetipsi gravis]] The spirits that are punished in purgatory are the more burdensome to themselves, the more intense the pain that presses them. They grieve too for their past sins and for the offence against God, since they persist in charity; yet by this grief they merit nothing, since they are not in the state of meriting, which ends with death, as does the way of this pilgrimage too. Hence (according to Damascene) what the fall was to the angels, death is to men [that is, after it the will can no longer turn to better or worse].

paras.t: Cur non tollis peccatum meum quantum ad pœnam, quod ante recessum a corpore abstulisti quantum ad culpam seu maculam vel obligationem ad pœnam æternam? Sic enim per contritionem deletum est, sed plene satisfactum non est. Ista sunt verba vehementis, dolorosi et amorosi simul et querulosi affectus: quæ magis pensanda sunt secundum intentionem mentalem, quam juxta sonum verborum. Ecce nunc in pulvere dormiam, id est, in venialibus meis, quantum ad debitum pœnæ manebo donec me liberes; vel, In pulvere, id est loco pœnali terreno; vel, In pulvere, id est mei ipsius humiliatione ac supplici veniæ affectione. Et si mane me quæsieris, id est, si cito vel quocumque tempore matutino me ad judicandum requisieris, seu tibi offerri præceperis, meque secundum rigorem justitiæ judicare volueris, non adjuncto dulcore clementiæ, non subsistam, id est, coram te stare et tuæ districtionis pondus ferre nequibo: ideo ad tuam pietatem confugio.
paras.en: [[7:21|Why dost thou not remove my sin|Cur non tollis peccatum meum]] as to the punishment, which thou didst take away before my departure from the body as to the guilt, or the stain, or the liability to eternal punishment? For so it was blotted out by contrition, but full satisfaction has not been made. These are the words of a vehement, sorrowful and loving, and at the same time plaintive affection: they are to be weighed rather by the intention of the mind than by the sound of the words. [[7:21|Behold now I shall sleep in the dust|Ecce nunc in pulvere dormiam]], that is, in my venial sins: as to the debt of punishment I shall remain in them until thou free me; or, [[7:21|in the dust|In pulvere]], that is, in an earthly place of punishment; or, [[7:21|in the dust|In pulvere]], that is, in the humbling of myself and a suppliant longing for pardon. [[7:21|and if thou seek me in the morning|Et si mane me quæsieris]], that is, if soon, or at whatever morning hour, thou shalt require me for judgment, or command me to be brought before thee, and wilt judge me by the rigour of justice, without the sweetness of mercy joined to it, [[7:21|I shall not be|non subsistam]], that is, I shall not be able to stand before thee and bear the weight of thy strictness: therefore I flee to thy mercy.

paras.t: Postremo, dum ista pro defunctis proferimus, affectuose atque intente agere id debemus, pensantes ineffabilem pœnarum eorum acerbitatem, vehementissimumque affectum quo sibi cupiunt subveniri; impotentiam quoque ipsorum, quoniam sibi ipsis non valent succurrere; itemque multiplicem, quem inde consequimur, fructum. Quum enim ex caritate pro eis quid agimus, non dubium quin vitam meremur æternam et caritatis ac gratiæ incrementum, aut certe ad tale incrementum aliquo modo disponimur. Defunctis autem seu animabus eorum nihil horum possumus promereri, quum non sint in statu proficiendi in caritate seu gratia; sed solum meremur eis pœnarum minorationem seu abbreviationem, et ex consequenti gloriæ accelerationem. Idcirco nobis ipsis per talia meremur vitam æternam, et caritatis ac gratiæ incrementum. Verumtamen, quo ex puriori Dei et proximi caritate egerimus ista atque similia, utpote non ad proprium commodum, sed ad Dei honorem ac gloriam, proximorumque salutem respicientes; eo amplius promeremur etiam nobis ipsis, ac crescimus. Idem equidem opus ex caritate procedens, est meritorium et satisfactorium: meritorium, quia ex caritate; satisfactorium, propter laborem adjunctum. Sicque prodest defunctis per applicationem ad eos: quibus etiam tanto plus prodest, quanto intentio atque dilectio amplius diriguntur ad ipsos. Nec dubium quin et animæ tales quum ad felicitatem pervenerint, orent fideliter pro oratoribus suis.
paras.en: Lastly, when we offer these things for the dead, we ought to do it affectionately and intently, weighing the unspeakable bitterness of their pains, and the most vehement longing with which they desire to be helped; their powerlessness too, since they cannot succour themselves; and likewise the manifold fruit we gain from it. For when we do anything for them out of charity, there is no doubt that we merit eternal life and an increase of charity and grace, or at least are in some way disposed to such an increase. But for the dead, or their souls, we can merit none of these things, since they are not in a state of advancing in charity or grace; we merit for them only the lessening or shortening of their pains, and in consequence the hastening of their glory. Therefore by such works we merit for ourselves eternal life and an increase of charity and grace. Yet the purer the charity towards God and neighbour with which we do these and like things, looking not to our own advantage but to the honour and glory of God and the salvation of our neighbours, the more we merit even for ourselves, and grow. For the same work, proceeding from charity, is both meritorious and satisfactory [that is, it both earns a reward and pays off the debt of punishment due to sin]: meritorious, because it is from charity; satisfactory, because of the labour joined to it. And so it profits the dead by being applied to them: and it profits them the more, the more the intention and love are directed to them. Nor is there any doubt that such souls, when they have come to happiness, pray faithfully for those who prayed for them.

paras.t: Merito quoque lectiones Officii pro defunctis, ex libro Job sumpta sunt, qui de generali resurrectione præ ceteris Prophetis evidentius vaticinatus censetur.
paras.en: Fittingly too the lessons of the Office for the dead are taken from the book of Job, who is held to have prophesied of the general resurrection more plainly than the other Prophets.

8.title: Expositio capituli octavi: Respondens autem Baldad Suhites, dixit.
8.title_en: Exposition of the eighth chapter: Then Baldad, the Suhite, answered, and said

paras.t: Expositores communiter dicunt, Gregorius quoque et Thomas id sentiunt, quod tres isti amici Job concorditer sentiebant, quod Deus in vita præsenti nulli homini infligat pœnam, nisi pro illius culpa. Hoc et ego aliquando sensi, quod scilicet concordabant in hoc, atque ob id putabant beatum Job divinæ derogare justitiæ, quia se dixit absque suo peccato plagatum, imo innocentem se esse ac justum, et nihilo minus flagellatum. Unde contra hoc tota eorum disputatio principaliter occupari videtur. Verumtamen, quum expositionem Alberti vidissem, incidi circa hoc dubitationem.
paras.en: The expositors commonly say, and Gregory and Thomas also hold, that these three friends of Job were of one mind in thinking that in the present life God inflicts punishment on no man except for his own fault. I too once thought so: that they agreed in this, and that for this reason they thought blessed Job was disparaging the divine justice, because he said that he had been struck without any sin of his, nay, that he was innocent and just, and was scourged nonetheless. Hence their whole disputation seems to be taken up chiefly against this. When I had seen the exposition of Albert, however, I fell into doubt about it.

paras.t: Ait namque Albertus in principio expositionis capituli tertii: Eliphaz ponit, quod gubernatio divina in rebus humanis est secundum merita, et quod bonis bona, et malis mala eveniant; sed quod aliquando lateat hominem, mala esse opera sua, et quod propter vilitatem naturæ homo sine peccato esse non possit. Propter quod dicit: Nihil in terra fit sine causa. Et: In angelis suis reperit pravitatem: quanto magis qui terrenum habent fundamentum, consumentur velut a tinea? Porro Baldad ponit, quod gubernatio non sit secundum merita, sed secundum ordinem optimum felicitatis humanæ. Et ideo, si Deus aliquando bonis mala pœnæ infligit, hoc in fine bonis multiplicibus recompensat; et si malis bona concedit, hoc fit ut justior sit eorum damnatio. Idque sonat in verbis suis. Nam dicit: Deus non projiciet simplicem, nec porriget manum malignis, donec impleatur risu os tuum. Præterea Sophar ponit, quod gubernatio Dei sit secundum solam ejus voluntatem, et illa quærenda non est, quia ab homine non potest cognosci. Ideo dicit: Forsitan vestigia Dei comprehendes, et usque ad perfectum Omnipotentem reperies? et: Si subverterit omnia, vel in unum coarctaverit, quis contradicet ei? Post hæc inducitur positio Eliu, qui cum tribus prædictis concordat, et maxime cum positione Sophar. Ideo dicit, quod Deus conteret multos et innumerabiles, et illius causa quærenda non est; et non addit ad hanc intentionem, nisi quod per mediatorem vel per se ipsum aliquando instruit, qualiter humana divinis debeant concordare. Et ideo dicit, Si fuerit angelus loquens pro eo unum de millibus; et quod per noctem erudit corda virorum et instruit disciplina. Gloriatur tamen de sapientia sua, quod hoc invenit post alios, et illam laudat in nubibus et fulgure.
paras.en: For Albert says at the beginning of his exposition of the third chapter [a note in the edition corrects this to "fourth": Eliphaz first speaks in chapter 4]: Eliphaz lays down that the divine government of human affairs is according to merits, and that good things befall the good and evil things the evil; but that it is sometimes hidden from a man that his works are evil, and that because of the baseness of his nature man cannot be without sin. For this reason he says: [[Job 5:6|Nothing upon earth is done without a cause|Nihil in terra fit sine causa]]. And: [[Job 4:18|in his angels he found wickedness|In angelis suis reperit pravitatem]]: [[Job 4:19|How much more shall they|quanto magis]] [[Job 4:19|who have an earthly foundation, be consumed as with the moth|qui terrenum habent fundamentum, consumentur velut a tinea]]? Baldad, then, lays down that the government is not according to merits, but according to the best order of human happiness. And so, if God sometimes inflicts the evils of punishment on the good, he makes it up to them in the end with manifold good things; and if he grants good things to the wicked, this is done so that their damnation may be the more just. And this is what his words convey. For he says: [[8:20|God will not cast away the simple, nor reach out his hand to the evil doer|Deus non projiciet simplicem, nec porriget manum malignis]], [[8:21|Until thy mouth be filled with laughter|donec impleatur risu os tuum]]. Further, Sophar lays down that God's government is according to his will alone, and that it is not to be inquired into, because it cannot be known by man. Therefore he says: [[Job 11:7|Peradventure thou wilt comprehend the steps of God, and wilt find out the Almighty perfectly?|Forsitan vestigia Dei comprehendes, et usque ad perfectum Omnipotentem reperies?]] and: [[Job 11:10|If he shall overturn all things, or shall press them together, who shall contradict him?|Si subverterit omnia, vel in unum coarctaverit, quis contradicet ei?]] After these the position of Eliu is brought in, who agrees with the three aforesaid, and most of all with the position of Sophar. Therefore he says that God [[Job 34:24|shall break in pieces many and innumerable|conteret multos et innumerabiles]], and that the cause of this is not to be inquired into; and he adds nothing to this meaning, except that God sometimes teaches, through a mediator or by himself, how human things ought to agree with divine ones. And so he says: [[Job 33:23|If there shall be an angel speaking for him, one among thousands|Si fuerit angelus loquens pro eo unum de millibus]]; and that by night[[Job 33:15||]] he teaches the hearts of men and instructs them with discipline[[Job 33:16||]]. Yet he glories in his own wisdom, that he found this out after the others[[Job 32:6||]] [the margin gives Job xxxii, 6–22], and praises it in the clouds and the lightning[[Job 37:2||]] [the margin gives Job xxxvii, 2–24].

paras.t: Hæc scribit Albertus loco jam nominato. Quibus, quantum ad ea quæ narrat de positione Baldad, obviare videtur quod in principio expositionis octavi capituli introducit, dicendo: Baldad convenit cum Eliphaz, quod mundus regitur secundum ordinem justitiæ: quod est retributio pro meritis. Sed addit duo, scilicet quod peccans, per pœnitentiam resurgere potest et judicium Dei effugere; item, quod si Deus aliquando punit in damnis vel rebus, dummodo punitus pœniteat, patienterque agat, multipliciter Deus recompensat in remuneratione pœnitentis. Ecce hoc loco subdit Albertus, quod secundum Baldad mundus regitur secundum ordinem justitiæ, quod est retributio pro meritis; superius vero asseruit, quod secundum Baldad gubernatio non fit secundum merita. Denique quod hic ait, ipsum Baldad duo addere positioni Eliphaz, scilicet quod peccans, per pœnitentiam resurgere, judiciumque Dei effugere potest, non videtur posse defendi; quia et ipse Eliphaz hoc ipsum apertissime fassus est, dicens: Beatus homo qui corripitur a Domino. Increpationem ergo Domini ne reprobes: quia ipse vulnerat, et medetur. Totumque residuum illius capituli pertinet ad hoc. Secundum quoque quod Albertus affirmat ipsum Baldad superaddere positioni Eliphaz, ipse Eliphaz tangit, dicendo: Scies quod pacem habeat tabernaculum tuum, et progenies tua quasi herba terræ. Ingredieris in abundantia sepulcrum, sicut infertur acervus tritici in tempore suo. Non intentione reprobandi Albertum Magnum hæc scribo, sed ut veritas elucescat: et is cui placet tenere Albertum, verba ejus resolvat, quæ mihi irresoluta videntur.
paras.en: This is what Albert writes in the place already named. But, as regards what he relates of the position of Baldad, it seems to be contradicted by what he puts forward at the beginning of his exposition of the eighth chapter, saying: Baldad agrees with Eliphaz that the world is ruled according to the order of justice, which is retribution for merits. But he adds two things: namely, that the sinner can rise again through penance and escape the judgment of God[[8:5||]] [the margin gives Job viii, 2–…, the last numeral not legible]; and further, that if God sometimes punishes with losses or in goods, provided the one punished repents and behaves patiently, God makes it up manifoldly in rewarding the penitent. See: here Albert states that according to Baldad the world is ruled according to the order of justice, which is retribution for merits; but above he asserted that according to Baldad the government is not according to merits. Then again, what he says here, that Baldad adds two things to the position of Eliphaz, namely that the sinner can rise again through penance and escape the judgment of God, does not seem defensible; for Eliphaz himself most openly professed this very thing, saying: [[Job 5:17|Blessed is the man whom God correcteth: refuse not, therefore, the chastising of the Lord|Beatus homo qui corripitur a Domino. Increpationem ergo Domini ne reprobes]]: [[Job 5:18|For he woundeth, and cureth|quia ipse vulnerat, et medetur]]. And the whole rest of that chapter bears on this. The second thing, too, which Albert affirms that Baldad adds to the position of Eliphaz, Eliphaz himself touches on, saying: [[Job 5:24|And thou shalt know that thy tabernacle is in peace|Scies quod pacem habeat tabernaculum tuum]], [[Job 5:25|and thy offspring like the grass of the earth|et progenies tua quasi herba terræ]]. [[Job 5:26|Thou shalt enter into the grave in abundance, as a heap of wheat is brought in its season.|Ingredieris in abundantia sepulcrum, sicut infertur acervus tritici in tempore suo]] I do not write this with the intention of finding fault with Albert the Great, but that the truth may shine out; and let him who is pleased to hold with Albert resolve his words, which seem to me unresolved.

paras.t: Itaque, cum B. Gregorio sanctoque Thoma id sentio, quod amici Job concorditer tenuerunt pœnam pro sola culpa infligi. Unde unanimiter arguunt contra Job, oppositum affirmantem. Diversis tamen argumentis utuntur, quamvis ad eamdem tendant conclusionem. Unde non sequitur, quod diversæ inter se fuerint opinionis ob id, quod varias habent assertiones ac multiplicia media seu multiformes præmissas: hoc quippe quotidie in disputationibus ita se habet; et in prosecutione præsentis capituli atque sequentium clare patebit, amicorum sancti Job unam esse opinionem circa providentiam Dei ac regimen universi.
paras.en: And so, with blessed Gregory and holy Thomas, I hold that the friends of Job were of one mind in holding that punishment is inflicted for fault alone. Hence they argue with one accord against Job, who affirms the opposite. Yet they use different arguments, though they tend to the same conclusion. So it does not follow that they were of different opinions from one another because they make various assertions and have many middle terms, or premisses of many forms [that is, the steps of a syllogism]: for so it goes every day in disputations; and in going through the present chapter and those that follow it will be clearly seen that the friends of holy Job have one opinion about the providence of God and the government of the universe.

paras.t: Postremo, aliqui expositiones suas litterales pro magna parte fundant in hoc, quod amici Job non posuerunt vitam post hanc vitam, sed animam rationalem esse mortalem. Quod dictum, superius evidenter ex verbis amicorum Job improbatum recordor, evidentiusque pelletur, nec aliquam (quantum capio) apparentiam habet. Nihilo minus textus sicut hucusque expositus est, ita deinceps, præstante Spiritu veritatis, litteraliter exponetur.
paras.en: Lastly, some ground their literal expositions in great part on this: that the friends of Job did not hold a life after this life, but held the rational soul to be mortal. I recall that this saying was clearly disproved above from the words of the friends of Job, and it will be refuted more clearly still; nor has it (as far as I can grasp) any appearance of truth. Nevertheless, as the text has been expounded up to now, so it will be expounded literally from here on, by the help of the Spirit of truth.

paras.t: Itaque Baldad post Eliphaz principalis, audita assertione beati Job, et objectione Eliphaz, responsione quoque Job ad verba Eliphaz, reputans objectionem Eliphaz concludentem, responsionemque Job insufficientem, imo insipientem et inconvenientia non parum augentem, nunc objicit contra Job, volens dicta Eliphaz confirmare. Itaque dicitur: Respondens autem, id est proportionate (ut sibi apparuit) loquens ad verba Job, Baldad Suhites, dicit: Usquequo loqueris talia præsumptuosa, ad tui justificationem, divinæque æquitatis derogationem spectantia, utpote quod sine tuo demerito sis percussus a Deo, et diei nativitatis tuæ maledixisti? quasi dicat: Periculose et pertinaciter verba multiplicas. Et spiritus multiplex sermonis oris tui? Spiritus quandoque pro ira seu indignatione accipitur, quandoque pro anima. Dupliciter ergo hoc verbum exponitur. Primo sic: Spiritus sermonis oris tui, id est ira seu indignatio vel impatientiæ passio, ex qua tua procedit locutio, est multiplex, magna, perseverans et varia; et nunc de isto, nunc de illo turbaris, ex turbationeque loqueris. Ita secundum Glossam, accipitur spiritus in Genesi, ubi Dominus loquitur: Non permanebit spiritus meus in homine in æternum, quia caro est. Potest tamen ibidem spiritus aliter sumi. Secundo sic: Spiritus sermonis oris tui, id est mens seu anima tua, quæ prorupit in verba præhabita, est multipliciter passionata, divisa, distracta, non in Deo simplificata ac recollecta. Ideo frivola profers et inordinata, non condependentia. His verbis consonat, quod infra ait contra Job Eliphaz: Docuit iniquitas tua os tuum, et imitaris linguam blasphemantium.
paras.en: And so Baldad, the chief after Eliphaz, having heard the assertion of blessed Job[[Job 3:1||]] and the objection of Eliphaz[[Job 4:1||]], and also Job's response to the words of Eliphaz[[Job 6:1||]] [the margin's reference here is hard to read; it seems to give chapters iii–vii], and judging the objection of Eliphaz conclusive and Job's response insufficient, nay foolish, and adding not a little to what was unfitting, now objects against Job, wishing to confirm what Eliphaz had said. And so it is said: [[8:1|answered|Respondens autem]], that is, speaking in proportion to the words of Job (as it seemed to him) [that is, to the point of what Job had said], [[8:1|Baldad, the Suhite|Baldad Suhites]], [[8:1|and said|dicit]]: [[8:2|How long wilt thou speak these things|Usquequo loqueris talia]], presumptuous things, tending to thy own justification and to the disparagement of the divine equity, as that thou hast been struck by God without any demerit of thine, and that thou hast cursed the day of thy birth? as if to say: Dangerously and stubbornly thou multipliest words. [[8:2|and how long shall the words of thy mouth be like a strong wind?|Et spiritus multiplex sermonis oris tui]] [literally "and the spirit of the speech of thy mouth is manifold": spiritus is wind or breath, and Denis takes it as anger and as soul]. Spirit is sometimes taken for anger or indignation, sometimes for the soul. This word, then, is expounded in two ways. First thus: the spirit of [[8:2|the words of thy mouth|sermonis oris tui]], that is, the anger or indignation or passion of impatience from which thy speech proceeds, is manifold: great, persistent and various; and now thou art troubled about this, now about that, and out of thy trouble thou speakest. So, according to the Gloss, spirit is taken in Genesis, where the Lord says: [[Gen 6:3|My spirit shall not remain in man for ever, because he is flesh|Non permanebit spiritus meus in homine in æternum, quia caro est]]. Yet spirit can be taken otherwise there too. Secondly thus: the spirit of [[8:2|the words of thy mouth|sermonis oris tui]], that is, thy mind or soul, which has burst out into the words spoken before, is manifoldly passionate [that is, stirred by the passions], divided, distracted, not made simple and recollected in God. Therefore thou utterest frivolous and disordered things that do not hang together. With these words agrees what Eliphaz says further on against Job: [[Job 15:5|thy iniquity hath taught thy mouth, and thou imitatest the tongue of blasphemers|Docuit iniquitas tua os tuum, et imitaris linguam blasphemantium]].
