paras.t: Numquid Deus supplantat, id est præcipitat aut opprimit, judicium, id est sententiæ prolationem seu æquitatis effectum judicando non recte? aut Omnipotens subvertit quod justum est? quasi dicat: Nequaquam; et tamen ex verbis tuis, o Job, hoc infertur, quoniam dicis te sine tua culpa percussum. Justum autem est unicuique reddere quod meretur. Si ergo justus et innocens es plagatus, contra justitiam fecit Deus. Ex hoc elicitur, quod Baldad concordavit cum Eliphaz, opinando quod Deus non nisi pro culpa infligeret pœnam: et etiam, quod non intellexit profunditatem verborum Job, quibus præcedentibus duobus capitulis, præsertim in principio capituli septimi, oppositum docuit. Ideo argumentum Baldad non procedit. Quamvis enim justum sit pro culpa pœnam infligi, non tamen semper est contra justitiam, infligere pœnam pro alia causa quam pro culpa, videlicet pro gratiæ incremento, pro gloriæ cumulo, pro bono communi, quod est proximorum ædificatio. Nec ratio justi consistit solum in hoc, ut retribuatur pro meritis; sed et in aliis multis salvatur ratio justi. Nam et Deus tam bonus et pius est, ut justum sit eum peccatoribus misereri. Ipse quoque tam sapiens est, ut justum sit eum justos adversitatibus exercere ad majorem eorum profectum, et pro bono communi fidelium. Unde hoc modo omnia argumenta amicorum Job carent vera syllogistica forma. Estque in eis fallacia aliqua; sed apud minus peritos prima facie quamdam apparentiam sortiuntur. Et nonnunquam superficialiter sumpta, rationabiliora apparent quam verba Job; sed secundum intentionem loquentium sumpta, longe aliter inveniuntur.
paras.en: [[8:3|Doth God pervert|Numquid Deus supplantat]] [supplantat, literally "trip up"], that is, throw down or overpower, [[8:3|judgment|judicium]], that is, the passing of sentence or the effect of equity, by judging not rightly? [[8:3|or doth the Almighty overthrow that which is just|aut Omnipotens subvertit quod justum est]]? as if to say: By no means; and yet this is what follows from thy words, O Job, since thou sayest that thou hast been struck without fault of thine. Now it is just to render to each what he deserves. If then thou hast been struck while just and innocent, God has acted against justice. From this it is gathered that Baldad agreed with Eliphaz in thinking that God would inflict punishment only for fault; and also that he did not understand the depth of Job's words, in which, in the two preceding chapters, and especially at the beginning of the seventh chapter, he taught the opposite. Therefore Baldad's argument does not hold. For although it is just that punishment be inflicted for fault, yet it is not always against justice to inflict punishment for some other cause than fault: namely, for the increase of grace, for the heaping up of glory, for the common good, which is the edification of one's neighbours. Nor does the notion of the just consist only in this, that retribution be made for merits; the notion of the just is preserved in many other things as well. For God is so good and kind that it is just for him to have mercy on sinners. He is also so wise that it is just for him to exercise the just with adversities, for their greater progress and for the common good of the faithful. Hence in this way all the arguments of Job's friends lack true syllogistic form. And there is some fallacy in them; but with the less skilled they have, at first sight, a certain appearance of truth. And sometimes, taken superficially, they appear more reasonable than Job's words; but taken according to the meaning of those who speak, they are found to be far otherwise.

paras.t: Etiamsi, id est quamvis, et quia (secundum mentem hujus Baldad), filii tui peccaverunt ei, id est contra Deum, et dimisit eos in manu, id est in vigore et actu, iniquitatis eorum, permittens eos usque ad horam mortis peccare, atque in actu et intenso affectu impietatis deprehendi ac obrui, quando videlicet erant pariter epulantes; tu tamen si diluculo, id est cito seu tempestive, consurrexeris ad Deum, id est, a terrenis, imis ac vitiosis affectibus mentem tuam ad Deum levaveris per veram contritionem: juxta id Ecclesiastici: Ne tardes converti ad Dominum, et ne differas de die in diem, subito enim veniet ira illius; et Omnipotentem fueris deprecatus pro remissione tuorum excessuum;
paras.en: [[8:4|Although|Etiamsi]], that is, though, and also because (according to the mind of this Baldad) [that is, Baldad means that the sin was the cause of what followed], [[8:4|thy children have sinned against him|filii tui peccaverunt ei]], that is, against God, [[8:4|and he hath left them in the hand|et dimisit eos in manu]], that is, in the force and act, [[8:4|of their iniquity|iniquitatis eorum]] [a note in the edition gives the reading suæ, as in the Vulgate], allowing them to sin up to the hour of death, and to be caught and overwhelmed in the act and the intense affection of impiety, when, that is, they were feasting together: [[8:5|Yet if thou wilt arise early|tu tamen si diluculo]], that is, quickly or in good time, [[8:5|to God|consurrexeris ad Deum]], that is, if thou raisest thy mind to God from earthly, low and vicious affections by true contrition, according to that of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 5:8|Delay not to be converted to the Lord, and defer it not from day to day|Ne tardes converti ad Dominum, et ne differas de die in diem]], [[Ecclus 5:9|For his wrath shall come on a sudden|subito enim veniet ira illius]]; [[8:5|and wilt beseech the Almighty|et Omnipotentem fueris deprecatus]] for the remission of thy excesses;

paras.t: si mundus mente a cogitationibus vanis et affectionibus passionum inordinatis, et rectus, id est justus in conversatione, incesseris, id est, per viam hujus peregrinationis ad futuram beatitudinem ambulaveris, non declinando ad dexteram aut sinistram; statim evigilabit ad te, id est, cito exaudiet te, seque tibi gratiosum præbebit per modum vigilantis, qui tibi in tuis adversis quasi dormiens fuit, solita beneficia sua subtrahens tibi: juxta id Psalmistæ, Exsurge, quare obdormis, Domine? Hinc in Joanne habetur: Si quis cultor est Dei, et voluntatem ejus facit, hunc exaudit. Et pacatum reddet tabernaculum justitiæ tuæ, id est domum et familiam tuam, tuæ justitiæ merito tibi donandam, ita quod pax erit tibi et cunctis tuis opibus atque domesticis; in tantum, ut priora tua, id est divitiæ et familiæ, quas aliquando habuisti, fuerint parva, comparatione sequentium bonorum tibi dandorum, et novissima tua, id est bona tibi in ultima tua ætate præstanda, multiplicentur nimis, id est, valde abundent.
paras.en: [[8:6|If thou wilt walk clean|si mundus]] in mind from vain thoughts and disordered affections of the passions, [[8:6|and upright|et rectus]], that is, just in thy way of life, [[8:6|walk|incesseris]], that is, if thou wilt journey along the way of this pilgrimage to the beatitude to come, not turning aside to the right or to the left: [[8:6|he will presently awake unto thee|statim evigilabit ad te]], that is, he will quickly hear thee, and show himself gracious to thee after the manner of one awake, who in thy adversities was as one asleep to thee, withdrawing from thee his accustomed benefits; according to that of the Psalmist: [[Ps 43:23|Arise, why sleepest thou, O Lord?|Exsurge, quare obdormis, Domine?]] Hence we have in John: [[John 9:31|if a man be a server of God and doth his, will, him he heareth|Si quis cultor est Dei, et voluntatem ejus facit, hunc exaudit]]. [[8:6|and will make the dwelling of thy justice peaceable|Et pacatum reddet tabernaculum justitiæ tuæ]] [a note in the edition gives the reading habitaculum, "dwelling", as in the Vulgate, for tabernaculum, "tent"], that is, thy house and household, to be given thee by the merit of thy justice, so that there will be peace for thee and for all thy goods and servants; [[8:7|In so much, that|in tantum, ut]] [a note gives the reading ut si, "that if", as in the Vulgate] [[8:7|if thy former things|priora tua]], that is, the riches and households which thou once hadst, [[8:7|were small|fuerint parva]] in comparison with the good things to be given thee afterwards, [[8:7|thy latter things|et novissima tua]], that is, the goods to be bestowed on thee in thy last age, [[8:7|would be multiplied exceedingly|multiplicentur nimis]], that is, would abound greatly.

paras.t: Quamvis autem ista Baldad promissio in ipso Job fuit impleta, quantum ad hoc, quod post maximam adversitatem ad maximam reductus est in hoc sæculo prosperitatem; universaliter tamen vera non est, nec in his qui pro suis plagantur peccatis, neque in his qui sine prævio suo demerito affliguntur: nam de utroque genere percussorum istorum multi usque ad mortem permanent in adversis.
paras.en: Now although this promise of Baldad was fulfilled in Job himself, in that after the greatest adversity he was brought back to the greatest prosperity in this world, yet it is not true universally, either of those who are struck for their own sins or of those who are afflicted without any demerit of theirs going before: for of both these kinds of the stricken, many remain in adversity until death.

paras.t: Insuper Baldad dictum suum nititur confirmare communi testimonio seniorum, et per scripta ipsorum. Interroga enim generationem pristinam, id est antiquam atque præteritam, non illos qui diu defuncti sunt alloquendo, sed dicta et scripta seu gesta eorum legendo; et diligenter investiga patrum memoriam, id est memorabilia facta; vel ea quæ eorum recordationibus continentur, quærendo ab his quid eorum occurrat memoriæ circa hæc: sicque de patribus adhuc viventibus loquitur Baldad. Juniores autem a senioribus eruditionem sumere debent, quemadmodum in Deuteronomio habetur: Interroga patrem tuum, et annuntiabit tibi; majores tuos, et dicent tibi. Et Ezechias loquitur Deo: Pater filiis notam faciet veritatem tuam. Unde Ecclesiasticus docet: Ne te prætereat narratio seniorum, et ipsi enim didicerunt a patribus suis: quoniam ab ipsis disces intellectum, et in tempore necessitatis dabis responsum.
paras.en: Moreover, Baldad tries to confirm what he says by the common testimony of the elders, and by their writings. [[8:8|For inquire of the former generation|Interroga enim generationem pristinam]], that is, the ancient and past one: not by speaking to those who died long ago, but by reading their sayings and writings or deeds; [[8:8|and search diligently into the memory of the fathers|et diligenter investiga patrum memoriam]], that is, the memorable deeds; or what is held in their recollections, by asking them what comes to their memory about these things: and so Baldad is speaking of fathers still living. Now the younger ought to take instruction from the older, as we have in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 32:7|ask thy father, and he will declare to thee: thy elders and they will tell thee|Interroga patrem tuum, et annuntiabit tibi; majores tuos, et dicent tibi]]. And Ezechias says to God: [[Is 38:19|the father shall make the truth known to the children|Pater filiis notam faciet veritatem tuam]]. Hence Ecclesiasticus teaches: [[Ecclus 8:11|Let not the discourse of the ancients escape thee, for they have learned of their fathers|Ne te prætereat narratio seniorum, et ipsi enim didicerunt a patribus suis]]: [[Ecclus 8:12|For of them thou shalt learn understanding, and to give an answer in time of need.|quoniam ab ipsis disces intellectum, et in tempore necessitatis dabis responsum]]

paras.t: Hesterni quippe sumus, id est heri nati, intelligendo per Heri, tempus non diu præteritum: sicut per Cras frequenter exprimitur tempus post pauca futurum. Et loquitur sic, ad insinuandum brevitatem vitæ præsentis. Et ignoramus quæ diu elapsa sunt, quia pauca conspeximus; et ea quæ scimus, minima sunt comparatione eorum quæ ignoramus; præsentisque brevitas vitæ non sinit nos omnia discere. Unde sacerdotes Ægypti gentiles dixerunt Soloni adhuc minus decrepito: Non est in vobis (scilicet Græcis) ulla cana scientia; ut habetur primo Timæi. Hincque subjungitur, quoniam sicut umbra dies nostri sunt super terram, id est instabiles, celerrime transeuntes, juxta illud Sapientiæ: Transibit vita nostra tanquam vestigium nubis, et sicut nebula dissolvetur. Umbræ enim transitus est tempus nostrum.
paras.en: [[8:9|For we are but of yesterday|Hesterni quippe sumus]], that is, born yesterday, understanding by "yesterday" a time not long past, as by "tomorrow" is often expressed a time to come after a little while. And he speaks thus to suggest the shortness of the present life. [[8:9|and are ignorant|Et ignoramus]] of the things that passed long ago, because we have seen few things; and the things we know are very small in comparison with those we do not know; and the shortness of the present life does not allow us to learn everything. Hence the gentile priests of Egypt said to Solon, who was not yet very old: There is not among you (that is, the Greeks) any hoary knowledge [that is, learning grown old with age]; as we have in the first book of the Timaeus [of Plato]. And hence is added: [[8:9|that our days upon earth are but a shadow|quoniam sicut umbra dies nostri sunt super terram]], that is, unstable, passing most swiftly; according to that of Wisdom: [[Wis 2:3|our life shall pass away as the trace of a cloud, and shall be dispersed as a mist|Transibit vita nostra tanquam vestigium nubis, et sicut nebula dissolvetur]]. [[Wis 2:5|For our time is as the passing of a shadow|Umbræ enim transitus est tempus nostrum]].

paras.t: Ipsi docebunt te verbo scripto aut memorabili facto; loquentur tibi, per se, vel per scripta quæ reliquerunt, et de corde suo proferent eloquia, id est non ficte aut false, sed ex corde pandent quod verum est, utpote quod dicta a me in isto capitulo, vera sint. Porro, sapientes de corde loquuntur, videlicet ex præmeditatione sagaci, et circumspecte; stulti autem, de ore, juxta quod Ecclesiasticus inducit: In ore fatuorum cor illorum, et in corde sapientium os illorum. Verba autem hic Baldad, quibus asserit pristinos et antiquos suæ assertioni consentientes, vera non sunt, si de vere sapientibus intelligantur, quamvis illis temporibus et ante multi fuerunt opinionis ejusdem cum amicis Job, scilicet Deum non infligere pœnam nisi pro culpa; quodque pœnitens rediret in vita hac ad prosperitatem terrenam.
paras.en: [[8:10|And they shall teach thee|Ipsi docebunt te]] by the written word or by memorable deed; [[8:10|they shall speak to thee|loquentur tibi]], by themselves, or through the writings they left; [[8:10|and utter words out of their hearts|et de corde suo proferent eloquia]], that is, not feignedly or falsely, but from the heart they will lay open what is true: namely, that what I have said in this chapter is true. Now the wise speak from the heart, that is, with shrewd forethought and circumspectly; but fools from the mouth, according to what Ecclesiasticus puts forward: [[Ecclus 21:29|The heart of fools is in their mouth: and the mouth of wise men is in their heart|In ore fatuorum cor illorum, et in corde sapientium os illorum]]. But these words of Baldad here, in which he asserts that the men of former and ancient times agree with his assertion, are not true if they are understood of the truly wise; although in those times and before many were of the same opinion as the friends of Job: namely, that God inflicts punishment only for fault, and that the penitent would return in this life to earthly prosperity.

paras.t: Consequenter Baldad dicta sua confirmat per similitudinem in naturalibus rebus compertam. Numquid vivere vita vegetativa, id est, crescere, florere, durare, potest scirpus, id est juncus, absque humore? Indiget enim indesinenter humore saltem sub terra latente. Circa quod scribit Albertus: Quoniam scirpus absque omni nodo est, nihil habet in quo stet nutrimentum ipsius. Idcirco non viret, nisi continue trahat humorem. Nodus enim in calamo vel planta ad hoc est, ad quod est stomachus vel intestinum, quod dicitur involutum in homine vel animali, ut ibi stet et inde dirigatur nutrimentum ad membra, nec cogatur continuo sollicitari pro nutrimento. Intenditque dicere, quod Job fuit sicut scirpus extra virens, et intus vanus, continue sumens humorem seu nutrimentum per avaritiam. Aut carectum crescere sine aqua? quasi dicat, Non nisi in aqua crescit: quia loca aquosa requirit. Carectum vero proprie dicitur locus, quo crescit herba, nomine carex; sed hic pro ipsa herba accipitur, quæ acuta atque durissima fertur. Unde Albertus: Carectum (inquit) gladiolus est, qui etiam nodum non habet in foliis, et viret extra, intusque vanum est; et per eamdem causam, qua scirpus, esse nequit sine continuo tractu humoris et aquæ; dilatatur quoque in foliis: quod scirpus non facit.
paras.en: Next Baldad confirms what he has said by a likeness found in natural things. [[8:11|Can the rush be green|Numquid vivere]] [vivere, "live"; a note in the edition gives the reading virere, "be green", which the Douay-Rheims follows] with vegetative life, that is, grow, flower and last, — [[8:11|the rush|scirpus]], that is, the juncus [another word for a rush], — [[8:11|without moisture|absque humore]]? For it needs moisture without ceasing, at least moisture hidden under the earth. On this Albert writes: Since the rush is without any knot, it has nothing in which its nourishment may stay. Therefore it is not green unless it draws moisture continually. For the knot in a reed or plant serves the purpose that the stomach serves, or the intestine, which is called the coiled one, in a man or an animal: that the nourishment may stay there and be directed from there to the members, and the plant not be forced to seek nourishment continually. And he means to say that Job was like the rush, green outside and empty within, continually taking in moisture or nourishment through avarice. [[8:11|or sedge bush grow without water|Aut carectum crescere sine aqua]]? as if to say: It grows only in water, because it needs watery places. Carectum properly means the place where a plant called carex [sedge] grows; but here it is taken for the plant itself, which is said to be sharp and very hard. Hence Albert: Carectum (he says) is the gladiolus [a plant with sword-shaped leaves], which also has no knot in its leaves, and is green outside and empty within; and for the same reason as the rush it cannot exist without a continual drawing of moisture and water; it also spreads out in its leaves, which the rush does not.

paras.t: Quum adhuc sit in flore, id est vigore atque virore scirpus sive carectum, nec carpatur manu, id est, violenter non extrahatur de terra, ante omnes herbas arescit, id est citius aliis per subtractionem vel defectum humoris aut aquæ. Præterea, secundum Albertum, scirpus verum non habet florem, sed loco floris in summitate sui emittit virgulas parvas et breves. Carectum quoque est duplex, videlicet majus et minus: majus, in extremis folii planum et lene est; minus autem, dentatum et asperum, valdeque incisivum, ut falx metentis: et hoc non carpitur manu, quia secaret manum carpentis seu capientis. Et intendit, quod Job ita odivit correptionem, quod tangi manu corripientis non potuit: ad tactum enim conturbatur, qui correptionem non sustinet.
paras.en: [[8:12|When it is yet in flower|Quum adhuc sit in flore]], that is, in vigour and greenness, the rush or the sedge, [[8:12|and is not plucked up with the hand|nec carpatur manu]], that is, is not pulled out of the earth by force, [[8:12|it withereth before all herbs|ante omnes herbas arescit]], that is, sooner than the others, through the withdrawal or lack of moisture or water. Further, according to Albert, the rush has no true flower, but in place of a flower it puts out at its top little short twigs. The sedge, too, is of two kinds, namely greater and lesser: the greater is flat and smooth at the edges of the leaf; but the lesser is toothed and rough, and very cutting, like the sickle of a reaper; and this one is not plucked with the hand, because it would cut the hand of him who plucks or takes it. And he means that Job so hated correction that he could not be touched by the hand of one who corrects: for he who does not bear correction is troubled at a touch.

paras.t: Sic viæ, id est operationes et studia, omnium qui obliviscuntur Deum, vel ejus non reminiscendo, vel ejus mandata non observando. Aliqui enim frequenter legunt, loquuntur, audiuntque de Deo, et tamen ei non obediunt, nec habent ejus memoriam amorosam, formatam et efficacem. Ideo dicuntur eum obliti, quemadmodum Deum non cognoscere asseruntur, qui mandatis ipsius non obsequuntur. Et spes hypocritæ, qui aliud intus abscondit, aliud forinsecus exhibet, peribit, id est, optato bono frustrabitur, aut certe cito privabitur: quod sicut sine humore non potest subsistere scirpus sive carectum, sic impia conversatio, vanaque spes damnabuntur, et non valent diu florere, eo quod careant rore gratiæ cœlestis, et aqua sapientiæ salutaris, fecundatione et irrigatione donorum Spiritus Sancti. Ideo dicit Psalmista: Iter impiorum peribit. Et iterum: Convertantur peccatores in infernum, omnes gentes quæ obliviscuntur Deum. In Ecclesiaste quoque habetur: Non sit bonum impio, nec prolongentur dies ejus; sed quasi umbra transeant, qui non timent faciem Domini. Et Sapiens: Spes impii tanquam lanugo est, quæ a vento tollitur; et quasi spuma, et tanquam memoria hospitis unius diei prætereuntis.
paras.en: [[8:13|Even so are the ways|Sic viæ]], that is, the works and pursuits, [[8:13|of all that forget God|omnium qui obliviscuntur Deum]], either by not remembering him or by not keeping his commandments. For some often read, speak and hear about God, and yet do not obey him, nor have a loving remembrance of him, formed and effective [that is, given its form by charity, and so living]. Therefore they are said to have forgotten him, just as those who do not follow his commandments are said not to know God. [[8:13|and the hope of the hypocrite|Et spes hypocritæ]], who hides one thing within and shows another outside, [[8:13|shall perish|peribit]], that is, will be cheated of the good it longs for, or at any rate soon deprived of it: for as the rush or the sedge cannot survive without moisture, so an impious way of life and a vain hope will be condemned, and cannot flourish long, because they lack the dew of heavenly grace and the water of saving wisdom, the fruitfulness and the watering of the gifts of the Holy Ghost. Therefore the Psalmist says: [[Ps 1:6|the way of the wicked shall perish|Iter impiorum peribit]]. And again: [[Ps 9:18|The wicked shall be turned into hell, all the nations that forget God|Convertantur peccatores in infernum, omnes gentes quæ obliviscuntur Deum]]. In Ecclesiastes too we have: [[Eccles 8:13|let it not be well with the wicked, neither let his days be prolonged, but as a shadow let them pass away that fear not the face of the Lord|Non sit bonum impio, nec prolongentur dies ejus; sed quasi umbra transeant, qui non timent faciem Domini]] [the margin's reference here is badly read; the passage is Eccles. viii, 13]. And the Wise Man: [[Wis 5:15|the hope of the wicked is as dust, which is blown away with the wind|Spes impii tanquam lanugo est, quæ a vento tollitur]]; [[Wis 5:15|and as a thin froth|et quasi spuma]], [[Wis 5:15|and as the remembrance of a guest of one day that passeth by|et tanquam memoria hospitis unius diei prætereuntis]].

paras.t: Non ei placebit vecordia sua, id est, Deo non placebit, imo et maxime displicebit vecordia, id est insania seu insipientia hypocritæ, cujus hæc insania est, quod in operibus ex genere bonis magis quærit hominibus placere quam Deo, laudem humanam quam divinam, commodum temporale quam fructum æternum. Ideo in Proverbiis scriptum est: Qui vanus et vecors est, patebit contemptui. Vel, Non placebit ei, id est hypocritæ, sua vecordia: quia dum viderit se optatis bonis fraudari, et ob suam vanitatem damnari, displicebit sibi insipientia sua, in quantum est meritoria pœnæ quam horret. Hinc in libro Sapientiæ impii dicunt: Quid nobis profuit superbia? aut quid divitiarum jactantia contulit nobis? Transierunt omnia illa tanquam umbra. Et sicut tela aranearum, quæ debilis est et parvo motu destruitur, fiducia ejus: quia (ut dictum est) spes ejus peribit, et vanis rebus innititur, atque æternis suppliciis punietur. Hinc loquitur Psalmista Deo: Propter iniquitatem corripuisti hominem, et tabescere fecisti sicut araneam animam ejus. Et Isaias: Opus eorum opus inutile; telas araneæ texuerunt.
paras.en: [[8:14|His folly shall not please him|Non ei placebit vecordia sua]], that is, it will not please God, nay, it will greatly displease him: the folly, that is, the madness or senselessness, of the hypocrite, whose madness is this, that in works good in their kind [that is, good by what they are, whatever the intention] he seeks to please men rather than God, human praise rather than divine, temporal gain rather than eternal fruit. Therefore it is written in Proverbs: [[Prov 12:8|he that is vain and foolish, shall be exposed to contempt|Qui vanus et vecors est, patebit contemptui]]. Or: [[8:14|His folly|sua vecordia]] [[8:14|shall not please him|Non placebit ei]], that is, the hypocrite: because when he sees himself cheated of the good things he longed for, and condemned for his vanity, his folly will displease him, inasmuch as it deserves the punishment that he dreads. Hence in the book of Wisdom the wicked say: [[Wis 5:8|What hath pride profited us? or what advantage hath the boasting of riches brought us?|Quid nobis profuit superbia? aut quid divitiarum jactantia contulit nobis?]] [[Wis 5:9|All those things are passed away like a shadow|Transierunt omnia illa tanquam umbra]]. [[8:14|and his trust|fiducia ejus]] [[8:14|shall be like the spider's web|Et sicut tela aranearum]], which is weak and is destroyed by a slight movement: because (as has been said) his hope shall perish, and it leans on vain things, and will be punished with eternal torments. Hence the Psalmist says to God: [[Ps 38:12|Thou hast corrected man for iniquity. And thou hast made his soul to waste away like a spider|Propter iniquitatem corripuisti hominem, et tabescere fecisti sicut araneam animam ejus]]. And Isaias: [[Is 59:6|their works are unprofitable works|Opus eorum opus inutile]]; they [[Is 59:5|have woven the webs of spiders|telas araneæ texuerunt]].

paras.t: Innitetur super domum suam, id est, in divitiis, sobole, familia, ceterisque ad se pertinentibus temporalibus rebus, spem suam constituet. Quocontra scriptum est: Quis ambulat in tenebris? Speret in nomine Domini, et innitatur super Deum suum. Et non stabit, id est, spes talis eum non liget in bono, sed corruet ipse cum sua fiducia, quia non innititur stabili fundamento, videlicet summo et incommutabili bono, sed rebus caducis. Propterea scriptum est in Jeremia: Maledictus homo qui confidit in homine, et ponit carnem brachium suum, et a Domino recedit cor ejus: erit enim quasi myricæ in deserto. Fulciet eam, id est, domum suam muniet contra adversa, et non consurget, id est, nec ipse, nec domus ejus ad veram ac stabilem prosperitatem perveniet.
paras.en: [[8:15|He shall lean upon his house|Innitetur super domum suam]], that is, he will set his hope on riches, offspring, household and the other temporal things that belong to him. Against this it is written: Who [[Is 50:10|hath walked in darkness|ambulat in tenebris]]? [[Is 50:10|let him hope in the name of the Lord, and lean upon his God|Speret in nomine Domini, et innitatur super Deum suum]]. [[8:15|and it shall not stand|Et non stabit]], that is, such hope will not hold him fast in good, but he will fall together with his trust, because he does not lean on a stable foundation, namely the highest and unchangeable good, but on perishable things. For this reason it is written in Jeremias: [[Jer 17:5|Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the Lord|Maledictus homo qui confidit in homine, et ponit carnem brachium suum, et a Domino recedit cor ejus]]: [[Jer 17:6|For he shall be like tamaric in the desert|erit enim quasi myricæ in deserto]]. [[8:15|he shall prop it up|Fulciet eam]], that is, he will fortify his house against adversity, [[8:15|and it shall not rise|et non consurget]], that is, neither he nor his house will come to true and stable prosperity.

paras.t: Humectus videtur (supple, scirpus), id est humore aqueo irrigatus, antequam veniat sol, humorem exsiccans, viriditatemque auferens, et in ortu suo, id est statim in ortu scirpi, germen ejus, id est fructus ejus nulli usui aptus, egreditur, quia celeriter crescit et fructificare videtur. Vel, In ortu suo, id est, sole oriente, germen ejus egreditur, id est, perit solis calore loca paludis siccante: siquidem humidum aqueum insipidum, faciliter epotabile atque siccabile est a sole. Per hoc intendit, quod simili modo impius seu hypocrita prosperatur et floret, antequam superveniat ei æstus adversitatis, seu fervor divini judicii, qui per solem notatur: quo veniente, falsa perit prosperitas, et latens aperitur impietas.
paras.en: [[8:16|He seemeth to have moisture|Humectus videtur]] (supply: the rush), that is, watered with watery moisture, [[8:16|before the sun cometh|antequam veniat sol]], which dries up the moisture and takes away the greenness; [[8:16|and at his rising|et in ortu suo]], that is, straightway at the springing up of the rush, [[8:16|his blossom|germen ejus]], that is, its fruit, fit for no use, [[8:16|shall shoot forth|egreditur]] [a note in the edition gives the reading egredietur, as in the Vulgate], because it grows quickly and seems to bear fruit. Or: [[8:16|at his rising|In ortu suo]], that is, when the sun rises, [[8:16|his blossom|germen ejus]] [[8:16|shall shoot forth|egreditur]] [egreditur, "goes out", here taken as "passes away"], that is, perishes by the heat of the sun drying up the marshy places: for a watery, tasteless moisture is easily drunk up and dried by the sun. By this he means that in like manner the impious man or the hypocrite prospers and flourishes before the heat of adversity, or the fervour of the divine judgment, which is signified by the sun, comes upon him: and when it comes, the false prosperity perishes and the hidden impiety is laid open.

paras.t: Super acervum petrarum radices ejus densabuntur, id est, radices scirporum in locis petrosis ac humidis multiplicabuntur, ita quod plurimi scirpi ibi concrescent, et inter lapides commorabitur, id est, scirpus manebit in hujusmodi locis lapidosis ad tempus.
paras.en: [[8:17|His roots shall be thick upon a heap of stones|Super acervum petrarum radices ejus densabuntur]], that is, the roots of the rushes will multiply in stony and moist places, so that very many rushes will grow up together there; [[8:17|and among the stones he shall abide|et inter lapides commorabitur]], that is, the rush will remain in such stony places for a time.

paras.t: Si absorbuerit eum de loco suo, id est, si quis extraxerit scirpum de loco quo stat, ut eum alibi plantet, negabit eum, et dicet: Non novi te, id est, scirpus negabit extrahentem, et dicet ei, Non novi te, id est, alibi non crescam sicut intendis, nec tibi consentiam. Itaque negat et dicit hæc non verbo, sed facto, non formaliter, sed materialiter: quemadmodum in Scripturis, inanimatis actus adscribuntur vitales, ut ibi: Valles abundabunt frumento; clamabunt, etenim hymnum dicent: sicque Deum laudare dicuntur. Vel sic: Negabit eum, id est, scirpum negabit locus ejus, et dicet, Non novi te, id est, mihi amplius non poteris implantari.
paras.en: [[8:18|If one swallow him up out of his place|Si absorbuerit eum de loco suo]], that is, if anyone pulls the rush out of the place where it stands, to plant it elsewhere, [[8:18|he shall deny him, and shall say: I know thee not|negabit eum, et dicet: Non novi te]], that is, the rush will deny the one pulling it out, and will say to him, [[8:18|I know thee not|Non novi te]], that is: I will not grow elsewhere as thou intendest, nor will I consent to thee. So it denies and says this not in word but in deed, not formally but materially [that is, not by an act of its own, but by what happens to it]: as in the Scriptures the acts of living things are ascribed to inanimate things, as here: [[Ps 64:14|the vales shall abound with corn: they shall shout, yea they shall sing a hymn|Valles abundabunt frumento; clamabunt, etenim hymnum dicent]]: and so they are said to praise God. Or thus: [[8:18|he shall deny him|Negabit eum]], that is, its place shall deny the rush, [[8:18|and shall say: I know thee not|et dicet, Non novi te]], that is: thou canst no more be planted in me.

paras.t: Hæc est enim lætitia viæ ejus, id est lætitia naturalis processus seu proprietatis scirpi, et rursum de terra alii germinentur, id est, ut ipso extracto, non idem ipse rursum nascatur, sed alii similes specie sibi succedant. Sicque lætitia metaphorice adscribitur scirpo, secundum quod unicuique rei corruptibili appetibile est perpetuari in simili sibi secundum speciem, ut ait Philosophus. Per ista intendit, quod impius per mortem sublatus, non revertetur ad vitam hanc, sed oblivioni tradetur, et alii in loco ejus succedent: ex quibus principaliter intenta concludit.
paras.en: [[8:19|For this is the joy of his way|Hæc est enim lætitia viæ ejus]], that is, the joy of the natural course or property of the rush, [[8:19|that others may spring again out of the earth|et rursum de terra alii germinentur]], that is, that when it has been pulled out, not the same one grows again, but others like it in kind succeed it. And so joy is ascribed to the rush metaphorically, in that for every corruptible thing it is desirable to be continued in something like itself in kind, as the Philosopher [Aristotle] says. By these things he means that the impious man, taken away by death, will not return to this life, but will be given over to oblivion, and others will succeed in his place: and from this he concludes what he chiefly intends.

paras.t: Deus non projiciet simplicem, id est, veraciter virtuosum, et mente in Deo simplificatum, qui in omnibus intentionem suam figit in Deo, talem utique Deus non spernit nec deserit; nec porriget manum, id est auxilium, malignis: quod in tantum verum est, o Job, quod experieris hoc in te ipso, si pœnitentiam egeris. Ideo subdit, donec impleatur risu os tuum, et labia tua jubilo, id est, tantam prosperitatem susceperis, quod tanta erit tibi inde jucunditas cordis, quod redundabit in corpus. Sicque ridebis, et ineffabili quodam gaudio perfunderis, ita quod mentis lætitiam exprimere labiis non valebis. Jubilus autem essentialiter inest menti, sed per redundantiam in corpore ponitur.
paras.en: [[8:20|God will not cast away the simple|Deus non projiciet simplicem]], that is, the truly virtuous man, made simple in mind in God, who in all things fixes his intention on God: such a one God certainly does not spurn or forsake; [[8:20|nor reach out his hand|nec porriget manum]], that is, help, [[8:20|to the evil doer|malignis]]: which is so true, O Job, that thou wilt experience it in thyself if thou doest penance. Therefore he adds: [[8:21|Until thy mouth be filled with laughter, and thy lips with rejoicing|donec impleatur risu os tuum, et labia tua jubilo]], that is, until thou receivest such prosperity that thy joy of heart from it will be so great that it will overflow into the body. And so thou wilt laugh, and be flooded with a certain unspeakable gladness, so that thou wilt not be able to express the joy of thy mind with thy lips. Now jubilation [jubilus, the Douay-Rheims's "rejoicing": joy too great for words] is in the mind essentially, but it is placed in the body by overflow.

paras.t: Denique, quamvis vera sint verba hæc secundum sanum piumque sensum, non tamen secundum loquentis intentionem. Baldad quippe inducit hæc contra Job, ad insinuandum quod Deus non desinit virtuosum adversitatibus exercere, sed a talibus eum tuetur; et quod impiis non det in vita hac prosperitatem saltem notabilem, seu magnam et longam: cujus oppositum constat ab initio sæpius contigisse. Verum est tamen, quod Deus non projicit simplicem, quantum ad spiritualia gratiæ bona, nec quantum ad talia, porrigit manum malignis in malitia sua manentibus, juxta illud Proverbiorum: Longe est Dominus ab impiis.
paras.en: Lastly, although these words are true in a sound and pious sense, yet they are not true according to the meaning of the one who speaks. For Baldad puts them forward against Job to suggest that God does not exercise the virtuous man with adversities [the Latin reads non desinit, "does not cease"; the sense requires "does not", perhaps non sinit], but protects him from such things; and that he does not give the impious in this life any prosperity that is at least notable, that is, great and long: the opposite of which, it is plain, has very often happened from the beginning. Yet it is true that God does not cast away the simple as regards the spiritual goods of grace, nor, as regards such goods, does he reach out his hand to the evil who remain in their malice; according to that of Proverbs: [[Prov 15:29|The Lord is far from the wicked|Longe est Dominus ab impiis]].

paras.t: Qui oderunt te, induentur confusione, et tabernaculum, id est opulentia seu prosperitas, et quidquid ad bona domus pertinet, impiorum non subsistet stabiliter, sed auferetur eis ac disperibit, secundum opinionem amicorum Job, quanquam secundum veritatem frequenter contingat, impios usque ad mortem, in omni terrena prosperitate florere, imo usque ad ultimam senectutem.
paras.en: [[8:22|They that hate thee, shall be clothed with confusion|Qui oderunt te, induentur confusione]]: [[8:22|and the dwelling|et tabernaculum]], that is, the wealth or prosperity, and whatever belongs to the goods of a house, [[8:22|of the wicked shall not stand|impiorum non subsistet]] firmly, but will be taken from them and will perish utterly; so according to the opinion of Job's friends, although in truth it often happens that the impious flourish in all earthly prosperity until death, nay, until extreme old age.

paras.t: Ideo quoque Baldad de hypocrita mentionem induxit, quoniam propter plagam quam vidit in Job, putavit eum non virtuosum fuisse ac simplicem, sed duplicem animo atque hypocritam: quod et alii duo, imo et Eliu, putaverunt; tamen ante hanc plagam tenuerunt eum pro viro eximie virtuoso.
paras.en: Baldad also brought in mention of the hypocrite for this reason: because of the stroke he saw in Job, he thought that he had not been virtuous and simple, but double-minded and a hypocrite. So too the other two thought, and Eliu as well; yet before this stroke they held him to be a man of outstanding virtue.

8.title: Mystica elucidatio ejusdem capituli octavi.
8.title_en: Mystical explanation of the same eighth chapter

paras.t: Sicut præhabitum est, per Job, quilibet veraciter justus et tribulationibus plenus signatur; per amicos autem ipsius, ficte virtuosi et sapientes in oculis propriis exprimuntur. Talis ergo quicumque ait ad Job, id est hominem virtuosum afflictum, nec aliquo modo a via justitiæ recedentem, sed veritatem in omnibus docentem et defendentem: Usquequo loqueris talia, et spiritus multiplex sermones oris tui? Injustis enim gravia esse solent verba justorum; et dum corrigi nolunt, recte prolata criminantur. Insuper, quum se increpari considerant, increpantem non ex rationis judicio, sed impetu passionis, variisque inordinatis affectionibus loqui testantur; quod item mensuram loquendi aut non perpendat, aut nesciat: imo se ipsos sapientiores ac meliores illo esse aut aperte profantur, aut implicite innuunt, sed et verba loquentis interrumpere solent. Ideo Sapiens ait: Sapientior sibi piger videtur septem viris loquentibus sententias.
paras.en: As was said before, by Job is signified any man who is truly just and full of tribulations; and by his friends are expressed those who are feignedly virtuous and wise in their own eyes. Any such man, then, says to Job, that is, to the virtuous man in affliction, who in no way departs from the way of justice but teaches and defends the truth in all things: [[8:2|How long wilt thou speak these things|Usquequo loqueris talia]], [[8:2|and how long shall the words of thy mouth be like a strong wind?|et spiritus multiplex sermones oris tui?]] For the words of the just are wont to be grievous to the unjust; and since they will not be corrected, they find fault with what is rightly said. Moreover, when they see themselves rebuked, they declare that the one rebuking them speaks not from the judgment of reason but from the impulse of passion and from various disordered affections; and likewise that he either does not weigh the measure of his speaking or does not know it: nay, they either openly declare or tacitly hint that they themselves are wiser and better than he, and they are wont even to interrupt the words of the speaker. Therefore the Wise Man says: [[Prov 26:16|The sluggard is wiser in his own conceit, than seven men that speak sentences|Sapientior sibi piger videtur septem viris loquentibus sententias]].

paras.t: Numquid Deus supplantat judicium? Prædicti ficte virtuosi et intus vani, ut amplius reputentur et prævalere putentur, aliqua vera et pulchra atque ad Dei excellentiam laudemque spectantia, tamen ad propositum secundum veritatem non pertinentia, jactanter solent proferre, quasi talibus verbis dicta aut facta justorum quibus reprehenduntur, repugnent, sicut et Baldad egisse hic legitur. Porro, quum Deus essentialiter verus, justus ac sapiens sit, nequaquam supplantat, sed conservat diligitque judicium, dicente Psalmista: Quia Dominus amat judicium. Et Isaias: Deus judicii Dominus. Sed quoniam incomprehensibilia sunt judicia Dei, interdum videtur hominibus humanum sensum sequentibus, non desuper unctis, esse supplantatio judicii, quod Deus æquissimo agit aut permittit judicio.
paras.en: [[8:3|Doth God pervert judgment|Numquid Deus supplantat judicium]]? [Denis's word *supplantat* means literally "trip up" or "overthrow"; the Douay-Rheims has "pervert".] Those aforesaid men, feignedly virtuous and inwardly vain, so as to be more highly esteemed and thought to prevail, are wont boastfully to bring forth things that are true and fair and that bear on the excellence and praise of God, yet in truth are not to the purpose, as though with such words they could refute the sayings or deeds of the just by which they are reproved; as Baldad is here read to have done. Now since God is essentially true, just and wise, He in no way perverts judgment, but keeps and loves it, as the Psalmist says: [[Ps 36:28|For the Lord loveth judgment|Quia Dominus amat judicium]]. And Isaias: [[Is 30:18|the Lord is the God of judgment|Deus judicii Dominus]]. But since the judgments of God are incomprehensible[[Rom 11:33||]], it sometimes seems to men who follow human sense, and are not anointed from above, that there is a perverting of judgment in what God does or permits by a most equitable judgment.

paras.t: Etiamsi filii tui, id est discipuli aut subditi seu imitatores, peccaverunt ei, et dimisit eos Deus in manu iniquitatis eorum, ita quod in mortali peccato defuncti sunt, æternaliterque damnati sunt; tu tamen si diluculo consurrexeris ad Deum, statim evigilabit ad te. Perversi dum caritative arguuntur, passionate redarguunt, et vitia sibi vere objecta aut similia in arguentem false retorquent. Ne tamen ex passionis ardore loqui cernantur, quasi amorose ad emendationem hortantur, veniamque promittunt. Sed hoc prorsus vitandum est: imo si quispiam etiam non vere reprehendatur, debet patienter audire, et ceteros suos defectus atque excessus advertere, nec reprehendentem pro tunc increpare aut durius alloqui.
paras.en: [[8:4|Although thy children|Etiamsi filii tui]], that is, thy disciples or subjects or imitators, [[8:4|have sinned against him, and he hath left them|peccaverunt ei, et dimisit eos Deus]] (God, that is) [[8:4|in the hand of their iniquity|in manu iniquitatis eorum]], so that they died in mortal sin and were eternally damned; [[8:5|Yet if thou wilt arise early to God|tu tamen si diluculo consurrexeris ad Deum]], [[8:6|he will presently awake unto thee|statim evigilabit ad te]]. When the perverse are charitably reproved, they reprove in return out of passion, and falsely turn back upon the one reproving them the vices truly charged against themselves, or the like. Yet lest they be seen to speak from the heat of passion, they exhort him to amendment as if lovingly, and promise him pardon. But this is to be wholly avoided: nay, even if someone is reproved untruly, he ought to listen patiently, and to consider his other defects and excesses, and not rebuke the one reproving him at that time, nor speak to him too harshly.

paras.t: Præterea verba hæc Baldad, quamvis beato Job non recte fuerint applicata, nihilominus secundum se sumpta, venustate ac veritate ornantur. Pater enim non portabit iniquitatem filii, nec econtra, ut Ezechiel asserit. Et quantumcumque alii perierint, quamdiu aliquis manet in vita hac, pœnitere potest ac veniam adipisci. Primo itaque debet peccator diluculo ad Deum consurgere, id est cito mentaliter pœnitere, et de bonis creatis, caducis et vanis, ad Creatorem suum se vertere per ejus cognitionem et amorem: deinde ad orationes se dare, pro malis delendis et bonis spiritualibus adipiscendis. Oratio quoque est præcipua pars satisfactionis. Tertio debet operationibus virtuosis constanter insistere, hoc est munde et recte incedere, Deoque in sanctitate et justitia deservire: quæ quum impleverit homo, Deus statim evigilabit ad eum, dando quod petit salubriter et constanter ac etiam pro se ipso, juxta illud Isaiæ: Miserans miserebitur tui; ad vocem clamoris tui statim, ut audierit, respondebit.
paras.en: Further, these words of Baldad, though not rightly applied to blessed Job, are nonetheless, taken in themselves, adorned with beauty and truth. For [[Ezech 18:20|the father shall not bear the iniquity of the son|Pater enim non portabit iniquitatem filii]], nor the other way about, as Ezechiel asserts. And however many others have perished, so long as a man remains in this life he can repent and obtain pardon. First, then, the sinner ought to arise early to God, that is, quickly to repent in mind, and to turn from created goods, fleeting and vain, to his Creator, by knowing and loving Him; next, to give himself to prayer, for the blotting out of evils and the obtaining of spiritual goods. Prayer, too, is the chief part of satisfaction. Thirdly, he ought to persevere steadily in virtuous works, that is, to walk clean and upright, and to serve God in holiness and justice; and when a man has fulfilled these things, God will presently awake unto him, giving what he asks for his salvation, and steadily, and even for His own sake, according to that word of Isaias: [[Is 30:19|he will surely have pity on thee|Miserans miserebitur tui]]; [[Is 30:19|at the voice of thy cry, as soon as he shall hear, he will answer thee|ad vocem clamoris tui statim, ut audierit, respondebit]].

paras.t: Postremo, secundum diversas considerationes, dicitur Deus super eumdem dormire et vigilare. Super impium enim dormit, in quantum eum relinquit, nec per gratiam visitat: super quem etiam vigilat, in quantum sibi pœnam pro culpa infligit. Propter quod ait per Jeremiam: Sicut vigilavi super eos ut evellerem, sic vigilabo super eos ut ædificem et plantem. Qui ergo cupit divinitus exaudiri, studeat divinæ voluntati per obedientiam conformari, irreprehensibiliter conversari, verbisque opera concordare. Alioqui advertat quod scriptum est: Qui declinat aurem suam ne audiat legem, oratio ejus erit exsecrabilis. Quo equidem divinæ voluntati quis conformiorem se ipsum præbuerit, ardentiusque Deum dilexerit, et irreprehensibilius ei servierit; eo erit carior, intimior et familiarior Deo, et eum tanquam amicum carissimum Deus copiose etiam in magnis exaudiet: imo affectum ejus antequam in verba prorumpat, aut incepta compleat, adspiciet et implebit, sicut per Isaiam testatur de talibus: Antequam clament, exaudiam eos; adhuc illis vociferantibus dicam, Ecce adsum.
paras.en: Lastly, according to different considerations, God is said both to sleep and to watch over the same man. For He sleeps over the wicked man inasmuch as He leaves him and does not visit him by grace; and He also watches over him inasmuch as He inflicts on him punishment for his fault. Wherefore He says by Jeremias: [[Jer 31:28|as I have watched over them, to pluck up|Sicut vigilavi super eos ut evellerem]], [[Jer 31:28|so will I watch over them, to build up, and to plant them|sic vigilabo super eos ut ædificem et plantem]]. Let him, then, who desires to be heard by God strive to be conformed to the divine will by obedience, to live blamelessly, and to make his deeds agree with his words. Otherwise let him consider what is written: [[Prov 28:9|He that turneth away his ears from hearing the law, his prayer shall be an abomination|Qui declinat aurem suam ne audiat legem, oratio ejus erit exsecrabilis]]. Indeed, the more conformable a man makes himself to the divine will, the more ardently he loves God, and the more blamelessly he serves Him, the dearer, the closer and the more familiar he will be to God; and God will hear him abundantly, even in great things, as a very dear friend: nay, He will look upon his desire and fulfil it before it breaks forth into words, or before he finishes what he has begun, as He testifies of such men by Isaias: [[Is 65:24|before they call, I will hear|Antequam clament, exaudiam eos]]; while they are still crying out I will say, [[Is 58:9|Here I am|Ecce adsum]] [the margin gives Is. lxv, 24 and Is. lviii, 9; Denis joins the two passages].

paras.t: Et pacatum reddet habitaculum justitiæ tuæ: id est, corpus tuum (in quo anima tua degit) faciet rationis judicio cum tranquillitate subjectum, ne de cetero more solito militet contra animam atque recalcitret; in tantum, ut priora tua fuerint parva, id est, pristina spiritualia gratiarum charismata modica fuerint respectu sequentis tuæ perfectionis: quia, ut ait Salvator, Abundanti dabitur, ut plus abundet; et profectus parit profectum, unaque actio virtuosa disponit ad aliam. Ideo monet Apostolus: Æmulamini charismata meliora. Et iterum: Abundantes in opere Domini semper. Et novissima tua, id est dona gloriæ tibi in patria conferenda, multiplicentur nimis. Deus enim, sicut citra condignum reprobos punit, sic supra condignum electos remunerat. Et quamvis sint quatuor dotes corporis glorificati, et tres animi, quantum ad principales pertinet dotes illorum, tamen in particulari innumerabilia nobis sunt munera ac gaudia Beatorum. Nam et innumerabiles eis sunt materiæ gaudiorum.
paras.en: [[8:6|and will make the dwelling of thy justice peaceable|Et pacatum reddet habitaculum justitiæ tuæ]]: that is, He will make thy body (in which thy soul dwells) subject in tranquillity to the judgment of reason, so that it no longer fights against the soul and kicks against it as it was wont; [[8:7|In so much, that if thy former things were small|in tantum, ut priora tua fuerint parva]], that is, if the former spiritual gifts of graces were slight in respect of thy perfection that is to follow: for, as the Saviour says, To him that aboundeth shall be given, that he may abound the more[[Matt 25:29||]]; and progress begets progress, and one virtuous act disposes to another. Therefore the Apostle admonishes: [[1 Cor 12:31|be zealous for the better gifts|Æmulamini charismata meliora]]. And again: [[1 Cor 15:58|always abounding in the work of the Lord|Abundantes in opere Domini semper]]. [[8:7|thy latter things|novissima tua]], that is, the gifts of glory to be bestowed on thee in the fatherland, [[8:7|would be multiplied exceedingly|multiplicentur nimis]]. For as God punishes the reprobate short of their desert, so He rewards the elect beyond their desert [that is, *citra condignum* and *supra condignum*: less, and more, than is strictly due]. And though there are four endowments of the glorified body and three of the soul, so far as their principal endowments go, yet in particular the gifts and joys of the Blessed are to us beyond number. For they have, too, numberless matters of joy.

paras.t: Interroga enim generationem pristinam: id est, testimonio Patriarcharum ac Prophetarum antiqui temporis hoc discere potes. Ideo subditur: Ipsi docebunt te. Prædicta enim verbis illorum probantur. Nam et de abundantia proficiendi in gratia fertur in Psalmo: Ibunt de virtute in virtutem. De exuberantia vero donorum gloriæ rursus ait Psalmista: Inebriabuntur ab ubertate domus tuæ, et torrente voluptatis tuæ potabis eos. Et in Isaia habetur: Oculus non vidit, Deus, absque te, quæ præparasti exspectantibus te. His verbis superbi et scioli confunduntur, qui a majoribus aut senioribus suis seu doctioribus discere aspernantur. Qui autem veraciter sapiens est, semper discere cupit, ut probat Cyrillus. Propter quod scriptum est: Sapientiam omnium antiquorum exquiret sapiens, et in Prophetis vacabit.
paras.en: [[8:8|For inquire of the former generation|Interroga enim generationem pristinam]]: that is, thou canst learn this from the testimony of the Patriarchs and Prophets of ancient time. Therefore it is added: [[8:10|they shall teach thee|Ipsi docebunt te]]. For what has been said is proved by their words. For of the abundance of progress in grace it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 83:8|they shall go from virtue to virtue|Ibunt de virtute in virtutem]]. And of the overflowing of the gifts of glory the Psalmist says again: [[Ps 35:9|They shall be inebriated with the plenty of thy house; and thou shalt make them drink of the torrent of thy pleasure|Inebriabuntur ab ubertate domus tuæ, et torrente voluptatis tuæ potabis eos]]. And in Isaias we have: [[Is 64:4|the eye hath not seen, O God, besides thee, what things thou hast prepared for them that wait for thee|Oculus non vidit, Deus, absque te, quæ præparasti exspectantibus te]]. By these words the proud and the smatterers are confounded, who disdain to learn from their elders or seniors or from the more learned. But he who is truly wise always desires to learn, as Cyril proves. Wherefore it is written: [[Ecclus 39:1|The wise man will seek out the wisdom of all the ancients, and will be occupied in the prophets|Sapientiam omnium antiquorum exquiret sapiens, et in Prophetis vacabit]].

paras.t: Numquid vivere potest scirpus absque humore? aut carectum crescere sine aqua? De his herbis et quid designetur per eas, dictum est præcedenti articulo. Quibus etiam verbis consonat in Evangelio Christus, dicens semen aruisse, quia humorem non habuit. Et de homine virtuoso loquitur Jeremias: Erit tanquam lignum quod transplantatur super aquas, quod ad humorem mittit radices suas, et non timebit quum venerit æstus, id est fervor adversitatis et ignis tentationis; erit enim Deus fiducia ejus. De quo in Proverbiis asseritur: Turris fortissima nomen Domini; ad ipsum currit justus, et exaltabitur. Itaque, ad manendum in virore virtutum gratiarumque flore, indesinenter egemus pluvia spirituali ac humore cælesti, videlicet inundatione internæ motionis, directionis, tactusque Spiritus Sancti, cujus actuali motione egemus in omni meritorio actu, dicente Apostolo: Deus est qui operatur in vobis velle et perficere. Ad quem loquitur Isaias: Domine, dabis pacem nobis; omnia enim opera nostra operatus es in nobis.
paras.en: [[8:11|Can the rush be green without moisture?|Numquid vivere potest scirpus absque humore?]] [[8:11|or sedge bush grow without water?|aut carectum crescere sine aqua?]] Of these plants, and of what is signified by them, we spoke in the preceding article. With these words Christ too agrees in the Gospel, saying that the seed withered because it had no moisture[[Luke 8:6||]]. And Jeremias speaks of the virtuous man: [[Jer 17:8|he shall be as a tree that is planted by the waters, that spreadeth out its roots towards moisture: and it shall not fear when the heat cometh|Erit tanquam lignum quod transplantatur super aquas, quod ad humorem mittit radices suas, et non timebit quum venerit æstus]], that is, the fervour of adversity and the fire of temptation; for God will be his trust [compare Jer 17:7, "the Lord shall be his confidence"]. Of whom it is asserted in Proverbs: [[Prov 18:10|The name of the Lord is a strong tower: the just runneth to it, and shall be exalted|Turris fortissima nomen Domini; ad ipsum currit justus, et exaltabitur]]. And so, to remain in the greenness of the virtues and the flower of the graces [the print is damaged here; *flore* is the likeliest reading], we have unceasing need of the spiritual rain and the heavenly moisture, namely the flood of the inward moving, direction and touch of the Holy Spirit, whose actual moving we need in every meritorious act, as the Apostle says: [[Phil 2:13|it is God who worketh in you, both to will and to accomplish|Deus est qui operatur in vobis velle et perficere]]. To whom Isaias says: [[Is 26:12|Lord, thou wilt give us peace: for thou hast wrought all our works for us|Domine, dabis pacem nobis; omnia enim opera nostra operatus es in nobis]].

paras.t: Non ei placebit, puta injusto atque hypocritæ, vecordia sua. In veritate nihil insanius, nihilque stultius cogitari potest aut vilius, quam Deo non obedire ac subdi; quam Creatorem non diligere, filialiterque timere ac jugiter venerari; quam caduca et vana ista terrena atque carnalia Deo immensæ bonitatis præferre; quam pro humanis laudibus agere prompte, quod pro Dei laude et gloria tædet implere; quam diabolo assentire conversando inique; quam pro his temporalibus, brevibus, carnalibusque deliciis æternam perdere felicitatem: postremo, quam taliter vivere, qualiter mori esset damnabile: et tamen sic agunt omnes iniqui. Idcirco prorsus vecordes sunt: tanto utique stultiores, quanto his quæ suæ salutis sunt neglectis, circa sæcularia prudentius occupantur, et corporis opes, decorem et delectationes magis quam animæ quærunt. Sed veniet hora, in qua sero displicebit eis eorum vecordia, quando et dicent illud: Nos insensati vitam justorum æstimabamus insaniam, et finem sine honore. Ergo erravimus a via veritatis, et justitiæ lumen non luxit nobis, et sol intelligentiæ non est ortus nobis.
paras.en: [[8:14|His folly|vecordia sua]] [[8:14|shall not please him|Non ei placebit]], that is, the unjust man and the hypocrite. In truth nothing more senseless, nothing more foolish or more base can be thought of than not to obey God and be subject to Him; than not to love the Creator, and fear Him as a son, and continually revere Him; than to prefer these fleeting and vain earthly and carnal things to God of boundless goodness; than to do readily for human praise what one is loath to fulfil for the praise and glory of God; than to consent to the devil by living wickedly; than to lose eternal happiness for these temporal, brief and carnal delights: lastly, than to live in such a way as it would be damnable to die in: and yet so do all the wicked. Therefore they are utterly senseless; and so much the more foolish as, neglecting the things that belong to their salvation, they busy themselves the more shrewdly about worldly things, and seek the wealth, comeliness and pleasures of the body more than those of the soul. But the hour will come in which their folly will displease them too late, when they too will say that word: [[Wis 5:4|We fools esteemed their life madness, and their end without honour|Nos insensati vitam justorum æstimabamus insaniam, et finem sine honore]]. [[Wis 5:6|Therefore we have erred from the way of truth, and the light of justice hath not shined unto us, and the sun of understanding hath not risen upon us|Ergo erravimus a via veritatis, et justitiæ lumen non luxit nobis, et sol intelligentiæ non est ortus nobis]].

paras.t: Sicut tela aranearum fiducia ejus, id est injusti atque hypocritæ. Quod enim incertissimo fundamento innititur, facillime labitur. Qui ergo in terrenis vanitati subjectis spem figunt, ruent atque peribunt, nec in illis unquam veram quietem invenient. Propter quod Augustinus loquitur Deo: Creasti nos propter te, et inquietum est cor nostrum, donec perveniat ad te. Et Psalmista: Mihi, inquit, adhærere Deo bonum est, ponere in Domino Deo spem meam. Innitetur super domum suam, et non stabit. Sic multi in sua progenie, opulentia, mansione confidunt; sed in illis non sortientur salutem, imo per impiam spem pœnam merentur æternam.
paras.en: [[8:14|and his trust shall be like the spider's web|Sicut tela aranearum fiducia ejus]], that is, of the unjust man and the hypocrite. For what rests on a most uncertain foundation falls most easily. Those, then, who fix their hope on earthly things subject to vanity shall fall and perish, and shall never find true rest in them. Wherefore Augustine says to God: Thou hast made us for Thyself, and our heart is restless until it come to Thee. And the Psalmist says: [[Ps 72:28|it is good for me to adhere to my God, to put my hope in the Lord God|adhærere Deo bonum est, ponere in Domino Deo spem meam]]. [[8:15|He shall lean upon his house, and it shall not stand|Innitetur super domum suam, et non stabit]]. So many trust in their offspring, their wealth, their dwelling; but they shall not obtain salvation in them; nay, by their impious hope they merit eternal punishment.

paras.t: Super acervum petrarum radices ejus, id est hypocritæ per scirpum signati, densabuntur, et inter lapides commorabitur. Per petram seu lapidem homo frequenter exprimitur. Itaque hypocritæ et injusti radices, id est occultæ et intimæ cogitationes seu affectiones, ex quibus prodeunt opera, quemadmodum ex radice virgulta, densabuntur super acervum petrarum, id est, abundanter fundantur super hominum favorem ac laudem seu dona: quia ad hæc illorum intentio fertur, et inter hæc commorantur, non Creatori, sed creaturæ placere quærentes; non Deo, sed hominibus cor suum principaliter infigentes: quod est cæcitas detestanda. Nempe, quo Deus benedictus omnibus melior digniorque consistit, eo plus in omnibus mentem dirigere, affectum firmare, finemque in ipso locare debemus, alia vana et frivola intuitu Dei in infinitum spernentes.
paras.en: [[8:17|upon a heap of stones|Super acervum petrarum]] [[8:17|His roots|radices ejus]], that is, of the hypocrite signified by the rush, [[8:17|shall be thick|densabuntur]], [[8:17|and among the stones he shall abide|et inter lapides commorabitur]]. By a rock or stone a man is often expressed. And so the roots of the hypocrite and the unjust man, that is, his hidden and inmost thoughts or affections, from which his works come forth as shoots from a root, shall be thick upon a heap of stones, that is, are abundantly founded upon the favour and praise or gifts of men: for their intention is borne towards these things, and among these they abide, seeking to please not the Creator but the creature, fixing their heart chiefly not on God but on men; which is a blindness to be abhorred. For truly, as much as God, the Blessed One, is better and worthier than all things, so much the more ought we in all things to direct our mind to Him, to fix our affection on Him and to place our end in Him, despising infinitely all other things as vain and frivolous in regard of God.

paras.t: Hæc est enim lætitia viæ, id est conversationis ejus, puta hypocritæ seu injusti, ut rursum de terra alii germinentur, id est, ut eo per mortem sublato, alii sibi similes ei succedant. Carnales enim et sæculares præsentia maxime diligentes, cognatos et caros cupiunt in hoc sæculo promovere, ditare, et superstites sibi in mundana prosperitate relinquere; idque solatiosum est eis, quod suos tales relinquunt, quasi arbitrantes se in suis manere.
paras.en: [[8:19|For this is the joy of his way|Hæc est enim lætitia viæ]], that is, of the conduct of the hypocrite or the unjust man, [[8:19|that others may spring again out of the earth|ut rursum de terra alii germinentur]], that is, that when he has been taken away by death, others like him may succeed him. For carnal and worldly men, who love present things above all, desire to advance and enrich their kinsmen and dear ones in this world, and to leave them surviving them in worldly prosperity; and it is a comfort to them that they leave such men of their own behind, as though they thought that they themselves remained in their own.

paras.t: Deus non projiciet simplicem, nec porriget manum malignis. Hoc in die judicii tam particularis quam universalis præsertim implebitur. In die enim generalis judicii omne malum pœnæ et culpæ aufertur electis, omnisque consolatio tollitur reprobis, nec quidquam divini consequuntur auxilii, nisi quod citra condignum torquentur. Interim vero in sæculo isto dona naturæ et bona fortunæ, aliaque diversa beneficia gratiæ gratis datæ, dantur a Deo communiter simplicibus et malignis. Deus namque in sua bonitate immensa iniquos conservat in esse, et pluit super bonos ac malos, solem faciens oriri super justos atque injustos: imo interdum malignis et pessimis de præfatis bonis plura divinitus conferuntur, quam electis et virtuosis, dum illos Deus prosperari permittit, istos autem instanter castigat. Præterea, quoniam Deus in vita præsenti flagellare et purgare solet electos per reprobos, ut electi purgati salventur, reprobi autem flagellantes juste damnentur; ideo Deus frequenter porrexit malignis manum, id est auxilium et triumphum adversus electos, ut patet in libris Judicum, Regum et Machabæorum. Sed quantum ad consecutionem felicitatis æternæ, non porrigit manum malignis ac reprobis, quos relinquit, quanquam variis modis eos quantum in se est, ad emendationem moveat et hortetur, per inspirationem secretam, per angelorum custodiam, per devotorum prædicationem, per miracula et Scripturas, per impressionem synderesis, ac per naturalis judicium rationis. Sed et malignis qui prædestinati sunt, porrigit manum tempore æternaliter præordinato, ita quod in caritate et gratia moriuntur. Sed et malis reprobis, interdum ex miseratione divina confertur gratia veræ contritionis; sed finaliter in ea non permanent. Unde malignis reprobis non præstatur finale auxilium consequendi salutem.
paras.en: [[8:20|God will not cast away the simple, nor reach out his hand to the evil doer|Deus non projiciet simplicem, nec porriget manum malignis]]. This will be fulfilled above all on the day of judgment, the particular as well as the universal. For on the day of the general judgment every evil of punishment and of guilt is taken away from the elect, and every consolation is taken from the reprobate, nor do they receive any divine help, except that they are tormented short of their desert. Meanwhile, in this world, the gifts of nature and the goods of fortune, and various other benefits of grace freely given [*gratia gratis data*: graces given for the good of others, such as prophecy, not for the holiness of the one who receives them], are given by God to the simple and the evil alike. For God in His boundless goodness keeps the wicked in being, and rains upon the good and the bad, making His sun to rise upon the just and the unjust[[Matt 5:45||]]: nay, sometimes more of the said goods are bestowed by God on the evil and the very wicked than on the elect and the virtuous, while God lets the former prosper and chastises the latter without respite. Moreover, since in the present life God is wont to scourge and purge the elect by means of the reprobate, so that the elect, being purged, may be saved, and the reprobate who scourge them may be justly damned, God has often reached out His hand to the evil, that is, given them help and triumph against the elect, as is plain in the books of Judges, Kings and Machabees. But as regards the attaining of eternal happiness, He does not reach out His hand to the evil and the reprobate, whom He leaves, although, so far as in Him lies, He moves and exhorts them in various ways to amendment: by secret inspiration, by the guardianship of the angels, by the preaching of devout men, by miracles and the Scriptures, by the prompting of synderesis [that is, the conscience's inborn grasp of the first principles of right action], and by the natural judgment of reason. And to the evil who are predestined He reaches out His hand at the time eternally foreordained, so that they die in charity and grace. To the evil reprobate, too, the grace of true contrition is sometimes given out of the divine mercy; but they do not persevere in it to the end. Hence the final help to attain salvation is not given to the evil reprobate.

paras.t: Donec impleatur risu os tuum, et labia tua jubilo. Quod item in judicio plene complebitur in unoquoque electo jam afflicto, per sanctum Job designato, qui tunc pereuntibus reprobis in mente et corpore, omni gaudio perfundetur, quemadmodum ait Salvator: Beati qui nunc fletis, quia ridebitis. Et iterum: Beati qui lugent, quoniam ipsi consolabuntur. Hinc per Malachiam Dominus ait electis: Egrediemini, et salietis quasi vituli de armento, et calcabitis impios. Hic est risus ex spirituali lætitia nascens, de quo in Proverbiis legitur: Ridebit in die novissimo. Est autem risus dissolutionis atque lasciviæ, de quo asserit Christus: Væ vobis qui ridetis, quia plorabitis et flebitis. De quo scriptum est in Jacobo: Risus vester in luctum convertatur, et gaudium in mœrorem. Porro, quod ait, Donec impleatur, etc., non est intelligendum, quod ore Sanctorum risu impleto, Deus postea porrigit manum malignis. Unde per Donec, excluditur tempus usque ad illud, non autem duratio sequens, sicut in Psalmo: Sede a dextris meis, donec ponam inimicos tuos, etc. Itemque: Deus, ne derelinquas me, donec annuntiem brachium tuum.
paras.en: [[8:21|Until thy mouth be filled with laughter, and thy lips with rejoicing|Donec impleatur risu os tuum, et labia tua jubilo]]. This too will be fully accomplished at the judgment in every one of the elect who is now afflicted, signified by holy Job, who then, while the reprobate perish, will be filled with every joy in mind and body; as the Saviour says: [[Luke 6:21|Blessed are ye that weep now: for you shall laugh|Beati qui nunc fletis, quia ridebitis]]. And again: [[Matt 5:5|Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted|Beati qui lugent, quoniam ipsi consolabuntur]]. Hence the Lord says to the elect by Malachias: [[Mal 4:2|you shall go forth, and shall leap like calves of the herd|Egrediemini, et salietis quasi vituli de armento]], [[Mal 4:3|And you shall tread down the wicked|et calcabitis impios]]. This is the laughter that springs from spiritual gladness, of which we read in Proverbs: [[Prov 31:25|she shall laugh in the latter day|Ridebit in die novissimo]]. But there is a laughter of dissoluteness and wantonness, of which Christ asserts: [[Luke 6:25|Woe to you that now laugh: for you shall mourn and weep|Væ vobis qui ridetis, quia plorabitis et flebitis]]. Of which it is written in James: [[Jas 4:9|let your laughter be turned into mourning and your joy into sorrow|Risus vester in luctum convertatur, et gaudium in mœrorem]]. Further, where he says, Until thy mouth be filled, etc., it is not to be understood that, once the mouth of the Saints has been filled with laughter, God afterwards reaches out His hand to the evil. For by *until* the time up to then is excluded, but not the duration that follows; as in the Psalm: [[Ps 109:1|Sit thou at my right hand: Until I make thy enemies|Sede a dextris meis, donec ponam inimicos tuos]], etc. And again: [[Ps 70:18|O God, forsake me not, Until I shew forth thy arm|Deus, ne derelinquas me, donec annuntiem brachium tuum]].

paras.t: Postremo, etiam sæpe in vita præsenti post gravem tentationem seu quamlibet diram tribulationem, electi quadam ineffabili consolatione ex occulta Sancti Spiritus visitatione piissima recreantur, magis plane quam verbis queant exprimere. Propter quod Paulus fatetur Corinthiis: Sicut abundant passiones Christi in nobis, ita per Christum abundat consolatio nostra. Et Psalmista devotissime loquitur Deo: Quam magna multitudo dulcedinis tuæ, Domine, quam abscondisti timentibus te! Et rursus: Secundum multitudinem dolorum meorum in corde meo, consolationes tuæ lætificaverunt animam meam. Dicit autem Gregorius: In æterna patria quum justorum mens in exsultatione rapitur, lingua in laudis canticum elevatur: qui quoniam tantum vident, quantum exprimere nequeunt, in risu jubilant. Ex quo sentire videtur Gregorius, quod in patria erit laus vocalis.
paras.en: Lastly, even in the present life, often after grievous temptation or any dire tribulation whatever, the elect are refreshed by a certain unspeakable consolation through the most loving hidden visitation of the Holy Spirit, plainly more than they could express in words. Wherefore Paul confesses to the Corinthians: [[2 Cor 1:5|as the sufferings of Christ abound in us: so also by Christ doth our comfort abound|Sicut abundant passiones Christi in nobis, ita per Christum abundat consolatio nostra]]. And the Psalmist says most devoutly to God: [[Ps 30:20|O how great is the multitude of thy sweetness, O Lord, which thou hast hidden for them that fear thee!|Quam magna multitudo dulcedinis tuæ, Domine, quam abscondisti timentibus te!]] And again: [[Ps 93:19|According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, thy comforts have given joy to my soul|Secundum multitudinem dolorum meorum in corde meo, consolationes tuæ lætificaverunt animam meam]]. And Gregory says: In the eternal fatherland, when the mind of the just is caught up in exultation, the tongue is raised to a song of praise; and since they see more than they can express, they rejoice in laughter. From which Gregory seems to hold that in the fatherland there will be vocal praise.

paras.t: Et tabernaculum, id est ædificatio terrenæ prosperitatis, impiorum non subsistet. Dum enim molem divitiarum, turrim honoris, consistorium deliciarum, contra paupertatem, tristitiam et depressionem vitæ præsentis sibi construere moliuntur, simul cum suis vanitatibus ruunt atque damnantur, juxta id Psalmi: Dejecisti eos dum elevarentur. Quomodo facti sunt in desolationem? Subito defecerunt; perierunt propter iniquitatem suam. Quod si interdum diu videantur florere, hæc tamen diuturnitas respectu durationis vitæ sequentis, minor et brevior est, quam ictus oculi ad innumerabilia et inexplicabilia millia annorum. Non ergo vitam hanc alicujus reputemus momenti, sed ad æternitatis considerationem mens nostra semper feratur.
paras.en: [[8:22|and the dwelling|Et tabernaculum]], that is, the building of earthly prosperity, [[8:22|of the wicked shall not stand|impiorum non subsistet]]. For while they labour to build for themselves a mass of riches, a tower of honour, a hall of delights, against the poverty, sadness and lowliness of the present life, they fall together with their vanities and are damned; according to that word of the Psalm: [[Ps 72:18|when they were lifted up thou hast cast them down|Dejecisti eos dum elevarentur]]. [[Ps 72:19|How are they brought to desolation? they have suddenly ceased to be: they have perished by reason of their iniquity|Quomodo facti sunt in desolationem? Subito defecerunt; perierunt propter iniquitatem suam]]. And if sometimes they seem to flourish for a long while, yet this length of time, in respect of the duration of the life to come, is less and shorter than the twinkling of an eye compared with countless and unutterable thousands of years. Let us not, then, reckon this life of any moment, but let our mind be borne always to the consideration of eternity.
